## 93. The sleepover: an invitation that can come from either side, and the impact columns the port had been inventing

The four files section 92 left behind are the family's last ninety-three rows, and the only
part of it that is a choice card: an invitation with four ways to spend the night, the night's
own log line written from either side of it, the four activities that can fill it, and the
twenty-eight excuses a refusal arrives in. They join the school year instead of getting a
function of their own, because the year already carries the gate (age 6..18), the rate, the
pronoun save and restore, the ledger and the tail that appends the full stop - and because
rendering the card through the shared choice-card path is what turned up the bug in 93.3.

### 93.1 The family

| file | rows | columns that matter |
|---|---|---|
| `a16_backtoschool-sleepover-invitation-dumb-enc` | 25 | Hero Min/Max Age, Hero Invites, NPC Invites, Crazy, Randomize Choices, Gender Bracket, Title, Scenario, CTA, Choice 1..4 with a Narrative and five impacts each |
| `a16_backtoschool-sleepover-acceptance-feedback-string-enc` | 36 | Invited To A Sleepover Version, Push Scenario Version, Sleepover Activity, Hero Min/Max Age, Hero Enjoyment, NPC Enjoyment, Commonness Score |
| `a16_backtoschool-sleepover-activitie-enc` | 4 | Activity, Sleepover Invite Friend String, Sleepover Age-Up String |
| `a16_backtoschool-sleepover-invitation-rejection-color-enc` | 28 | String - Hero, String - NPC, Believability Score, Commonness Score, Hero Minimum/Maximum Age |

The invitation's age window is eleven overlapping spellings of 7..17, with `(7,17)` and
`(10,17)` on seven rows each. Twenty-three of the twenty-five rows let the hero do the
asking and twenty-three let the friend, and twenty-one allow both, so a coin decides the
direction on almost every row; only two rows are friend-only. `Gender Bracket` is the literal
`<sleepover-companion>` on all twenty-five rows - the table is written for whichever friend it
is about - `Crazy` is set on six rows and `Randomize Choices` on seventeen, and neither is
read (93.4). The CTA is `What will you do?`, with a trailing space on nineteen of the
twenty-five rows, which the card carries and the log does not.

The twenty-five titles are five strings, fourteen of which keep the trailing space the column
carries: `Slumbering Scares ` (7), `Sleepover Shenanigans` (6), `Nighttime Nonsense` (5),
`Midnight Mayhem ` (4), `Bedtime Beauty ` (3). The year's own tail trims it (93.4). The
cards' own cells name the friend 113 times as `<sleepover-companion>` and twelve times in the
possessive, alongside the family's usual machinery: `<rb>` twelve, `<car-type>` five,
`<rb2>` four, `<random-first-name>` three and one `<num7-15>`. Every one of those resolves
through a table the port already had except the two companion spellings, which are the two new
cases in 93.2.

### 93.2 The invitation, the answer, and the night

The row says who asks. `Hero Invites` and `NPC Invites` are both set on twenty-one rows, so
the port coins the direction there and lets a single-sided row decide itself; the direction is
then what picks the column the port reads for the refusal (`String - NPC` when the hero did the
asking, `String - Hero` when the friend did) and which half of the acceptance table it uses.

The companion is the classmate the port already keeps for the dance and the house party
(92.5 item 5) - the corpus's own friend list does not exist here, so a classmate of the right
gender stands in. The year draws that classmate before the card resolves, which is why the two
resolver cases only read it back:

~~~
} else if (token == "sleepover-companion-possessive") {
  // The same classmate, in the possessive: ten of the invitation's own
  // narratives say "<sleepover-companion-possessive> mother" (REPORT.en.md 93).
  const std::string v = hero_ == nullptr ? std::string() : hero_->schoolClassmate;
  if (v.empty()) out += text.substr(i, close - i + 1);
  else out += v + "'s";
} else if (token == "sleepover-companion") {
  // The sleepover tables name the friend they are about, and the port knows
  // one classmate - the same one the dance and the house party use. The year
  // draws it before the card resolves, so this case only reads it back.
  const std::string v = hero_ == nullptr ? std::string() : hero_->schoolClassmate;
  if (v.empty()) out += text.substr(i, close - i + 1);
  else out += v;
}
~~~

The activity comes first, out of the four-row table, because the acceptance rows point back at
it through their own `Sleepover Activity` column - `play video games` on eight, `watch a
movie` on six, `bake together` and `camp in the backyard` on four each, and blank on
fourteen, which is a row that fits any activity.

The answer itself is the port's coin. The rejection table ships a `Believability Score` (two
on seven rows, three and four on six each, five on five, one on four) and a
`Commonness Score`, and nothing that says how often a friend says yes, so the port asks with a
0.25 coin when the hero did the inviting and 0.35 when the friend did. A refusal marks the
rejection row, titles the card `A sleepover invitation`, upper-cases the direction's own
string and takes two happiness. An acceptance marks the invitation row, keeps the classmate's
gender for the pronouns, then picks the log line out of the acceptance table - filtered to the
row's age window and to its activity, and weighted by `Commonness Score` (three on twelve
rows) - and adds its `Hero Enjoyment` (four on twelve rows, three on seven, one and five on
six each, two on five) on top of the points the night's own choice carries. The activity's own
two strings follow, the host's side of it only when the hero did the asking, and then the
port's own sentence and the ledger line.

Last comes the night itself: `renderRow(inv, ir, life, out, forcedChoice)` renders the
invitation row's four choices with their own narratives and impacts, and the year copies the
title and body back out of it so the tail cannot clobber them with something else. The branch
table of the whole year is now:

| branch | weight | available when |
|---|---|---|
| field trip | 8 | age 6..18, the family's own gate |
| school dance | 8 | the same |
| prom | 12 | once a life, and the life is at least 15 |
| house party | 6 | age 6..18 |
| sleepover | 7 | age 7..17 and all four tables load |

### 93.3 The impact columns the port had been inventing

`renderRow` reads five impact columns per choice, and it used to read all five
unconditionally. An absent column is not a score of zero in this engine: `Table::num` returns
0 for a column the table does not have, and `pointsForImpact(0)` is not a no-op either - the
game maps a score of 0 to a coin that pays -1 or +1. So every choice card whose table spelled
its impacts differently from the engine's canonical five was silently moving two attributes.
Fifty-eight tables in the corpus carry a `Choice 1` column; the engine's own spellings are
`Karma Impact` (68 tables), `Happiness Impact` (48), `Discipline Impact` (44),
`Intelligence Impact` (28) and `Appearance Impact` (28), while the scenario family the
dumb-scenario and school families belong to writes `Smarts Impact` (20 tables) and
`Looks Impact` (8) instead. Both were being read as absent, and both paid the coin.

The first probe run of this section is the proof: 41 smarts changes (16 draws of +1 and 25 of
-1), 40 looks and 23 karma across 110 cards, none of which any of the four tables asked for.
The fix reads each column only if the table has it, and lets Intelligence and Appearance also
answer to the scenario family's spelling:

~~~
// An absent column is not a score of 0: the table maps a score of 0 to a
// drawn -1 or +1, so reading a column the row does not carry moved smarts
// and looks on every card that spells its own impacts differently
// (REPORT.en.md 93). Only a column the row really has is applied, and
// Intelligence/Appearance also answer to the scenario family's own
// Smarts/Looks spelling (20 and 8 choice tables use it).
struct ChoiceImpact {
  const char* engine;
  const char* scenario;
  int AgeUp::*field;
};
const ChoiceImpact imps[5] = {
    {"Karma Impact", nullptr, &AgeUp::karma},
    {"Discipline Impact", nullptr, &AgeUp::discipline},
    {"Happiness Impact", nullptr, &AgeUp::happiness},
    {"Intelligence Impact", "Smarts Impact", &AgeUp::smarts},
    {"Appearance Impact", "Looks Impact", &AgeUp::looks},
};
for (const ChoiceImpact& im : imps) {
  const std::string col = std::string(im.engine) + suffix;
  if (t.has(col)) { out.*(im.field) = pointsForImpact(int(t.num(row, col))); continue; }
  if (im.scenario == nullptr) continue;
  const std::string alt = std::string(im.scenario) + suffix;
  if (t.has(alt)) out.*(im.field) = pointsForImpact(int(t.num(row, alt)));
}
~~~

The distinction that matters for reading the numbers afterwards: a blank cell inside a column
the table really has is a score of 0, and a score of 0 really does draw -1 or +1. The
invitation's own cells are mostly like that - of the hundred Smarts cells 66 are blank, of the
hundred Looks cells 89 are blank, of the hundred Karma cells 69 - so a card can honestly move
smarts by 1 on a row that never mentions smarts. What it must not do is move it on a table that
has no Smarts column at all, which is what the port was doing.

`Relationship Impact` is the busiest column in the invitation table (86 of its 100 cells are
non-blank: +1 on 35, -1 on 28, -2 on 12, +2 on 11) and it is not applied, because it is the
friend's relationship and the port keeps no friend relationship - the same shortcut the dance
and the party already document. `Friend Impact`, which the dumb-scenario friend set uses, is
unapplied for the same reason.

### 93.4 Shortcuts

1. The 0.30 school-year rate and the sleepover's weight of 7 against the year's other four
   (8, 8, 12, 6) are the port's own, and the 7 exists only to keep one card a year spread over
   five branches.
2. The refusal coin (0.25 when the hero asks, 0.35 when the friend does) is the port's own. The
   corpus ships a `Believability Score` and no decider.
3. `Crazy` (6 rows) and `Randomize Choices` (17 rows) are unread. The port's `renderRow`
   always draws the branch from the seed, which is the effect `Randomize Choices` asks for, and
   `Crazy` has no column in the port's card model to land on.
4. The classmate stands in for the corpus's friend list, as in 92.5 item 5. Its gender is the
   port's own 50/50 and is not read off the name, so a female name can carry a male pronoun in
   the corpus's own sentence.
5. `<car-type>`, `<random-first-name>` and `<num7-15>` resolve through tables the port
   already had; `<rb>`, `<rb2>` and the inline slash lists go through the scenario token
   machinery `renderRow` already runs.
6. The card's title has its trailing space trimmed by the year's tail, which trimmed only the
   body before this section. The trim stays in that tail and not in `renderRow`, because
   `renderRow` also renders the rows the benchmark pushes out of the captured trace, and a
   title the game itself kept is not the port's to change.
7. `Relationship Impact` and `Friend Impact` are unmapped (93.3). One card a year.

### 93.5 Verification

The probe is `/tmp/qdir/slpres.py`: 240 lives (relationships on and off x sixty seeds x both
genders, to age 30, in the United States, with the school flag set), selecting every event whose
table starts with `a16_backtoschool-sleepover` and checking each card against the candidate
rows of its own table - the refusal's direction and column, the acceptance's activity and age
window, the choice against the row's own four cells, the narrative against the matching
`Narrative N`, the deltas against that branch's impacts plus the acceptance row's enjoyment,
the ledger counter's monotonicity and a sweep for leftover brackets:

~~~

kinds {'accepted': 70, 'refused': 40, 'refused-pal': 16, 'refused-hero': 24}
tables {'a16_backtoschool-sleepover-invitation-dumb-enc': 70, 'a16_backtoschool-sleepover-invitation-rejection-color-enc': 40}
choice index {1: 20, 2: 16, 3: 16, 4: 18}
activities {'watch a movie': 28, 'camp in the backyard': 18, 'bake together': 20, 'play video games': 4}
ledger lines 70 bad 0
happiness {6: 8, -2: 40, 7: 8, 0: 4, -5: 8, -7: 4, 10: 4, 5: 8, 1: 4, 2: 4, 3: 4, -4: 4, 9: 4, 4: 6}
smarts {1: 28, -1: 32, 8: 8, 4: 2} looks {-1: 40, 4: 4, 1: 22, -4: 4} karma {-4: 16, 1: 14, -1: 16, -8: 8, 8: 4, 4: 12}
mismatches {}
acceptance line seen {'y': 70}
RESIDUE 0 []
~~~

The proportions are what the tables say. The forty refusals split sixteen to twenty-four by who
did the asking and every one of them costs exactly the two happiness the port charges; the
seventy acceptances touch all four choices of the night (20, 16, 16, 18) and the same four
activities the table has, with `play video games` rarest because it is the one the acceptance
table only fits on eight of its rows. The happiness values are `points(2) = 8` and
`points(-2) = -8` plus an enjoyment of 1..5, the -5 and -7 being the low enjoyment of a
negative branch, and every smarts and looks value is a score-0 coin, which is the corpus's own
blank cell doing what the game does with it. The ledger line is monotonic on all seventy cards
and no card carries a bracket.

## 94. The celebrity dating app: a roster nothing pointed at, six tables of career, and a
picker the port collapsed

Every family the port has wired so far was found the same way: a table pointed at it. The
`a16_celeb` family is the first one that nothing points at - a grep for its seven file names
across `gamedata_plain/` returns the files themselves and no row anywhere - so its consumer
had to be read out of the code, and the code turns out to be two features: a celebrity dating
app the Love menu opens (94.3) and the guest the royal interaction summons (94.4). Both draw
from the same roster, and the app is the only one of the two that needed new tables loaded.

### 94.1 The family

| file | rows | columns that matter |
|---|---|---|
| `a16_celebrities-enc` | 453 | Celebrity, Gender |
| `a16_celeb-dating-app-names-enc` | 405 | First Name, Last Name, First Name Gender, Celebrity Category, Skin, Country, Commonness Score |
| `a16_celeb-dating-app-actor-enc` | 20 (14 with content) | Genre, Minimum/Maximum Salary, Fame Score, Retirement Age, Commonness Score, Country Whitelist |
| `a16_celeb-dating-app-musician-enc` | 11 | Genre, the same five numbers, Country Whitelist |
| `a16_celeb-dating-app-athlete-enc` | 7 | Sport, Gender, the same five numbers, Country Whitelist |
| `a16_celeb-dating-app-influencer-enc` | 7 | Platform, the same five numbers, no whitelist |
| `a16_celeb-dating-app-ceo-enc` | 1 | Minimum/Maximum Salary, Fame Score, Retirement Age - no Commonness, no whitelist |

Nine hundred and four physical rows, eight hundred and ninety-eight of them with content. The
roster itself is flat - a name and a gender, 264 male and 189 female - and it is the one table
of the family a `renderRow` card could never use, because it carries no sentence at all.

The names table is the picker's pool. Six categories: athlete 92, musician 82, actor 73,
influencer 54, ceo 52 and model 52. Two hundred and five male rows and two hundred female, six
skin tones (102, 110, 72, 63, 47, 11) and a commonness of 2 to 5 with two hundred and five rows
on 3. Its country column is blank on 343 rows and then `kr` (22), `au, gb` (20), `in` (19)
and `in, us` (1). Thirty-three of the rows are not names at all but templates -
`<random-first-name-male>` on 25, `<random-first-name-female>` on 8, and all 33 with
`<random-surname>` (94.5 item 5).

The career tables are one row per job: actor has fourteen genres of its twenty rows (six blank)
with salaries from 500K to 80M, a fame score of 1..5, a retirement age of 55..80 and a
commonness of 1..5; musician eleven genres, athlete seven sports - the Gender column blank on
basketball and soccer, `female` on volleyball, `male` on the other four - influencer seven
platforms, and a single CEO row (550K..1.5M, fame 3, retirement 65). Three rows are gated by
country: `Bollywood` to `in`, `K-pop` to `kr` and `rugby` to `au, gb`, whose cell is
the family's only quoted one and which the loader reads as a single value, comma and all.

### 94.2 The consumer

`il2cpp_dump.txt` names the family on one class - the game-data holder the dumb-scenario and
zoo sets live on - as six lists in a row (`_celebDatingAppActorSet`, `...MusicianSet`,
`...CeoSet`, `...InfluencerSet`, `...AthleteSet`, `...CelebrityNamesSet`) plus
`_celebritySet` for the roster, and it names the tables' readers as
`DataHub.LoadCelebDatingAppActorSet` and its four siblings, `GetRandomCEOCelebData`,
`GetRandomActorCelebData` and the rest.

The feature is a `Scenario` with a picker: `ScenarioCelebrityDatingApp` carries a cost,
three cached selected indices (age, desired gender, celebrity type) and the methods
`GetAgeRangeArray`, `GetDesiredGenderArray`, `GetDesiredCelebrityTypeArray` and
`GetLoverCandidateWithMinAgeAndMaxAgeAndGenderAndCelebrityType`; its answer opens
`ScenarioCelebrityDatingAppResult` with the lover it built. The important absence is
`ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush`: the app is opened from the Love menu, it is never pushed.
That is why the port had to own the trigger (94.5 item 1).

The lover it builds is `Game.SimCelebrityLover`, which adds to an ordinary `SimLover` a fame
type, a genre, a fame score, a company, a platform, a sport, a team, a retirement age, a
minimum and maximum salary and a career model level - exactly the columns the career tables
carry. The app's own strings are in the metadata: `Celebrity Dating App` (#15327),
`Date the celebrity of your dreams` (#17200), the three pickers (#33859..#33861),
`The celebrity dating app has paired you with {0} named {1}.` (#41823), its first-person
twin (#41824), `The celebrity dating app was unable to pair you with anyone of your desired
specifications.` (#41825) and `I used the celebrity dating app.` (#25558).

### 94.3 The app

The app is a rule inside `relationshipYear`, not a year of its own: it belongs to the branch
that runs when the hero has no lover, and it bails on a forced choice so it can never take a
year a pushed card already owns. Its six kinds are a table in the port, not a table in the
corpus:

~~~
static const CelebKind kinds[6] = {
    {"actor", "a16_celeb-dating-app-actor-enc", "Genre", "actor", "Actor"},
    {"musician", "a16_celeb-dating-app-musician-enc", "Genre", "musician", "Musician"},
    {"athlete", "a16_celeb-dating-app-athlete-enc", "Sport", "athlete", "Athlete"},
    {"influencer", "a16_celeb-dating-app-influencer-enc", "Platform", "influencer", "Influencer"},
    {"ceo", "a16_celeb-dating-app-ceo-enc", "", "", "CEO"},
    {"model", "a16_model-career-progression-enc", "Model Type", "", "Model"}};
~~~

The sixth row is the exception that the corpus forces: the names table has a `model` category
on 52 rows and there is no `a16_celeb-dating-app-model-enc` to go with it, so the model
borrows the port's own model ladder - the same table section 78 wired - and reads its trade off
`Model Type` and its fame off `Can Be Famous`. The CEO is the other way round: a table with
one row and no commonness column, so its draw is uniform and its occupation string is the
display alone.

The country whitelist is read by one lambda. The hero's own country code comes out of
`a16_countries-enc.json` (the file the port already loads for `<country>` and the mafia),
and a row passes when its whitelist cell is blank or when the hero's code is one of the codes
in it; a table with no such column - influencer, CEO - admits every row, and a hero whose
country has no code admits everything too:

~~~
auto knownHere = [&](const Table& t, size_t row, const char* column) {
  if (ccode.empty() || !t.has(column)) return true;
  const std::string list = lower(trim(t.at(row, column)));
  if (list.empty()) return true;
  ...          // comma separated, trimmed, lower cased, one code at a time
};
~~~

The app fills three pools: the kinds whose career table survives the country and gender tests,
the career rows of the drawn kind, and the name rows of that category and the wanted gender.
The card is then built in code - it has no table of its own - with the game's own title,
tagline and picker line, the drawn category as the choice, and two log lines: the pairing
sentence with the occupation the career row names, and the ledger line `That was celebrity
date number N.` behind it. The narrative is the game's first-person line. The lover it hands
back carries the name, the wanted gender, an age three years either side of the hero's own, a
status of dating, a relationship of 60, a drawn craziness and pride, and the career record -
fame type, genre, skin, fame score, retirement age and salary. It moves no attribute at all,
which is what the probe checks on every card (94.6).

### 94.4 The royal guest, and a correction to 87

The roster's other consumer was already in the port and was inventing its guest. The royal
interaction (kind 7 of `royalYear`, REPORT.en.md 87) drew a first name and a surname out of
the port's own pools and a coin for the gender, with a 453-row roster of real names and their
genders sitting unread:

~~~
if (ensureTable("a16_celebrities-enc")) {
  const Table& roster = tbl("a16_celebrities-enc");
  const size_t a = royalRng_.below(uint32_t(roster.size()));
  cel = roster.at(a, "Celebrity");
  celFemale = lower(roster.at(a, "Gender")) == "female";
  cel2 = roster.at(royalRng_.below(uint32_t(roster.size())), "Celebrity");
}
~~~

The invented draw survives as the fallback for a missing table, the way every other table in
the port degrades. The probe now counts the guest against the roster: 219 celebrity cards, 219
of them naming one of the 453 names, 94 distinct names, and 75 cards whose own sentence uses a
female pronoun against 88 that use a male one (94.6).

### 94.5 Shortcuts

1. The trigger and the price are the port's. The game opens the app from the Love menu and
   charges a code-side cost; the port offers it on a 0.06 coin to a hero of 18 or more with no
   lover, and charges nothing.
2. The game's three pickers - age range, desired gender, celebrity type - collapse to one. The
   port keeps the type picker (the card's choice), pins the gender to its own pairing
   convention (the opposite of the hero's) and gives the candidate the hero's own age plus or
   minus three, because the corpus's career rows carry a retirement age and no birth year.
3. The fame score is a record and not an effect. The port's only consumer of `h.fame` is the
   cult's threshold (REPORT.en.md 63), and a randomly offered card must not move it.
4. `The celebrity dating app was unable to pair you with anyone of your desired
   specifications.` is kept as the game's own guard, not as a reachable branch: 104 cards
   across four countries never once met it, because every category has both genders in the
   names table and every gated career row has blank siblings. It stays for the case a table
   ships without them.
5. Thirty-three name rows are templates rather than names. They are filled from the port's own
   first-name and surname pools at draw time, which is what the game itself would do with them.
6. The model category borrows the port's model ladder (94.3). A seller of `a16_model-career
   -progression-enc` would not change the app; a `a16_celeb-dating-app-model-enc` would.
7. The app's own store text (`#45183`) and the IAP that opens it are not modelled - the port
   has no paywall for a card it draws itself.
8. The country whitelist is honoured as a positive list. A blank cell means anywhere, and a
   hero in a country the port cannot code is admitted everywhere.

### 94.6 Verification

The probe is `/tmp/qdir/celres.py`: 640 app lives (four countries x relationships on and off
x forty seeds x both genders, to age 60) and 60 royal lives, checking each app card's title,
tagline and fixed deltas, that it never fires before 18, that its choice is one of the six
displays, that the occupation in its pairing line is a real cell of that category's table (and
that the CEO and the model are spelled as their own rows are), that the drawn name sits in the
names table under the right category, gender and country whitelist, that the career row passes
the same whitelist, the ledger line's monotonicity, a sweep for leftover brackets, and - on
every royal card - that the body names a member of the 453-row roster:

The six kinds all arrive (24 model, 24 actor, 24 CEO, 16 influencer, 8 musician, 8 athlete) and
every one of the 104 cards pairs: the failure literal never fires. The occupations are the
tables' own - a platform for the influencer, a genre for the actor and the musician, a sport

uniform draw, which is why `CEO` and the three model tiers are as frequent as they are. The
gated rows are rare and real: `Bollywood` appeared after 486 lives in India, `K-pop` after

## 95. The region under the city: a place table with no renderer, a birth city the port never
drew, and an office pool that ate its own stack

The last three sections each wired a family whose consumer was easy to name: the school year
read the field-trip tables, the relationship year read the sleepover ones, the celebrity app
read its seven. This family is read by the game's own place dictionary, and the port had
nothing in the dictionary to answer with. The gap turned out to be three separate holes: a
token with no value, a value with no draw, and a fill that re-entered itself until the stack
ran out.

### 95.1 The family

`a16_city-regions-enc` is 246 rows of `Country Code,City,Region` (247 physical lines, the
extra one a whitespace padding row). Thirty country codes appear - `us` 57, `gb` 28, `es` 15,
`it` 13, `br` 12, `de` 12, `au` 11, `ca` 10, `mx` 10, `fr` 9, `in` 8,
`jp` 8, `ch` 7, then `py`/`se`/`sv` 4, `ad`/`ao`/`ar`/`gt`/`ht`/`ie`/
`ni`/`tn`/`ug` 3, `bz`/`pg` 2 and `aw`/`gy`/`ws` one each - and the 246 rows
name 246 distinct (country, city) rows and 196 distinct region names.

The country rows themselves are the other half of the place dictionary: every one of the 102
countries in `gamedata_json/a16_countries-enc.json` carries its own `Cities` array, 418
cities in total, and the region table knows 243 of them (in 30 countries). The remaining 72
countries have no region code at all, so a hero born in one of them answers with the country
itself - which is exactly what the office pool does at the national level.

The consumer is code-side, and the dump names all three parts of it: `class DataCityRegion`
(il2cpp_dump.txt:7529) with `<CountryCode>`, `<City>` and `<Region>` backing fields, the
game-data holder's `field 0x6d0 System.Collections.ArrayList _cityRegionSet`
(il2cpp_dump.txt:17420) sitting between `_politicalHeadlineSet` and
`_dumbScenarioPoliticalOfficeSet`, and `method @0x73f2b9ec28 System.Void
LoadCityRegionSet()` (il2cpp_dump.txt:18439).

What asks for a region is `a16_country-political-systems-enc` - 102 rows, one per country,
15 columns - and it asks with exactly two tokens: `<jurisdiction adjective>` 67 times and
`<region>` 67 times. Its `Title Regional` column is `<jurisdiction adjective> governor`
for 53 countries, its `Title Regional Specific` is the `governor of <region>` form, and the
port renders the level's own title (the third hole below).

### 95.2 The birth city

`Sim::heroToken` has answered `city` for a long time, and that is what hid the hole: the
token resolved to the empty string and the resolver keeps an empty value verbatim, so a row
that writes `<city>` shipped the literal. `createLife` chose a country and
`h.region = regionForCity(c.code, h.city)` with `h.city` still empty; only
`pinCountry` - the `--script` path - ever drew a city, and the port has no other birth path.
Every normal life therefore had no city: the birth line read `I was born a male in , Nigeria.`
and the probe counted 33 raw `<city>` literals in 334 lives before the fix.

The draw is one line, and the stream is the reason it is not two:

~~~
  if (h.city.empty() && !c.cities.empty())
    h.city = c.cities[placeRng_.below(uint32_t(c.cities.size()))];
  h.region = regionForCity(c.code, h.city);
~~~

`placeRng_` is the port-private place stream section 95 introduces for exactly this reason:
`createLife`'s `rng_` stream is matched value-for-value against the game's own attribute
snapshots (the ctor note at src/sim.cpp:2700), so a new draw on it would move every attribute
after it. `pinCountry` keeps its own single `rng_` draw and the guard leaves it alone, so a
pinned life consumes the place stream exactly once, as before.

### 95.3 The office pool, and the four countries that ran out of stack

The probe found a crash before it found the leak: Andorra, Hong Kong, Papua New Guinea and
Puerto Rico died with rc -11 (SIGSEGV) at seed 4, and the binary built from the previous
commit died on the same four (rc 139), so it was the office pool and not this section. Under
AddressSanitizer the report is one line and an infinite cycle:

~~~
==63520==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-overflow on address 0x00016ab56f00 (pc 0x000104b0bf18 bp
    resolveInto (src/sim.cpp:2308) -> resolve (src/sim.cpp:2305) ->
    ensureOfficeFields (src/sim.cpp:4973) -> politicalToken (src/sim.cpp:21720) ->
    resolveInto (src/sim.cpp:2422) -> ...
~~~

`ensureOfficeFields` ended with `h.office = resolve(trim(t.at(row, pick.title)))`. The four
countries open a regional office whose title is the token-bearing `<jurisdiction adjective>
mayor` (or `governor`, or `chief executive`) and open no national one, so the level draw
keeps landing on that row; resolving its title reaches `politicalToken`, whose on-demand fill
runs `if (office.empty() && life_) ensureOfficeFields(life)` - and the office is still empty,
because the assignment has not returned yet. The fix assigns the raw title first:

~~~
  const std::string officeTitle = trim(t.at(row, pick.title));
  h.office = officeTitle;
  h.office = resolve(officeTitle);
~~~

The same probe found the second leak: `<jurisdiction>` 34 times and `<political-office>`
20 times, always in `a16_dumb-scenarios-political-campaign-enc` (whose own token census is
`<opponent>` 52, `<jurisdiction>` 29, `<political-office>` 25, `<lover>` 16,
`<insult>` 8, `<opponent-possessive>` 6, `<jurisdiction-possessive>` 5,
`<lover-possessive>` 3). A campaign card is about the office the hero is running for, and for
a hero whose country offers no office at all (15 of the 102 rows open no level) the on-demand
fill returns early and the row rendered the raw literal. The gate is the honest reading of the
card:

~~~
  if (campaign && h.office.empty()) {
    ensureOfficeFields(life);
    if (h.office.empty()) return false;
  }
~~~

It sits after both of `politicalYear`'s own coins, so the gates' RNG order is unchanged.

### 95.4 Shortcuts

1. `<region>` has no rendered consumer yet, and this section does not invent one. The
   game's own `governor of <region>` form is a separate render path - `field 0x48
   System.String <TitleRegionalSpecific>k__BackingField` (il2cpp_dump.txt:7836) and
   `GetTitleForOfficeAndPlaceAndIsSpecificAndIsCapitalized(System.Int32, SimPlace,
   System.Boolean, System.Boolean)` (il2cpp_dump.txt:7868) - which the port does not call;
   `heroToken("region")` answers any card that does write the token, and the region reaches
   the screen through the country's jurisdiction word instead (`in your state` for a United
   States hero, where `Region Jurisdiction` is `state`).
2. The birth city comes off `placeRng_` rather than the game's own draw. That is the
   deliberate exception: the attribute stream is snapshot-matched, and a place draw cannot go
   there without moving every attribute behind it.
3. The region for a city is the table's own row - the same-city rows first, the country's
   other rows when the city is not in the table, nothing when the country has no code. The
   game's picker is a different draw, and the port has no captured stream for it.
4. Fifteen of the 102 political-systems rows open no office. Those countries now offer no
   campaign card at all rather than a card with a hole in it, and the probe asserts it.
5. The four countries that crashed now render the ordinary campaign card (see the cards
   below), which is the game's own behaviour for an office holder - the port simply stops
   losing the year to a segfault.

The probe is `/tmp/qdir/ctyres.py` (a *res.py, so the harness picks it up). It pins every

## 96. The movie theater: a place table the game keeps in four slots, a card whose body has
no string to read, and an expansion pack that is not a card family

The last four families each arrived with a table and a consumer: the school year read the
field trips, the relationship year the sleepovers, the dating app its seven, the census the
region table. This one has both and neither of them is the card. `a16_movies-enc` is a film
list, the game holds four of its rows at a time in its own place object, and the card that
asks whether to go is a scenario class whose sentence is built at runtime - so the section had
to read the card out of the metadata literals and write two of its lines. The twelve
`genesis_movie_*` files sitting in the same directory look like the rest of the family and
are an expansion pack (96.5).

### 96.1 The family

`a16_movies-enc` is 244 rows of `Title,Genre` (245 physical lines, the extra one a
whitespace padding row). Seventeen genres appear - Children 44, Comedy 33, Documentary 23,
Romantic Comedy 20, Drama 16, Sports 16, Adventure 15, Horror 14, Thriller 13, Fantasy 13,
Sci-Fi 8, Western 5, War 5, Musical 5, Mystery 5, Indie 5, Action 4 - and 56 of the 244
titles are templates over exactly four tokens: `<random-first-name>` 30, `<random-surname>`
30, `<random-first-name-male>` 8 and `<random-first-name-female>` 8.

The consumer is code-side and the dump names all of it: `class DataMovie`
(il2cpp_dump.txt:11778), whose `Genre` is a `System.Int32` rather than the table s genre
word - the loader maps the word to the enum - the game-data holder s
`field 0x10 System.Collections.ArrayList _movieSet` (il2cpp_dump.txt:17282),
`method @0x73f2b73ce0 System.Void LoadMovieSet()`, the three pickers
`GetRandomNonChildrenMovie()`, `GetRandomMovieForChildren()` and
`GetRandomMovieOfGenre(System.Int32)` (il2cpp_dump.txt:19443-19445), and
`EmojiForMovieGenre(System.Int32)` @0x73f3025558.

The four slots are the game s own place cache. `SimPlace` carries `0x158 DataMovie
AvailableMovie` with the `0x160 <AvailableMovieTitle>` string beside it, `0x168
AvailableChildrensMovie` / `0x170`, `0x178 AvailableComedyMovie` / `0x180` and `0x188
AvailableDocumentaryMovie` / `0x190` (il2cpp_dump.txt:57100-57550), and
`RefreshAvailableMovies()` @0x73f2ed1ebc fills them: one general film, one children s film,
one comedy and one documentary, drawn when the hero stands somewhere that shows films.
`Sim::placeMovie(int slot)` (src/sim.cpp:23328) is that cache, keyed the way the game keys
it - slot 0 the general film, 1 the children s, 2 the comedy, 3 the documentary - and it
returns the title it cached.

### 96.2 Two card bodies with no string to read

The card is `ScenarioMovieTheaterPull` (@0x73f3bc1cd0 `RefreshScenario`,
@0x73f3bc2104 `ChoiceSelectedAtIndex`, @0x73f3bc246c `EmojiString`, fields
`_genre`/`_movie`/`_movieTitle`/`_requireRewardedVideo`), with
`ScenarioMovieTheaterPullWatched` (@0x73f3bc2240 ctor(String,int), @0x73f3bc24cc
`DismissSelected`), `ScenarioMovieTheaterPushWatched` (@0x73f3bc2710
ctor(String,String,String,ArrayList)), `ScenarioOpportunityChildhoodMovie`
(@0x73f3bc29b0 `RefreshScenario`, @0x73f3bc3820 `ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush`,
@0x73f3bc3954 `MovieAvailable`), `ScenarioOpportunityMovie` (@0x73f3bc3a80, with
@0x73f3bc44e4 `NormalMovieAvailable`, @0x73f3bc3fe4 `ChildrensMovieAvailable` and
@0x73f3bc40bc `GetChildToGo`) and `ScenarioRelationshipMovieTheater` (@0x73f3bc6f14,
@0x73f3bc7ac8 `NormalMovieAvailable`, @0x73f3bc79cc `ChildrensMovieAvailable`,
@0x73f3bc7cb8 `ChoiceSelectedAtIndex`, five ctors for the five companions) plus its
watched variant @0x73f3bc7de8. The sibling `ScenarioPushConcert` and
`ScenarioRelationshipConcert` classes have exactly the same shape, so this is a template
the game reuses per activity rather than a per-table renderer the port can register.

No table in `gamedata_plain/` carries any of that text, and `obs_corpus` has no captured
movie card - `scenarios.csv` has no row for it, and the only movie line in `logs.csv` is
the actor card `I got my shot to direct a film and chose to make an action movie.` at age 19
(trace_game7.json). The vocabulary therefore came out of the metadata literals, and the
literals are choices and narratives only:

~~~
choices      #21912 Go to a movie             #21947 Go to the movies
             #21948 Go to the movies with {0}  #21894 Go see a children s film
             #21895 Go see a comedy            #21896 Go see a documentary
             #21897 Go see it                  #21898 Go see {0}
             #46052 Watch the movie instead
narratives   #23948 I decided to watch the movie instead.
             #25792 I went with {0} to go see {1}.
             #25782 I went to the theater to see {0}.
             #49733 You went to the theater to see {0}.
             #47780 You are unable to find an interesting movie to take {0} to go see.
             #47782 You are unable to find an interesting new {0} to go see.
stats        #30523 MoviesWatched             #30522 Moviegoer
             #30508 Movie Buff                #30512 Movie Junkie
             #21907 Go to 5 movies in one life
names        #30516 Movie Theater             #30517 Movie Theater Cashier
~~~

The two bodies are the one part with no string behind them. A literal sweep for
`movie theater is showing`, `taking you to the movie theater` and every other fragment of
an invitation returns nothing in `il2cpp_dump.txt`: `RefreshScenario` builds the sentence
at runtime out of the place, the film and the companion, so there is nothing to port. The port
keeps the game s vocabulary as far as it exists - every choice cell is a game literal, the two
narratives are #25782 and #23948, the ledger line counts the `MoviesWatched` stat of #30523,
and the film named in every line is the row the table gave - and writes the two invitations
itself:

~~~
  young   Your {parent} is taking you to the movie theater to see <movie-children>.
  adult   The movie theater is showing <movie>.
~~~

### 96.3 The four slots

The cache lives on the hero, because the game s lives on the place the hero is standing in and
the port has no place visit (`struct PlaceMovie { std::string title; int row = 0; }`,
`PlaceMovie movies[4]`, `std::string movieCity` and `int moviesWatched` at
include/bl/game.h:580-583). Four rows are drawn once per city and cleared when the city
changes, which is the port s stand-in for `RefreshAvailableMovies`:

~~~
  if (h.movieCity != h.city) {          // a different theater: the cache is the place s
    h.movieCity = h.city;
    for (PlaceMovie& m : h.movies) { m.title.clear(); m.row = 0; }
  }
~~~

The genre filter is the pickers: slot 0 keeps every non-Children row, and the other three keep
exactly their own genre word (src/sim.cpp:23337-23360):

~~~
  static const char* const kGenre[4] = {"", "Children", "Comedy", "Documentary"};
  if (slot == 0 ? genre == "Children" : genre != kGenre[slot]) continue;
~~~

The draw is `pool[placeRng_.below(uint32_t(pool.size()))]` - the port-private place stream
section 95 introduced, for the same reason: `createLife` s `rng_` stream is matched
value-for-value against the game s attribute snapshots, so a place draw cannot go there without
moving every attribute behind it - and the 56 template titles are filled the way section 94
filled the names table, with `drawFirstName` and `drawSurname`:

~~~
  while ((p = title.find("<")) != std::string::npos) {
    const std::string tok = title.substr(p, title.find(">", p) - p + 1);
    if (tok == "<random-first-name>")              title.replace(p, tok.size(), drawFirstName(placeRng_.chance(0.5)));
    else if (tok == "<random-first-name-male>")    title.replace(p, tok.size(), drawFirstName(false));
    else if (tok == "<random-first-name-female>")  title.replace(p, tok.size(), drawFirstName(true));
    else                                           title.replace(p, tok.size(), drawSurname());
  }
~~~

### 96.4 The card and its three outcomes

`Sim::movieYear` (src/sim.cpp:23377) is hooked into the year chain at src/sim.cpp:3501,
right after the Dumb-scenario pool and before the celebrity app:

~~~
  if (movieYear(life, out, forcedChoice)) return true;
~~~

It bails on a forced choice, on age under 4, and on a 12% coin off `placeRng_` - the game s
own card is one the player opens from a place screen, so the odds are the port s (96.6, item 2).
A hero of 12 or under gets the childhood shape, a hero with a lover gets the companion option,
and the film for the visit is drawn before the options so the invitation can name it:

~~~
  young   Go see it                    (the children s film)
          Watch the movie instead
  adult   Go see it                    (the general film)
          Go to the movies with <lover> (when the hero has a lover, slot 0)
          Go see a comedy              (slot 2, when there is no companion)
          Go see a documentary         (slot 3, when there is no companion)
          Watch the movie instead
~~~

Going is worth `pointsForImpact(1)` happiness - 4 points - and going with a lover
`pointsForImpact(2)`, 8; staying home draws the coin `pointsForImpact(0)` measures, so it is
worth plus or minus one. Everything else is untouched: `karma`, `smarts`, `looks` and
`discipline` all render 0, and the probe asserts it. Going writes the game s own ledger line
and one of its two narratives:

~~~
  went        That was movie number <n>.
              I went to the theater to see <film>.          (#25782)
  companion   That was movie number <n>.
              I went with <lover> to go see <film>.         (#25792)
  home        I decided to watch the movie instead.          (#23948)
~~~

The counter is the port s `h.moviesWatched`, which is #30523 s `MoviesWatched` recorded on
the hero - the port has no stat screen to show it on.

### 96.5 The Movie Director bundle

The twelve `genesis_movie_*` files next to `a16_movies-enc` are the Movie Director
expansion pack and not a card family. They are tile and action lists in JSON whose entity
references point at a filmography the port has no model for - `<film.cast.lead.actor_id>` -
whose conditions read `scenario.movieDirector.profile_fromCastmember`, and whose DataSources
are `gfc:movie_director:filmography` and `gfc:movie_director:talent_network`; beside them
sit `genesis_movie_director` (188 rows), `genesis-md-creative-vision-followups-enc` (2255),
`genesis-md-daily-review-enc` (418), `genesis-md-audience-reception-enc` (227),
`genesis-md-festival-screening-enc` and `genesis-md-festival-scenarios-enc` (36 each),
`genesis-md-film-reception-weights-enc` (4) and `genesis_movie_director_defaults` (40).

The literals around it say what it is: `Movie Director Bundle` #30511, `The Movie Director
Expansion Pack--Step behind the camera and call all the shots.` #41607, `You have been
granted honorary access to Movie Director!` #48681, `Direct your own films, make A-List
connections, and more!` #17754, plus its own progression counters `NumMovieDirectorViews`
#32353, `CurrentLifeIsMovieDirector` #16853, `FilmingProgressPct` #20158,
`Filmography` #20159 and `FilmsReleased` #20160. That is a paid container with its own
screens - a place the player walks into - and the port has no place screen and no purchase
path, so the twelve files stay unwired. They are recorded here so the next reader does not
mistake them for a hole in the same family.

### 96.6 Shortcuts

1. The two card bodies are the port s prose (96.2). Every choice cell, both narratives and the
   ledger line are the game s own literals.
2. The trigger is port-owned. The game decides when the opportunity arrives with its own
   `ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush` (@0x73f3bc520c on the opportunity class, and the same
   method on `ScenarioOpportunityChildhoodMovie` @0x73f3bc3820), and a scripted life has no
   push channel, so the port spends a 12% coin off `placeRng_` at age 4 and up.
3. The invitation names the general film and the log names the genre film. The game caches
   `AvailableMovie` for the visit and calls its genre picker when the choice is made, so a
   comedy card can read as one film and log another - `placeMovie(opt.slot)` is where the port
   draws that second one, at the same point in the flow.
4. There is no children model in the port (src/sim.cpp:14191 records the shortcut), so the
   childhood card s inviter is the literal `mother` rather than
   `ScenarioOpportunityChildhoodMovie` s drawn inviter with its own pronoun.
5. `h.moviesWatched` is a record only: the port has no achievement machinery (a grep for
   `achievement` across src/ and include/ is empty), so #21907 `Go to 5 movies in one life`
   has nothing to fire.
6. The four slots are keyed by city, not by visit. The game refreshes them when the hero arrives
   somewhere; the port draws four rows the first time a city is asked and keeps them until the
   city changes, so a hero who stays put sees a stable marquee.

genre the body s film belongs to, the exact choice set for the hero s age and company, the last

## 97. The generic pastime pool: the table three other features already drew from, and a
card the game pushes that the port has to coin

Every family so far arrived with a table nobody else read. This one is the opposite:
`a16_pastimes-enc` is the generic half of a family whose private halves the port already
runs - the pet, the mob and the commune each draw a pool of their own and each writes the
same sentence with its own subject - and the generic table had no consumer at all. The card
that reads it is not a table either. The game reaches it through a push scenario whose body
and both choices survive as metadata literals, and whose one missing line is the one the
port had to write (97.2).

### 97.1 The family

`a16_pastimes-enc` is 271 rows of `Pastime,Holiday`: 224 rows with an empty gate and 47
carrying an `x`, 269 distinct tails (two are duplicated - `to dinner` and `to pick
flowers`) and 18 rows that are not plain tails. A cell is a TAIL, not a sentence: the verb
belongs to the caller, so the table reads `to the park`, `bowling`, `golfing`, `to the
gym`, `to the movies`, `to watch a play`.

The private halves are already in the port, each with its own draw:
`a16_pet-pastimes-enc` (src/sim.cpp:11107, the card `Time with <pet>`),
`a16_mafia-pastimes-enc` (src/sim.cpp:9513, the card `An evening with the family`) and
`a16_cult-communard-spend-time-enc` (src/sim.cpp:8164, `Time with my followers`), with
`a16_zoo-animal-spend-time-color-enc` beside them. Four sibling tables and four cards, one
per subculture, and nothing read the generic pool they are variants of.

The consumer is code-side and the dump names it: `class DataPastime`
(il2cpp_dump.txt:12628, the `Pastime` string plus its `Holiday` flag), the holder field
`_pastimeSet` (il2cpp_dump.txt:17276), `LoadPastimeSet()` @0x73f2b72520 and the picker
`GetRandomPastime()` @0x73f2d0ca3c. The picker disassembles into array fills, a
`CountNotNull`, a branch on `IsChristmasSeason()` and a
`GetRandomNumber(System.Int32,System.Int32)` - which is what the `Holiday` column is for:
the 47 gated rows are the season half of the pool.

Four scenario classes hold a `_pastime` string, and two of them carry the card shape. The
pull class `ScenarioRelationshipSpendTimeGeneral` (il2cpp_dump.txt:49726, `_person` 0x170,
`_hero` 0x178, `_life` 0x180, `_pastime` 0x188) and the push class
`ScenarioPushSpendTime` (il2cpp_dump.txt:41798, `_parent` 0x170, `_lover` 0x178,
`_child` 0x180, `_sibling` 0x188, `_person` 0x190, `_takingHero` 0x198, `_pastime`
0x1a0, `_isPersonYourFather` 0x1a8), with `ScenarioMobsterSpendTimePush`
(il2cpp_dump.txt:43878) and the skip-school family `ScenarioSchoolSkipPush`
(il2cpp_dump.txt:50410, `_student` 0x170, `_classmate` 0x178, `_pastime` 0x180) after
them. The pull class s `RefreshScenario()` @0x73f2a05b64 reads the year pair off
`[person+0x120]` and `[hero+0x20]` for its first-time-this-year branch, calls
`LivesInSamePlaceAsHero()` @0x73f30e6b28, tests willingness through a vtable slot, calls
`ImpactKarma` on the person (1 or -1) and then `TryPushSeasonsScenario()`,
`HandleFirstTimeThisYear()`, `ShowSpendTimeFeedback()`, `HandleAchievements()` and
`GetRelationshipImpactByPerson()` @0x73f2a06864. Its `PrepareBracketParser()`
@0x73f2a05c90 fills the person dictionary and calls `GetRandomPastime()`,
`RelationshipTemplate()` @0x73f30e3bc8, `get_PlaceOfResidence()` @0x73f30d6494 and
`get_Country()` @0x73f2ec51ec: two slots, the pastime and the person.

### 97.2 The card, its literals, and the one line with no string to read

The two slots are in no table. The corpus has no captured spend-time card and no content
file spells the sentence, so the vocabulary is the metadata literals again - and this family s
literals are thin: exactly ten strings carry `<person-relationship>`, and they are
refusals and acceptances rather than a card.

~~~
token        #9352 <pastime>                 #9364 <person-relationship>
refusal      #9365 <person-relationship> refused to go <pastime> with me.
             #9366 ... with you.            #9367 <person-relationship> refused to see me.
             #9368 ... to see you.
acceptance   #9369 <person-relationship> took me <pastime>.
             #9370 ... took you <pastime>
             #25284 I took <person-relationship> <pastime>.
             #49542 You took <person-relationship> <pastime>.
impossible   #48109 You can not spend time with <person-relationship> because <he/she>
             lives in <person-place> and you live in <hero-place>.
named forms  #19880 Family {0}, {1}, refused to go {2} with me.
             #30722 My bandmate, {0}, refused to go {1} with me.
             #30755 My communard, {0}, refused to go {1} with me.
             #30992 My {0}, {1}, refused to go {2} with me.
~~~

The card that carries those two slots is a push, and its text is five more literals: the body
`Your {0}, {1}, wants to go with you.` (#50800, inside the 50795-50809 cluster of
`Your {0}, {1}, ...` sibling lines), the two choices `Go with {0}` (#21961) and
`Refuse to go with {0}` (#35522), and the title, which is the game s own button `Spend
Time` (#39665) with `Spend Time With All` (#39666) and `Spend time with {0}` (#39678)
beside it. The port took the push shape for exactly that reason: every slot of the card is a
game literal - the body, both choices and both acceptance lines - where the pull class s own
sentence has no body string at all, only the two template slots.

One line has nothing to read. No literal has the hero refusing a pastime invite: the refusals
above are the person saying no to the hero, and the two hero-side refusals near the family
(#24944 `I refused to go with my ` and #24945 `I refused to go with my {0}{1} on {2}.`)
are holiday lines. So the refusal narrative is the port s own prose, marked in the code as
such and listed as a shortcut in 97.5.

### 97.3 Who can ask, and the four gates

`Sim::spendTimeYear` (src/sim.cpp:23492) hangs off the year chain right after the movie
card (src/sim.cpp:3527) and follows the rules the other code-built cards follow. A pushed
choice owns the year, so `forcedChoice >= 0` returns early; a hero under six cannot be
asked; the year s invite is a coin on the family s own stream, `spendRng_.chance(0.10)`
(the stream the constructor adds at src/sim.cpp:625); and the person has to be willing.

That last gate is the game s own. `RefreshScenario()` weighs the invite by the
relationship - `GetTotalHeroRelationshipStrength()` is what `ShowRefusalFeedback()`
reads - so the port draws the partner against the hero s own `relationship` score
(`h.relationship / 100`) and gives a relative a flat coin. A refusal there is not a card: it
is the year nobody asked, which is the same silence the pull class would show, minus the
person-side karma.

The pool is the family vector plus the partner. Both slots of the card carry a name -
#50800 s second slot and the only slot of `Go with {0}` - and the port never names a parent
(include/bl/sim.h:49 records why), so a parent can fill neither the clause nor the choice
label and stays out; the siblings, the children and the partner are all named. The partner s
word comes off the two fields the port already carries, `loverStatus` and `loverFemale`:
`wife`, `husband`, `girlfriend`, `boyfriend`.

`HeroTakesOther()` @0x73f2a066b0 is code-side - a list of relationship words it tests with
`Contains` - so the port reads the direction off the ages: the person takes the hero out
when the person is older, the hero takes them when not. That is what chooses between the two
acceptance literals, and it is why one sibling can produce either line in different lives.

An accepted invitation also moves the partner s `relationship` by five, clamped at 100 - the
port s reading of the code-side `GetRelationshipImpactByPerson()`, which the game calls from
`HandleFirstTimeThisYear()`. A relative moves nothing, because the port keeps no score for
one.

### 97.4 The pastime, the one-of lists and the Holiday column

`Sim::pickPastime` (src/sim.cpp:23474) draws the tail and returns its row, the same
provenance rule the movie card uses: `out.row_id` is the real row of the real table. The
pool is the Holiday split - the 47 gated rows when the life s calendar month is December, the
month the port s own holiday set already gives Christmas (kHoliday, src/sim.cpp:499), and the
224 ordinary rows otherwise. A life with no fixed date takes the ordinary half, so the gate is
deterministic per run rather than a coin of its own.

Eighteen rows are not plain tails. Seventeen write a one-of list inline -
`<apples/oranges/strawberries/blueberries/peaches/lemons/limes/grapes>`,
`<mountains/forest/country/city/hills>`, `<checkers/chess/backgammon/Connect 4>`,
`<plungers/broomsticks/straws/wrapping paper rolls/umbrellas/breadsticks/pool noodles/cue
sticks/toy lightsabers/rulers/sticks/bamboo shoots>` and the rest - and three name a token
instead: the two `<musician>` karaoke rows and the boy s choir. `fillOneOf`
(src/sim.cpp:563) is the one-of half: the first slash inside a pair turns it into a list and
the member is drawn from the family s stream, while a pair with no slash is handed on
untouched, so `<musician>` reaches the resolver, which already answers it through
`referenceToken("musician")` (src/sim.cpp:1699). The filled tail goes through `resolve()`
like every other rendered string, which is what makes `to watch <musician> music videos` a
real invitation instead of a raw token.

### 97.5 Shortcuts

1. The invite s coin (0.10 a year) and the relative s willingness (a flat 0.5) are the port s:
   `ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush()` @0x73f3ce99f8 is code-side, and the game also reaches
   the card from the menu (97.3).
2. The person takes the hero out when the person is older, the hero takes the person
   otherwise: `HeroTakesOther()` is a code-side list, not a recovered rule (97.3).
3. Parents cannot ask, because the port leaves their name empty and the card has no slot that
   can do without one (97.3).
4. The refusal narrative is written here: no literal spells the hero refusing a pastime
   invite (97.2).
5. An unwilling person produces no card and no person-side karma, where the pull class would
   have shown a second card (97.3).
6. The five points the partner gains on an accepted invitation are the port s reading; the
   game s own impact is code-side (97.3).
7. The Christmas gate is the port s month rule rather than the game s `IsChristmasSeason()`,
   and a life with no fixed date never meets the 47 gated rows (97.4).
8. The two other consumers of the same table are still unwired: `ScenarioSchoolSkipPush`
   (the skip-school family) and `ScenarioMobsterSpendTimePush` (97.1).

A new probe (spdres.py) drives 160 lives across both genders, two year budgets and both
relationship settings, and checks every spend-time card in them: the title, the two slots of

literals, the refusal line, the happiness delta per outcome and no other delta, and a sweep of
every rendered line for a raw `<...>` token.

## 98. The skip-school card: the same pastime pool asked for by a classmate, and the three
actions a push scenario's own literals hold

The pastime pool has a second consumer, and it is the one 97 named and left unwired:
ScenarioSchoolSkipPush. It is a push aimed at a pupil rather than at an adult, so it does not
arrive on the school year's own coin either - it is a rule of its own, tried before the school
year claims the year - and all three of its actions come out of the family's own literals. Where
97 had to write exactly one line by hand, this card writes none: its refusal borrows the
generic choice pair 97 already renders.

### 98.1 The family

`class ScenarioSchoolSkipPush : Scenario` (il2cpp_dump.txt:50410) holds three fields and one
of them is the pool: `_student` (SimOccupationStudent, 0x170), `_classmate` (SimClassmate,
0x178) and `_pastime` (System.String, 0x180). Its methods are `.ctor()` `0x73f2a6402c`,
`RefreshScenario()` `0x73f2a64110`, `ChoiceSelectedAtIndex(System.Int32)` `0x73f2a6499c`,
`GetClassmateSkipper(System.Boolean)` `0x73f2a64494` and
`ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush()` `0x73f2a65248`.

RefreshScenario has the shape the other push cards have: a one-time dictionary fill (nine
`FillDictionary` calls) and then `mov w0, #1; bl GetClassmateSkipper` with the result stored at
`[x19+0x178]` - the scenario picks the classmate who will do the skipping itself, and the
argument is the literal `1`. The card's text is not in the disassembly at all: those fills name
the game's own dictionary ids, so the vocabulary lives in the metadata, not in the code. The
classmate is therefore both a field and a draw, and the port's one classmate is the same
person the school year already uses (98.3).

What that vocabulary is, by id: the push body `#50285` - `Your classmate, {0}, wants you to skip
class with {1} and go {2} instead.` - the title `#39189` `Skipping School`, the two actions that
are the family's own, `#39183` `Skip school` and `#39179` `Skip class and do something else`,
and the three outcomes `#25105` `I skipped school and went {0} with my classmate, {1}.`,
`#25104` `I skipped school and went {0} instead.` and `#24954` `I refused to skip school with my
classmate, {0}.`. Beside them sit the achievement `#39184` `Skip secondary school 3+ times` -
the literal that says which school levels the card belongs to (98.3) - and a set of app-side
forms the port has no surface for, because it has no confirmation dialog: `#39175` `Skip School`,
`#39181` and `#39182` `Skip it` and `Skip it altogether`, `#39363` `So, skip school?`, `#11941`
`Are you sure you want to skip school?`, `#46539` `Where else would I skip?` and `#49324`
`You skipped school and went {0} instead.`.

The refusal action is not among the family's own. The card has three actions and only two of
them are its literals; the third is the generic pair 97 already renders, `Refuse to go with {0}`
(`#35522`). Two cards of different families refusing in the same words is the game's own habit,
not an invention of the port.

### 98.2 The card

The port builds the year like this (Sim::skipSchoolYear, src/sim.cpp:23574): the body is
`Your classmate, <name>, wants you to skip class with <him|her> and go <tail> instead.`, the
second slot filled from `h.schoolClassmateFemale`, the third from the pool (98.4); the title is
`Skipping School`; the prompt is the port's usual `What will you do?`; and the single choice is
one of three, drawn with equal weight:

- `Skip school` (`#39183`) - the hero goes with the classmate. The narrative is `#25105`,
  `I skipped school and went <tail> with my classmate, <name>.`, and it names the classmate
  again, so the line and the body share one name.
- `Skip class and do something else` (`#39179`) - the hero skips with nobody. The narrative is
  `#25104`, `I skipped school and went <second tail> instead.`
- `Refuse to go with <name>` (`#35522`) - the narrative is `#24954`,
  `I refused to skip school with my classmate, <name>.`

The three outcomes are the port's own happiness readings in the units the rest of the port uses:
`pointsForImpact(2)` (eight) for going with the classmate, `pointsForImpact(1)` (four) for going
somewhere else alone, and `pointsForImpact(0)` (the plus or minus one) for refusing. There is no
ledger line: the family has no stat line for a skipped class, and inventing one would put prose
of the port's own into a card that needs none.

### 98.3 Who can ask: the four gates

1. A forced choice suppresses the year, the rule every code-built card in the port takes.
2. The hero has to be in school at all - `h.schooling`.
3. The hero has to be in secondary school. The gate reads the band off the age rather than off
   `h.schoolLevel`, because that field is only brought up to date by the school year itself and
   therefore goes stale in any year another rule claims: `schoolLevelFor()` (src/sim.cpp:20287)
   gives 2 at 11 to 13 and 3 at 14 to 17, which is the middle and high school the achievement
   literal counts, and level 4 (college, 18 to 22) is out.
4. A classmate has to exist - `h.schoolClassmate`, which the port draws once when the school
   starts (src/sim.cpp:20369, `personName("classmate")` and a coin for the gender) and the
   scenario re-draws in the cards that need one (src/sim.cpp:22165, :24943-24948,
   :25051-25056).

Who the classmate is comes from the game, but the coin that says a classmate asks this year does
not: `ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush()` `0x73f2a65248` is code-side and the port reads the
whole gate as 0.12 a year on the feature's own stream (98.5).

The placement in the chain is part of the gate. The rule is tried before the school year itself
(src/sim.cpp:3518), not after it: a push aimed at a pupil has to get its chance on a school
year, and the school year claims the year at 0.6 on its own coin, so a rule parked behind it
would be starved to the point of never firing. It draws on its own stream, so no earlier
subsystem's sequence moves - and 97's own probe was re-run afterwards to show exactly that: the
spend-time census is bit-for-bit what 97 recorded (98.6).

### 98.4 The pastime, the second draw, and the trouble

The pastime itself is the same draw 97 performs, and it is the same call: `pickPastime()` now
takes the stream it draws from (src/sim.cpp:23474, `int Sim::pickPastime(Rng& rng, std::string&
tail)`), so each feature keeps its own sequence. 97's call site passes `spendRng_`
(src/sim.cpp:23632) and this card passes `skipRng_` (include/bl/sim.h:477, seeded in the
constructor, src/sim.cpp:626).

The 'skip class and do something else' action draws a SECOND tail from the pool: the body named
the place the classmate proposed, and the hero who goes alone goes somewhere else. The row the
card carries - `out.row_id`, the row of the pastime it names - therefore follows the narrative
rather than the body: it is the body's row when the hero keeps the invite or refuses, and the
second draw's row when the hero goes elsewhere. The probe checks both by matching the named tail
against that row's own pattern (98.6).

A skipped class costs trouble. `h.schoolTrouble` is the school family's own counter and it is
read in four places - at three or more it costs a grade point (src/sim.cpp:20538), it decays by one a
year (:20542), at two it can open the school's trouble card (:20608), and a row can require it
(:20773, `Requires Trouble`) - so this card is the second writer of it after the school year's
own events and it adds one on any skip, with the classmate or alone.

### 98.5 Shortcuts

1. The 0.12 coin is the port's: `ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush()` `0x73f2a65248` is code-side,
   and the card is also reachable from the game's own push scheduler, which the port does not
   model.
2. The level band is read off the age rather than off `h.schoolLevel`, which goes stale (98.3).
3. The three actions are drawn with equal weight; the game's own weighting is in the scenario's
   code, not in a table.
4. 'Skip class and do something else' takes a second draw from the same pool; the game's second
   place is whatever its own logic picks, and the port reads it as another pastime (98.4).
5. The happiness numbers (eight, four, plus or minus one) are the port's reading; the game's own
   impacts are code-side.
6. The trouble the skip costs is the port's reading of the school family's own counter (98.4).
7. The classmate who asks is the one classmate the port keeps, where `GetClassmateSkipper()`
   picks one out of the class each time.
8. The confirmation forms (`#39363`, `#11941`, `#46539`, `#39175`, `#39181`, `#39182`) stay
   unrendered: the port has no dialog surface, so the card is a single screen with three
   actions, the same shape the other code-built cards take.
9. `ScenarioMobsterSpendTimePush` is now the last consumer of the pastime pool that is still
   unwired.

### 98.6 Verification

checks every skip-school card in them: the title, the body's name, the pronoun against the
classmate's own gender, the choice label against the body's name, the row the card carries
against the tail the narrative names (the body's row when the hero keeps the invite or refuses,
the second draw's row when the hero goes alone), each of the three narratives against its
literal, the happiness delta per outcome and no other delta, and a sweep of every rendered line
for a raw `<...>` token. The lives have school switched on, which is what makes a pupil exist at
all: the earlier pastime probe ran lives with no school and saw no skip card.

## 99. The mobster spend-time card: a pastime from the mafia's own country-keyed table, a
colleague who outranks you, and the one push the family's subsystem sends itself

98's last shortcut pointed here, and it was half right. `ScenarioMobsterSpendTimePush` is
indeed the last unwired card of the spend-time family, but it is not a consumer of the pool 97
named: read against the class, it never touches `a16_pastimes-enc` at all. Its pastime comes
from the mafia's own table, `a16_mafia-pastimes-enc`, through
`GetRandomMafiaPastimeForCountryCode(System.String)` - the draw the mafia year already
performs for its own card (src/sim.cpp:9550). What this card shares with 97 and 98 is the
shape (one pastime tail, one turn, two actions), not the table; the correction is recorded
here rather than edited into 98.

What it does share with both of them is the thing that made those sections short: every word
it renders is the family's own. The body, the accepted line and the refused line are three
literals whose slots are a rank word, a name and a tail, and the two actions are the generic
pair 97 and 98 both rendered. The port writes no prose for this card either.

### 99.1 The family

`class ScenarioMobsterSpendTimePush : Scenario` (il2cpp_dump.txt:43878) holds three fields:
`_mobster` (SimMobster, 0x170), `_specialJob` (SimSpecialJobMafia, 0x178) and `_pastime`
(System.String, 0x180). Its methods are `.ctor(SimSpecialJobMafia)` `0x73f3e1b938`,
`RefreshScenario()` `0x73f3e1b980` and `ChoiceSelectedAtIndex(System.Int32)` `0x73f3e1bb7c`.

The class has no `ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush()`. That is the difference that matters
against 97 and 98: their cards sit on the game's random push scheduler and the port models the
coin it finds there, this one is pushed by the mafia subsystem, so there is no schedule to
read and the port coins the card on its own stream (99.3).

RefreshScenario (127 instructions) is a one-time dictionary fill of seven entries and then the
card's three slots. `DataMafiaMob get_Mob()` `0x73f3090460` with
`GetRandomMafiaPastimeForCountryCode(System.String)` `0x73f2cf3534` yields the tail and stores
it at `[x19+0x180]`; `GetRankString()` `0x73f30dbbe8` and `GetName()` `0x73f30dbb00` yield the
other two; and `String.Format(string, Object, Object, Object)` `0x73f52a7210` with the three
of them in that order writes `Scenario.Body` (`[x19+0x48]`). Two `ScenarioChoice` objects are
then built with `.ctor(System.String, Boolean, Boolean)` `0x73f2eb9c50` - the third argument
true on both, so both are the actionable kind - and appended to the array list at
`[x19+0x108]`, which is `Scenario`'s `ChoiceArray`. The labels and the format strings are
static metadata fields, so the card's vocabulary is once again not in the disassembly.

By id, that vocabulary is: the body `#19883` `Family {0}, {1}, wants to go {2} with
you.\n\nWhat will you do?` - literal and prompt in one string, which the port splits into its
body and its own `What will you do?` line - then the accepted line `#25793` `I went {0} with
Family {1}, {2}.` and the refused line `#25253` `I told Family {0}, {1} that I was too busy to
go {2} with {3}.`, the only four-slot line in the family. Around them sit the mafia family's
neighbouring cards: `#19876` `Family {0}, {1},`, the concert push's body `#19878`, the team-
building card's body `#19879`, `#19880` `Family {0}, {1}, refused to go {2} with me.`, and
`#25252`, the concert card's refusal - which `#25253` differs from by exactly the `to` and the
`concert`, and that is how the two refusals of a shared family are told apart.

ChoiceSelectedAtIndex (544 instructions) shows how the game reads its own card back: the
chosen label is lowercased (`String.ToLower()` `0x73f52aa938`) and matched with
`String.Contains` against two static string arrays - one holding the accept phrase, one the
refuse phrase. The action is not classified by index; it is classified by the words the card
put on its own buttons. Behind each branch sit the impacts (99.2) and a response line drawn
with `PickRandomFromStringArray(ArrayList)` `0x73f32b0608`, which is why the game can say
different things on the same outcome and the port says one: the port reads the literals, not
the arrays the game draws from.

### 99.2 The card

The port builds the year like this (Sim::mobsterSpendYear, src/sim.cpp:23667). The tail comes
from the mafia table (99.4); the rank word comes from `mafiaRankTitle()` (src/sim.cpp:9161),
which reads the mafia mob's own `Rank N` column for the rank drawn; the name comes from the
mafia token resolver's `<mafia-colleague>` slot (src/sim.cpp:9116), the one named colleague
the port keeps. The body is `Family <rank>, <name>, wants to go <tail> with you.` (the first
half of `#19883`), the title is `Spend Time` (the game's own family button, `#39665`, the same
reading 97 took - this class builds no title string of its own), the prompt is the port's
usual `What will you do?`, and the single choice is one of two, drawn with equal weight:

- `Go with <name>` (`#21961`) - the narrative is `#25793`, `I went <tail> with Family <rank>,
  <name>.`, and the happiness reading is `pointsForImpact(2)` (eight).
- `Refuse to go with <name>` (`#35522`) - the narrative is `#25253`, `I told Family <rank>,
  <name> that I was too busy to go <tail> with <her|him>.`, and the happiness reading is
  `pointsForImpact(-1)` (minus four).

The pronoun in the refusal is the resolver's own: the colleague slot's `speakAs` is what sets
the port's `pronounOtherFemale_`, so the line agrees with the name it prints
(src/sim.cpp:23669).

Both branches move the hero's standing in the family, and the move depends on who asked. The
game asks `IsGodfather()` `0x73f30dbc68` first. Which object the question is asked of is not
visible in the disassembly, and the port asks it of the hero (99.5): when it holds, accepting
is `ImpactStanding(4)` `0x73f30987a0` and refusing is `ImpactStanding(-5)`. When the asker is
not the godfather the game compares the mobster's rank against the hero's own and moves the
standing by one either way - `ImpactStanding(1)` up, `ImpactStanding(-1)` down - but only when
the mobster outranks the hero; a colleague at or below the hero's rank moves nothing at all.
The port reads that as `h.mafiaStanding += godfather ? 4 : (senior ? 1 : 0)` and
`h.mafiaStanding -= godfather ? 5 : (senior ? 1 : 0)`, with `senior` the same rank comparison
the game performs.

Two of the game's moves the port cannot carry. The card lands a second impact on the mobster
himself (the 0x508 vtable slot, weight 4 on the way in and 3 on the way out), and it builds a
follow-up object at the end (`.ctor(System.String, Single)` `0x73f2ec31f8`, after two random
rolls). The port keeps no per-person relationship with a mafia colleague, and it has no card
scheduler to hand a follow-up to. Both are recorded in 99.5.

There is no ledger line and no karma move: the family's own stat is the standing, and the port
moves it.

### 99.3 Who can ask: the four gates

1. A forced choice suppresses the year, the rule every code-built card in the port takes.
2. The hero has to be in the family - `h.mafia` - and old enough. The port requires eighteen:
   the card's body prints a rank word, and a made man is not a child. The game's own age test is
   code-side, like the rest of its eligibility.
3. An 0.08 coin. The card has no `ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush()`, so the coin that says the
   family asks this year comes from the mafia subsystem, and the port coins it on its own stream
   (include/bl/sim.h:487, `Rng mobRng_`, seeded in the constructor at src/sim.cpp:627, so no
   earlier subsystem's sequence moves).
4. The table has to yield a pastime and the colleague has to resolve with a name and a rank word -
   the same two-part check 97 makes, for the same reason: both slots of the card carry a
   rendered string.

The placement in the chain is part of the gate. The rule is tried immediately before the mafia
year itself (src/sim.cpp:3547, one line above `mafiaYear`), not after it: the mafia year
claims a share of the years for its own card, so a rule parked behind it would be reached far
too rarely.

### 99.4 The pastime, the country column, and the rank

`a16_mafia-pastimes-enc` is 104 rows of `Pastime` and `Specific Mob Country`. The country cell
is a lowercase ISO code and the table is overwhelmingly country-neutral: 69 of the 104 rows
leave it empty, the named rows are `it` 9, `jp` 7, `cn` 6, `ie` 6 and `mx` 6, and exactly one
row carries two codes at once, `cn, jp`. The draw is the one the mafia year already performs
(src/sim.cpp:23657): a row whose country cell equals the hero's `h.mafiaCountry`, and when no
row matches, a row from the whole table. A comma list never matches, because the comparison is
against the whole cell, so that one row is only reachable through the fallback - the same
behaviour the shipped year has had since its own section.

The rank word is drawn too (src/sim.cpp:23692, `mobRng_.below(4) + 1`): ranks one to four.
Five is left out on purpose. The mob table's fifth rank is the one with a gender-split title
column (`Rank 5 Male` / `Rank 5 Female`, the godfather and his female form), the godfather is
already the special case the standing branch tests for, and drawing him would need a gender
the card does not carry. Above the hero is the card's point, so the draw covers the four ranks
that can be above, below or level with him, and the hero's own rank decides which standing
move happens.

The table now has two consumers in the port: this card, and the mafia year's own 'An evening
with the family' (src/sim.cpp:9550, which resolves the same `Pastime` cell). The probe counts
both, which is why its log carries a second number beside the cards (99.6).

### 99.5 Shortcuts

1. The 0.08 coin is the port's. The class has no `ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush()`, so the
   game's rate and its actor live in the mafia subsystem, which the port does not model.
2. The eighteen-year age floor is the port's; the game's own test is code-side, and the reason
   the port keeps a floor is that the body prints a rank word.
3. The two actions are drawn with equal weight; the game's weighting is code-side.
4. The happiness numbers (eight and minus four) are the port's reading; the game's own impacts
   are code-side.
5. The standing moves (four and minus five for the godfather, one either way for a man above the
   hero's rank, nothing otherwise) are the port's reading of a chain the game evaluates in its
   own code, and the comparison is the strict one - a colleague at the hero's own rank moves
   nothing. The state they move, `mafiaStanding`, is not part of the simulator's event output,
   so the probe can check that the card renders and cannot check that the standing moved: this
   move is code-visible only, and it is the only part of the card's outcome that is.
6. The card's second impact - the one the game lands on the mobster himself - and the follow-up
   object it builds are not modelled: the port keeps no per-person relationship with a mafia
   colleague, and it has no scheduler to hand a follow-up to (99.2).
7. The title is the port's borrow. `RefreshScenario` sets a body and two choices and no title
   string at all, so the port renders the mafia family's own `Spend Time` button (`#39665`),
   which is the same borrow 97 recorded.
8. The game draws its response line from an array of variants; the port renders the single
   literal it read, so the same outcome reads the same every time.
9. The rank draw covers one to four, so in the port the asker is never the godfather. The game's
   `IsGodfather()` question has to be asked of somebody, and the port asks it of the hero: a
   hero who is the godfather gets the big move (four or minus five) when a subordinate invites
   him out. The game's own rank range for the asker, and the branch that fires when the asker
   holds the family's top rank himself, are not reproduced.
10. The country column's comma list (`cn, jp`) is unreachable through the country filter, exactly
   as in the shipped mafia year; that row is drawn only through the fallback (99.4).

### 99.6 Verification

A new probe (mobres.py) drives 80 mafia lives across both genders and two year budgets and
checks every mobster spend-time card in them: the title, the body's rank word against the mob
table's own `Rank N` columns, the body's name against the choice label, the tail the accepted
line repeats against the row the card carries, both narratives against their literals - the
refusal's pronoun included - the happiness delta per outcome and no other delta, an eighteen-year
floor on the ages the cards land at, and a sweep of every rendered line for a raw `<...>` token.
The lives are the earlier probes' lives with the family joined, which is what makes a made man
exist to be asked at all. The mob table is loaded the way the mafia year loads it, and the
row pattern is built from its `Pastime` column, so a one-of list in a cell is checked as the
alternation it is.

One number in the log is a census rather than a check. The colleague is drawn per card by the
mafia token resolver ("one name per token per card"), so a life can name several mobsters and the
count of distinct names is not a mismatch.
