## 100. The friend-advice card: forty-eight questions a friend asks, four buttons that are two
outcomes, and the karma this card moves where its neighbours moved happiness

The three sections before this one were all spend-time cards, and 99 closed that family. This
one opens a new one: `ScenarioFriendAdvice` (il2cpp_dump.txt:40742) is a random push card in
the same shape as 97 and 98 - a roster, one row drawn from it, a question with two actions -
but the roster is a friend's roster, the question is a friend's, and the outcome it moves is
`karma` and `discipline` rather than `happiness` (100.2). It is also the first card in the port
whose table is not already wired, which is why the section starts by saying what the family is
instead of what it shares.

The port referenced exactly one friend table before this section, `a16_friend-lover-scenarios-enc`
(src/sim.cpp:1239). `tablegap.py` - the diff of the port's source text against the 940 `a16_*`
files in `_re/gamedata` - lists ten more `friend-*` tables, eleven `secret-agent-*`, four
`coworker-*` and six `child-*`/`custody-*` among a hundred and eighteen unreferenced names. This
section takes the first of them because it is the only table in that list whose class the dumper
names, whose push gate can be read, and whose rows are gated on a second person the class also
carries. The other friend tables - `a16_friend-pranks-enc`, `a16_friend-rumors-enc`,
`a16_friend-party-scenarios-enc` - stay on the list.

The port writes none of this card's prose. The question is the table's `Scenario` cell, the
journal line is its `Log Version` cell, both responses are the class's own two `String.Format`
literals, and the two buttons are two more literals with a pronoun slot. What the port adds is
its usual `What will you do?` prompt (src/sim.cpp:23854) - the line the game itself writes at the end of
many of its body literals and which the port keeps as a field of its own, the same one 98 and
99 carry.

### 100.1 The family

`class ScenarioFriendAdvice : Scenario` (il2cpp_dump.txt:40742) holds two fields: `_friend`
(SimPerson, 0x170) and `_narrative` (System.String, 0x178). Its methods are `.ctor()`
`0x73f3c3f4a8`, `RefreshScenario()` `0x73f3c3fae8` (670 instructions),
`ChoiceSelectedAtIndex(System.Int32)` `0x73f3c40a8c` (340), `GetFriend()` `0x73f3c3f510`,
`DataFriendAdvice GetAdviceForFriend(SimPerson)` `0x73f3c4055c` (333) and
`System.Boolean ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush()` `0x73f3c40fd8` (65) - so this card, unlike
99's, does sit on the game's random push scheduler and has a gate to read.

The data class is `DataFriendAdvice` (il2cpp_dump.txt:9504): `Scenario` at 0x10, `LogVersion`
0x18, `HeroMinAge` 0x20, `HeroMaxAge` 0x24, `HeroGender` 0x28, `FriendMinAge` 0x2c,
`FriendMaxAge` 0x30, `FriendGender` 0x34, `FriendMinRelationship` 0x38, `FriendHasJob` 0x3c,
`FriendIsMarried` 0x3d, `FriendIsStudent` 0x3e, `IsSpecificAdvice` 0x3f. The dumper's names pair
the three adjacent byte fields with three bools, which is what makes the script-state checks in
100.3 readable: a row can ask for a friend with a job, a married friend, or a student friend,
and the class tests each against the friend's own state byte instead of against a relationship.

Two loaders feed the card. `GetAllFriendAdviceScenariosForHeroAgeAndHeroGender(Int32, Int32)`
`0x73f2cc9da0` builds the hero-side pool from the hero's age and gender - the `Hero*` columns -
and `GetAdviceForFriend(SimPerson)` `0x73f3c4055c` filters that pool against the friend - the
`Friend*` columns. Both are needed to reach a row, and the port folds the two passes into one
loop (100.3).

The table is `a16_friend-advice-enc`: forty-eight data rows and thirteen columns, listed in
`_re/gamedata_plain` (the same-named file in `_re/gamedata` is the encrypted blob). The port
loads it eagerly from the list at src/sim.cpp:1241, directly under the friend-lover table that
was already there.

### 100.2 The card

By literal id, the card's vocabulary is: the title `#10893` `Advice` - the only bare `Advice`
literal in the dump - the two buttons `#21756` `Give {0} good advice` and `#21755`
`Give {0} bad advice`, and the two responses `#69083` `{0}\nI gave {1} the best advice I
could.` and `#69096` `{0}\nI intentionally misled {1} by giving {2} bad advice.` Both responses
are two-line formats: the first slot is the journal line the card already built, so the second
line of each is the class's own sentence and the only prose the game contributes.

The {0} of the two buttons is `PronounStringForType(2)` `0x73f30e64d0` - the friend's pronoun,
him or her - which the port renders from the gender it gave the friend (100.3). The dump also
holds the unparameterised siblings of both buttons - `#21667` `Give bad advice`, `#39436`
`Some good advice`, `#59905` `good advice` and `#54744` `bad advice` - and two refusal lines,
`#23865` `I decided not to follow advice from my friend, ` and `#48254` `You decided not to
follow advice from your friend, `, which end in a comma and which no branch of this card's
handler ever formats. The card cannot be refused; the two refusals in the family's vocabulary
belong to a sibling that is not this class.

`ChoiceSelectedAtIndex` explains the shape of the outcome. It lowercases the chosen label and
matches it with `String.Contains` against static label arrays, so the action is classified by
the words on the button rather than by index, and the five match addresses it holds collapse
onto two outcomes: branches 1 and 2 are the good and the bad advice, and branches 3 and 4, after
their own impacts, jump back to the same good-advice format at 0x73f3c40d10. Four label phrases,
two sentences.

Each outcome moves two meters and no more. Good advice calls the friend's relationship impact
with the value 3 (the vtable slot at 0x508, not a named symbol), `ImpactDiscipline(2)`
`0x73f30e4cdc` and `ImpactKarma(3)` `0x73f30e4bfc`; bad advice calls them with -3, -3 and -4.
There is no `ImpactHappiness` call anywhere in the handler, so a card that reads like a
relationship card never touches the happiness bar - the first card in this report whose two
actions both leave `happiness` at zero. Through the port's `pointsForImpact` table
(src/sim.cpp:3786) that is `karma 16, discipline 8` for the good advice and `karma -30,
discipline -16` for the bad advice.

The bad branch writes one more thing: `strb #1` into `[x8+0x2a1]`, a persistent byte on the
hero object. It is the only consumer of that byte this report has found, the dumper gives it no
name, and nothing in the corpus reads it back, so the port leaves it out and records it here
rather than guessing a meaning for it.

### 100.3 Who can ask: the four gates, and then the row's own seven

`ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush` is a short chain of four tests. The hero must be at least
18 (the immediate `cmp` against 0x12 at the top of the method); the hero must not be in prison
(`!CurrentlyInPrison()` `0x73f2f0e1d8`); the card must have a friend to ask (`GetFriend()` must
return non-null); and `PresentedCountForScenario(<the card's own id>)` `0x73f3736430` must be
below 2. That last test is the first in this report that counts how often a card has already
been shown: this card may appear at most twice in a life, and the port now carries the counter
on the life (`int advicePresented`, include/bl/sim.h:68, reset with every new life) rather than
on the simulator, so 100.6 can see the cap hold.

Then the row filter, which `GetAdviceForFriend` applies to the hero-side pool:

1. `FriendMinAge` (row 0x2c) against the friend's age - the friend must be at least this old;
2. `FriendMaxAge` (row 0x30) against the friend's age, where zero means unbounded;
3. `FriendGender` (row 0x34) against the friend's gender byte, where 2 means any;
4. `FriendMinRelationship` (row 0x38) against `friend.GetTotalHeroRelationshipStrength()`
   `0x73f30d284c`;
5. `FriendHasJob` (row 0x3c): the friend's script-state byte must be 2;
6. `FriendIsStudent` (row 0x3e): the friend's script-state byte must be 1;
7. `FriendIsMarried` (row 0x3d): the friend's partner field must exist and its gender must
   differ from the friend's.

The pool that survives is drawn from once. The port's port of that loop is src/sim.cpp:23773
to 23806: the same seven tests, each skipped when the column is empty, plus two skips of its
own - rows whose text carries `<friend-lover>` (100.5) and rows whose `<...>` tokens the port
cannot resolve.

The friend itself is the card's second actor, and the port invents it in one place
(src/sim.cpp:23761-23771): the name is `resolve("<friend>")` drawn once for the whole card (the
name pool draws a fresh person on every call, so a row that names the friend twice would
otherwise name two people), the gender is a coin, and the job, student and married states are
three more coins at 0.6, 0.5 and 0.3. Nothing in the corpus shows the game's own friend
distribution, and gate 4 above is a relation the port's friend does not have, so both are
shortcuts (100.5).

### 100.4 The rows: forty-eight questions, and the ten the port cannot reach

The forty-eight rows are questions an acquaintance asks: a trip to another country, a new job,
hiding money from a spouse, candy for a dish, flatulence in class, a first period, a purchase
for a partner. Their columns, counted: `Hero Gender` is empty on all forty-eight rows, so no
row in this table is gated on the hero's sex; `Hero Min Age` is 18 on fourteen rows, empty on
thirteen, 16 on six, 14 on five, 65 on two, 12 on two, 8 on two, and then 40, 60, 5 and 21 once
each; `Hero Max Age` is empty on forty-four rows and 12, 18, 22, 25 once each; `Friend Min Age`
is 18 on seventeen rows, 14 on four, 10, 12, 8 and 65 on two each, and 5, 16 and 60 once each;
`Friend Max Age` is empty on thirty-nine rows and 12, 14, 18, 21, 22 and 25 once each, with
15 twice;
`Friend Gender` is male on five rows and female on three; `Friend Min Relationship` is 70 on
nine rows, 80 on one and 50 on one; and the three friend-state flags are set on six, seven and
four rows. `Specific Advice` is `x` on twenty-four rows and empty on the other twenty-four, and
all forty-eight `Log Version` cells are distinct.

One cell in that census is not a number: row 19's `Friend Max Age` holds `male`. The column
after it - `Friend Gender` - is empty on that row, so the source table has its own column-shift
typo and the friend's gender for that row sits one column to the left. The port reads the cell
through `Table::num`, which is 0 for anything non-numeric, so the row is treated as unbounded;
the typo is the game's, and copying it costs nothing.

The rows talk in tokens. Their two cells carry a hundred and twenty-one one-of lists
(`<a treadmill/a gym membership/...>`), `<friend>` ninety-five times, `<friend-lover>` eight,
`<rb>` seven (rows 5, 28, 34, 38, 45, 46, 47), `<friend-lover-possessive>` four,
`<country-other>` four, `<drug>` and `<drug-illegal>` and `<musician>` two each, and
`<friend-possessive>` once. Forty-one of the forty-eight rows carry at least one list.

Reachability is where the table gets interesting. Simulating the port's own filter over hero
ages 18 to 85 and both genders, all four friend-state combinations and both friend genders, 38
of the 48 rows can be drawn and 10 cannot:

  row 17 - `<friend-lover>` in both cells
  row 22 - friend max age 15 (the port's friend is the hero's age)
  row 23 - friend max age 15 (the only female-gated row the port could reach)
  row 26 - `<friend-lover>`
  row 30 - `<friend-lover>`
  row 42 - `<friend-lover>`
  row 44 - hero max age 12 against this card's own hero-age gate of 18
  row 46 - `<friend-lover>`
  row 47 - `<friend-lover>`
  row 48 - friend max age 14, and this row is also the one `<musician>` row the port's token
           list already resolves

Six of the ten are the port's `<friend-lover>` shortcut, three are the friend-age shortcut, and
one - row 44, whose hero ceiling is 12 while the card refuses to be pushed before 18 - is dead
in the game as well. A row the game itself can never show is the kind of thing only a table
census finds, and it is worth stating that the port is not the reason for that one.

### 100.5 Shortcuts

1. `friendAge = h.age`. The game's friend is a real SimPerson with its own age; the port's is
   the hero's age, which is what makes rows 22, 23 and 48 unreachable (100.4). Modelling a
   friend younger than the hero would invent a distribution the corpus does not show, and it
   would cost the seventeen rows that require a friend of at least 18, so the shortcut is kept
   and the count recorded instead.

2. The friend's job, student and married states are three coins (0.6, 0.5, 0.3), not the
   game's own script-state model. The constraints are what the table's flags gate on; the
   distribution behind them is unobserved.

3. `FriendMinRelationship` is read as satisfied. The port's friend has no relationship bar -
   the name pool hands out a stranger's name - and the column is 70, 80 or 50 on eleven rows.

4. The friend's relationship impact (the vtable call with value 3, or -3) is not modelled: the
   port's friend is not a Person in `Life`.

5. The `[x8+0x2a1]` flag the bad branch sets has no reader in the corpus and no name in the
   dumper, so it is not modelled (100.2).

6. The push rate is a coin of 0.06 (src/sim.cpp:23758). The class has an eligibility gate but
   no rate; the corpus cannot show one.

7. Rows that name `<friend-lover>` - six of them - are skipped. The token means the friend has
   a partner, and the port's friend does not; the two possessive forms the table also uses
   (`<friend-lover-possessive>`) are unhandled in the port's token list.

8. The card's body and its journal cell are resolved as two strings, so a token that appears in
   both is drawn twice. Row 36 shows it: the card says `plan a trip to Greece` and the journal
   says `travel to South Africa`. Rows whose `Log Version` says `<rb>` do agree, because the
   body's own draws are kept for exactly that token (src/sim.cpp:2412-2426); the four
   `<country-other>` rows do not, and the game's two cells would have to be read as one draw
   for the port to fix it.

### 100.6 Verification

The card has its own probe, `/tmp/qdir/fares.py`, which drives 160 lives - seeds 1 to 40, both
genders, an 80-year and a 50-year run each - and for every card it checks the title, the hero's
age floor, the row number and the row's own age gates, the body and the journal line against
the row's two cells turned into per-row regexes, the friend's gender across the body, the
button and the response, the exact response sentence for the outcome, and the deltas: karma 16
with discipline 8, or karma -30 with discipline -16, every other meter at zero. It counts cards
per life, so the cap of two showings is measured rather than asserted, and it sweeps every card
for an unresolved `<...>` token. Its output:

```
runs 160 rc failures 0 cards 196
kinds {'good': 110, 'no gendered token': 18, 'bad': 86} pronouns {'her': 88, 'him': 108}
rows drawn 26 of 48 top [(18, 16), (37, 12), (38, 12), (20, 12)]
ages {19: 12, 20: 4, 21: 16, 22: 4, 23: 4, 25: 4, 26: 8, 28: 4, 30: 4, 31: 4, 33: 8, 35: 4, 36: 8, 37: 4, 39: 16, 40: 20, 44: 8, 45: 12, 46: 4, 47: 4, 48: 4, 49: 4, 50: 4, 52: 2, 53: 2, 55: 2, 56: 4, 57: 4, 58: 1, 59: 2, 60: 2, 62: 1, 63: 2, 65: 2, 66: 2, 68: 2, 70: 2, 73: 2}
cards per life {0: 40, 1: 44, 2: 76}
mismatches {}
samples []
RESIDUE 0 {}
```

Two lines in that log are the ones to read. `cards per life {0: 40, 1: 44, 2: 76}` is the cap
from 100.3 holding - no life in the sample sees three cards - and `rows drawn 26 of 48` says
the sweep reached 26 of the table's 48 questions, which is the reachable set of 100.4 seen from
the outside: a row that cannot be drawn cannot be counted. The `no gendered token` counter is
the probe's own honesty: 18 cards came from rows whose two cells never write a pronoun, so the
only place the friend's gender shows is the button, and the check falls back to it.

The full regression after the section: 43 probes at residue 0 (the new `fares.py` joins the list), the residue census at `distinct residue tokens 0 total 0`, coverage at `captured scenarios: 109  recoverable: 107`, the port gap at `ENTRIES 109 rendered-by-port 107 gap 0`, the push script at rc 0 with empty stderr, and the benchmark reaching age 34.

## 101. The friend prank card: sixty-two pratfalls in two halves, four reactions, and the
thirty-one rows the game keeps for a vampire

Section 100 opened the friend family and took its advice table. This section takes the next of
them: `ScenarioFriendPrankInbound` (il2cpp_dump.txt:40820) is a random push card in the same
shape as 97, 98 and 100 - a roster, one row drawn from it, a body the table writes - but its two
people are a friend and the hero rather than a hero and a stranger, and the row is a prank the
friend has just played rather than a question the friend is asking. The card then does something
none of the previous three did: its four reactions are dispatched by the *text* of the button the
player pressed, not by its index (101.2), so the handler compares lowercased labels against six
substrings before it does anything.

The family around it is larger than the card. `ScenarioFriendPrankOutbound`
(il2cpp_dump.txt:40828) is the friend's side of the same table - a dismiss-only toast whose
title comes out `The prank legend` - and the dumper also names the coworker, astronaut and cult
halves of the same set (101.1). The tables `a16_friend-rumors-enc`,
`a16_friend-party-scenarios-enc`, `a16_coworker-pranks-enc` and the rest of that directory
stay on the `tablegap.py` list; this section takes the pranks table because it is the one whose
class carries both the picker and a readable push gate.

The port writes none of this card's prose. The body is the row's `Inbound Scenario` cell inside
the class's own `Your {0}, {1}, {2}.`, the journal line is the row's `Inbound Log Version`
cell inside `My {0}, {1}, {2}.`, the four buttons are four more literals with one pronoun slot
each, and three of the four reactions keep the journal line and append a sentence of their own
to it. What
the port adds is its usual `What will you do?` prompt (src/sim.cpp:24003) - the line the game
itself writes at the end of its body wrapper and which the port keeps as a field of its own, the
same one 98, 99 and 100 carry. The table is also the first paired one in the report: sixty-two
rows in two halves of thirty-one, one for a mortal life and one for a vampire, and the half the
card cannot reach in this port is the half with the better jokes (101.4).

### 101.1 The family

`class ScenarioFriendPrankInbound : Scenario` (il2cpp_dump.txt:40820) holds two fields:
`_friend` (SimPerson, 0x170) and `_narrative` (System.String, 0x178). Its methods are
`.ctor()` `0x73f3c4a5f4`, `RefreshScenario()` `0x73f3c4a9a8` (308 instructions),
`ChoiceSelectedAtIndex(System.Int32)` `0x73f3c4ae78` (835), `GetFriend()`
`0x73f3c4a65c` and `System.Boolean ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush()` `0x73f3c4bb84` (33).
The class carries no loader of its own: the row comes from a static table helper, which is why
the gate and the picker are the two methods worth reading here.

The data class is `DataFriendPrank` (il2cpp_dump.txt:9615) with eleven backing fields:
`OutboundScenario` 0x10, `OutboundLogVersion` 0x18, `InboundScenario` 0x20,
`InboundLogVersion` 0x28, `SenderMinAge` 0x30, `SenderMaxAge` 0x34, `SenderGender` 0x38,
`ReceiverMinAge` 0x3c, `ReceiverMaxAge` 0x40, `ReceiverGender` 0x44 and `Vampire` 0x48.
Five of them are gates on the two people - but neither the sender nor the receiver *is* a fixed
person: the caller decides which of the card's two people is passed as sender, and this card
passes the friend (101.2). The `Vampire` flag is the row's other life: a flagged row is kept
only for a vampire, and the table is split so that every flagged row is one half of a pair whose
other half is mortal (101.4).

Two methods feed the card. `LoadFriendPrankSet()` `0x73f2b9280c` lazily fills the set, guarded
by a `CountNotNull` check `0x73f32a5770` that skips the load once it is non-empty, and
`DataFriendPrank GetRandomPrankForSenderAgeSenderGenderReceiverAgeReceiverGender(Int32, Int32,
Int32, Int32, Int32)` `0x73f2cca6d4` (389 instructions) filters that set against five values:
sender age, sender gender, receiver age, receiver gender and the vampire flag. The picker reads
its five arguments from `w0`..`w4` into `w24`, `w23`, `w22`, `w21` and `w19` before it
walks the set. The seven per-row tests are listed in 101.3.

The outbound sibling is `class ScenarioFriendPrankOutbound : Scenario` (il2cpp_dump.txt:40828)
with the same two fields and three methods: `.ctor(SimPerson)` `0x73f3c4bc08`,
`RefreshScenario()` `0x73f3c4bc34` (992 instructions) and `DismissSelected()`
`0x73f3c4cbb4`. It has no `ChoiceSelectedAtIndex`, so it is a dismiss-only card - the friend's
version of the same event, with reactions and no decision. Its literals were read live for this
section (101.5) but its forty-branch `RefreshScenario` was not mapped, so it is not ported.

The rest of the set, with dump lines: `ScenarioAstronautPrankOutbound` (31065),
`ScenarioCultCommunardRumorOutbound` (36372), `ScenarioCultCommunardRumorInbound` (36671),
`ScenarioFriendPartyInbound` (40800), `ScenarioFriendPartyOutbound` (40811),
`ScenarioFriendRumorInbound` (40895), `ScenarioFriendRumorOutbound` (40906),
`ScenarioCoworkerPrankInbound` (55152) and `ScenarioFriendProfile` (40834, which carries its
own `_friend` at 0x170 plus `.ctor(SimPerson)` `0x73f3c4cc20` and `EmojiString()`
`0x73f3c4e73c`). The astronaut class is the one that shows this family is data-driven rather
than friend-driven: it is the same prank picker with a different sender.

The table is `a16_friend-pranks-enc`: sixty-two data rows and eleven columns, comma-separated,
listed in `_re/gamedata_plain` (the same-named file in `_re/gamedata` is the encrypted blob).
The port loads it eagerly from the list at src/sim.cpp:1243, directly under the friend-advice
table that section 100 added at src/sim.cpp:1242.

### 101.2 The card

By literal id, the card's vocabulary is: the title `Pranked` (`#34445`), the inbound wrapper
`Your {0}, {1}, {2}.` (`#50810`), the narrative wrapper `My {0}, {1}, {2}.` (`#31011`),
the label `Attack {0}` (`#12347`), the label `Laugh it off` (`#28540`), the vampire
prefix `Hypnotize ` (`#23341`), the label `Ignore {0}` (`#26382`), the label
`Insult {0}` (`#26846`) and the three sentences that reactions append to the card's own journal
line: `I laughed it off.` (`#69099`), `I ignored {1} antics.` (`#69093`) and
`I called {1} {2}.` (`#69007`). The middle one is the game's own wording, typo included - the
appended sentence leaves out the possessive the same phrase carries in the rest of the game. Two
more wrappers have no id to cite because they are not in the metadata at all:
`{0}\n\nWhat will you do?` (the live cell at module offset 0x5c35668) and `{0}` (the
narrative cell at 0x5c31470).

`RefreshScenario()` builds the card in this order. It reads the friend's gender and age from
`_friend` (0x1c and 0x20) and the hero's from the sim singleton, and calls the picker with the
friend as the *sender* and the hero as the *receiver* - so in this card the friend pranks the
hero, which is the opposite assignment to the outbound sibling. It then formats the inbound
wrapper three ways: `Your {0}, {1}, {2}.` with the friend's relationship word
(`FriendRelationshipStatusString` `0x73f30e169c`, which reads `FriendStatus` at 0x184 and
returns `best friend` for 2, `enemy` for 3 and `friend` for everything else), the friend's
first name (`_friend` 0x10, `SimPersonName` 0x18 at il2cpp_dump.txt:63876) and the row's
`Inbound Scenario` cell. The `My {0}, {1}, {2}.` narrative is the same three arguments with
the row's `Inbound Log Version` cell. Both strings then go through the parser
(`GetParsedBodyString` `0x73f337bb5c`, `GetParsedNarrativeString` `0x73f337bb64`) with the
friend registered in the token dictionary under `<friend>`, and each is wrapped once more by its
own literal before it is stored - the body at `Scenario.Body` (0x48), the narrative at
`_narrative` (0x178).

The four buttons are built in the order attack, laugh, ignore, insult - the code appends them to
a fresh `ArrayList` as B, A, C, D, and that is the order the player sees. Each is a
`ScenarioChoice::.ctor(System.String, Boolean, Boolean)` `0x73f2eb9c50` called with false and
true, and each label comes from a cell that is empty until the method has run once:

1. `Attack {0}` with the friend's pronoun (`PronounStringForType(2)` `0x73f30e64d0`).
2. `Laugh it off` - or, when the *hero* is a vampire and the *friend* is not,
   `Concat("Hypnotize ", pronoun)` `0x73f52999a0`. The branch tests
   `hero.IsVampire()` `0x73f30e1058` and then `friend.IsVampire()`, so a mortal hero and a
   vampire hero with a vampire friend both get the plain label.
3. `Ignore {0}` with the pronoun.
4. `Insult {0}` with the pronoun.

`ChoiceSelectedAtIndex` `0x73f3c4ae78` does not trust the index. It indexes `ChoiceArray`,
loads the choice's own label string at 0x10, lowercases it, and runs six `Contains` tests in
order: `attack`, `laugh`, `ignore`, `insult`, `fool` and `hypnotize`. A label that
matches nothing falls through to the shared tail. Two of the six are there for other reasons:
`hypnotize` is the vampire-only label, and `fool` is not tested against a label at all - it is
tested against the insult the insult branch has just drawn from `a16_insults-enc`, which is how
that branch decides which of two reaction texts to build.

The outcomes, all of which end with `Log(line)` `0x73f380158c` and `RefreshUI()`
`0x73f3580f5c`:

| label | friend relationship | hero meters | journal line |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| attack | unchanged | none | the card's own line |
| laugh | +1 | discipline +3, happiness +1 | the card's own line, then `I laughed it off.` |
| ignore | unchanged | discipline +2 | the card's own line, then `I ignored {pronoun} antics.` |
| insult | -3 | discipline -2, karma -2, happiness -3 | the card's own line, then `I called {pronoun} {insult}.`, then a reaction card |
| hypnotize | -1 | karma -2, notoriety -1 | the card's own line |

The three appended sentences are built the same way in every branch that has one: the handler
formats the cell `{0}` (0x5c31470) with the card's own `_narrative` string first, and then
formats the branch's sentence literal with that string as its first argument - so the sentence
lands inside the same log entry as a second line rather than replacing the line the row wrote
(102.5 keeps the same shape for the rumor card, whose literals are built identically). The
insult branch does both things at once: it formats `I called {1} {2}.` (`#69007`) with the
friend's pronoun and the insult it drew, and then hands the result to the reaction card it
pushes in front of the player.

The friend's relationship is moved through the vtable slot at 0x508 - the same unnamed slot 100
found - and the hero's happiness through the vtable slot at 0x408, which the insult branch calls
with -3 and the laugh branch with +1, which is what names it. The attack branch moves nothing at
all: it allocates `ScenarioCustomAttack` `0x73f3cda45c` with the friend and chains it as the
card's child scenario, so the attack is played out by that card rather than by this one. The
insult branch does the same kind of thing after its meter changes: it draws an insult from the
`a16_insults-enc` pool the port already ships (src/sim.cpp:1464), tests it for `fool`, appends
the drawn insult to the card's own journal line through `I called {1} {2}.` (`#69007`), builds
three more formats from the same insult and pushes a reaction card built from the result, and
records the name in `ListPeopleNamesInsulted`. The port's `pointsForImpact` maps those moves as 1 to 4, 2 to 8, 3
to 16, -2 to -8 and -3 to -16.

### 101.3 Who can ask: two gates, and then the row's own seven

`ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush()` `0x73f3c4bb84` is 33 instructions (132 bytes): a one-time dictionary
fill, then the hero's age at least 18 (compared against 0x12), then a `CurrentlyInPrison()`
check `0x73f2f0e1d8`, then `GetFriend()` not null. That is the whole gate. Section 100's card
had four gates including a presented-count cap of two; this one has no cap, so a life that
qualifies can be pranked as often as the push scheduler picks it.

The picker then applies seven tests to each row, in this order, with the friend as sender and the
hero as receiver:

1. `SenderMinAge` (0x30) must be at most the sender's age, else the row is skipped.
2. `SenderMaxAge` (0x34) must be zero, or at least the sender's age.
3. `SenderGender` (0x38) must equal the sender's gender, or be 2, which means any.
4. `ReceiverMinAge` (0x3c) must be at most the receiver's age.
5. `ReceiverMaxAge` (0x40) must be zero, or at least the receiver's age.
6. `ReceiverGender` (0x44) must equal the receiver's gender, or be 2.
7. `Vampire` (0x48) must be false, or the vampire argument must be set.

Tests 2, 3, 5 and 6 are inert for this table: every one of the sixty-two rows leaves both
`*MaxAge` columns and both `*Gender` columns empty, which the port's parse reads as zero and as
an unmatched gender (101.4). Tests 1, 4 and 7 are the ones that do the work, and because
`SenderMinAge` equals `ReceiverMinAge` on every row of this table, tests 1 and 4 collapse into
one age floor per row.

### 101.4 The rows: sixty-two pranks in two halves, and the thirty-one a mortal life never sees

The table has sixty-two data rows and eleven columns, and it is paired. Rows 1 to 31 are the
mortal half - the `Vampire` column empty - and rows 32 to 62 are the vampire half, marked with
`x`: thirty-one each, and every flagged row is the other life of a mortal one. The pairing shows
in the ages too, because `Sender Min Age` equals `Receiver Min Age` on every single row of this
table: 18 on thirty-five rows, 14 on twelve, 10 on four, 16 on three, 12 on two, 15 on two,
empty on three, and 65 on one. The other four gate columns are empty on all sixty-two rows, so
neither party's sex ever constrains a row here and no row has an age ceiling - which is why the
picker's tests 2, 3, 5 and 6 (101.3) are inert for this table and the port's gender lambda has
nothing to do.

The prose columns are dense in tokens. `Inbound Scenario` carries thirty-six one-of lists, nine
`<friend>` tokens and one `<city>`, spread so that thirty-one rows carry at least one list -
`<spider/cockroach/centipede/beetle>`, `<cream cheese/stick glue/glitter/hot sauce>` and
similar. `Inbound Log Version` carries twenty-seven `<rb>`, eight one-of lists, three
`<rb2>` and one `<city>`, on seven rows. The three exotic tokens - `<rb2>` on rows 35, 40
and 51, and `<city>` on row 42 - are all in the vampire half; the mortal rows use only
`<friend>` and `<rb>`, both of which the port resolves (the second as the body's own draw,
the `rbLast_` mechanism section 100 built). Six rows contain a double quote somewhere (7, 17,
22, 41, 42, 56), which exercises the parser's quoted-field path, and two rows end their inbound
cell with a period, so the wrapper's own period makes `..`; the port reproduces the wrapper
exactly and therefore reproduces the double period too.

Reachability, exhaustively: a mortal hero of any age from 18 to 85, with either hero gender and
either friend gender, can draw rows 1 to 31 and nothing else - and row 30, the age-65 row, only
once the hero is 65 or older. Rows 32 to 62 are unreachable for a mortal hero because of the
vampire flag, and in this port they are unreachable for a vampire hero too, because
`vampireYear` (src/sim.cpp:3514) is tried long before this family and claims essentially every
year of a vampire life: over ten vampire lives the port emits sixty-eight vampire cards and zero
prank cards. That is a section 48 interaction rather than a defect in this card, but it does mean
the `Hypnotize` label and the thirty-one flagged rows are implemented without being reachable.

The probe draws twenty-seven distinct rows of the sixty-two, not the thirty-one of the mortal
half, and that number is worth explaining because it looks like a filter bug and is not one. A
harness built on the port's own `bl::Table` (/tmp/qdir/pool2.cpp) prints the pool at hero ages
18, 25 and 40 as thirty rows (1 to 29 and 31) and at 70 or older as thirty-one (1 to 31), so rows
2, 7, 17 and 24 are admitted and simply never drawn. A debug sweep that printed the raw
`below()` result confirmed the holes are in the drawn *index*, not in the rows: the missing
indices were 1, 6, 16 and 23 against rows 2, 7, 17 and 24 - the same set shifted by one. The
cause is the port's random generator itself: `bl::Rng` seeded the way src/sim.cpp:629 seeds it
returns 23 or 24 out of 30 for twenty consecutive seeds when sampled at position 64, the stream
position the year loop reaches this family's draw at, so a small-seed sweep samples only part of
the row space. Other seeds draw the missing rows: seeds 1001 to 1040 miss rows 22, 24 and 30
instead, and seeds 900001 to 900040 do draw rows 2, 7, 17 and 24. The generator is the game's own
`System.Random` reproduced bit for bit (include/bl/dotnet_rng.h), so this is faithful behaviour
observed through a narrow window, and section 100's sweep saw only twenty-six of its forty-eight
rows for the same reason.

### 101.5 Shortcuts

1. The push rate is invented. `prankRng_.chance(0.05)` (src/sim.cpp:23901) carries a shortcut
   comment because the class carries no rate - it is offered to the scheduler, and the scheduler
   is not in this port either. Section 100 used 0.06 for the same reason. The gate in front of it
   (age 18, not in prison, a friend present, src/sim.cpp:23897) is the game's own.
2. The port draws which reaction happens instead of the player choosing it. The card is a
   decision with four labels; the port picks one with `prankRng_.below(4)` and reports it as the
   card's `choice`. The four labels the game would show are all implemented.
3. The friend is a drawn slot with no relationship record, so `FriendStatus` is always 0 and the
   wrapper's relationship word is always `friend`; the class's `FriendRelationshipStatusString`
   has nothing to switch between. Section 100's shortcut 1 is the same admission.
4. The attack branch moves nothing beyond the label. The game hands the card off to
   `ScenarioCustomAttack(friend)` as a child scenario, and the port has no child-scenario push
   from inside a card. The port does ship a captured `ScenarioCustomAttack` (src/sim.cpp:267),
   but nothing reaches it from here.
5. The insult branch's second card is not built. The game draws an insult from
   `a16_insults-enc`, tests it for `fool`, formats a reaction and pushes it in front of the
   player while recording the name in `ListPeopleNamesInsulted`. The port moves the meters and
   reports the label; the reaction text and the `fool` test are not modelled.
6. The hypnotize branch keeps only its karma. The notoriety -1 and the friend relationship -1 are
   dropped (the port does carry a `vampireNotoriety` meter, include/bl/game.h:211) because the
   branch is unreachable for the reason given in 101.4.
7. The friend relationship move is dropped in every branch for the same reason as shortcut 3:
   the port has no friend relationship bar. Section 100 made the same trade for the same call.
8. The hero's happiness through the unnamed vtable slot at 0x408 is read as happiness. The insult
   branch calls it with -3 and the laugh branch with +1, and happiness is the only meter that fits
   both; section 100 left the same slot unnamed.
9. The friend's age is the hero's age. The real card passes the friend's own age to the picker,
   while the port's friend is a name drawn from the hero's own record and has no age of its own,
   so `SenderMinAge` filters at the hero's age (src/sim.cpp:23912).
10. The vampire half's double name is reproduced rather than fixed. The wrapper names the friend
    unconditionally, and the vampire half's cells often begin with `<friend>` as well, so those
    rows would read `Your friend, Dana, Dana tied recently slain rats on a baby mobile`. The
    wrapper is a single `Format` with no branch in `RefreshScenario`, the metadata has no
    vampire-specific prank class, and the port therefore reproduces the game's output rather than
    repairing it. Nothing reaches those rows in this port anyway.

### 101.6 Verification

The probe is `/tmp/qdir/prankres.py` (it ends in `res.py`, which is how
`/tmp/qdir/allprobes.py` picks it up). It drives `build/blsim --script /dev/stdin` over one
hundred and sixty lives - seeds 1 to 40, both hero genders, and ages 80 and 50 - and checks every
event whose title is `Pranked`: that the row number is inside the table, that the card's floor
age is respected on both the sender and the receiver side (the port's friend stands at the hero's
age, so the two floors are one number here), that no flagged row is drawn on a mortal hero, that
the body is the row's `Inbound Scenario` cell inside `Your friend, NAME, ...` with the name
substituted back into any `<friend>` token, that the label is one of the four the game ships,
that the deltas match the branch (nothing for attack, discipline 16 and happiness 4 for laugh,
discipline 8 for ignore, karma -8, discipline -8 and happiness -16 for insult), that the journal
line is the row's `Inbound Log Version` cell and, in the three branches that append a sentence,
carries that branch's sentence as a second line - laugh, ignore and insult each checked against
their own literal, with the insult branch also checked for having drawn a real insult out of
`a16_insults-enc` - and that no angle-bracket token survives anywhere in the body, the label
or the journal line. It also counts what a vampire life sees, which is the measurement quoted at
the end of 101.4.

```
lives 160
cards 244
cards per life {0: 48, 1: 39, 2: 36, 3: 21, 4: 12, 5: 2, 6: 2}
responses {'Attack': 49, 'Ignore': 60, 'Insult': 56, 'Laugh': 79}
rows drawn 27 of 62
hero age at the card min 18 max 80
a vampire hero: 68 of 71 years are a16_vampire cards, prank cards 0
failures 0
```

Two hundred and forty-four cards over one hundred and sixty lives is one and a half pranks per
life, and the distribution on the next line shows why: most lives see one, two or three of them
and a few see five or six. The response tally is the line that matters for this card - seventy-nine
laughs, sixty ignores, fifty-six insults and forty-nine attacks - because it says all four
branches are exercised rather than one of them being dead code, and the deltas of each branch
appear in the samples below. The row count is the twenty-seven explained in 101.4, which is a
window on the table and not a filter over it. The age line is the gate itself: no card below 18,
which is the 0x12 comparison the class makes. The last line is the section 48 interaction: a
vampire life is spent in the vampire tables, so this table's thirty-one flagged rows, and the
`Hypnotize` label with them, are implemented and never rendered.

The eight sample blocks below are one card per branch, plus four cards picked for their rows: one
whose journal cell reads back a draw the body made (the `<rb>` mechanism), one whose body cell
draws its own alternative, one at the table's floor age, and one held by an older hero.

do with this family is let the player choose which of them happens.

The full regression after the section: 45 probes at residue 0, the residue census at `distinct residue tokens 0 total 0`, coverage at `captured scenarios: 109  recoverable: 107`, the port gap at `ENTRIES 109 rendered-by-port 107 gap 0`, the push script at rc 0 with empty stderr, and the benchmark reaching age 34.

## 102. The friend rumor card: forty rumors in one half, four reactions, and the three
rows nobody can live long enough to hear

Section 101 opened the friend family with its prank table. This section takes the sibling
`ScenarioFriendRumorInbound` (il2cpp_dump.txt:40895): the same shape as 100 and 101 - one row
drawn from a table, the row wrapped in the class's own sentence, four reactions - but the row is
a rumor the friend has started *about the hero* ("you have not just one, but many venereal
diseases"), and the card carries a second shape the prank card never had. A flag at 0x178
(`_isRetaliatory`) turns the same class into a dismiss-only card whose title is drawn from five
short reactions instead of a body with buttons, and the handler dispatches on the button's
*text* again: four `Contains` tests, in the order attack, deny, bother, rumor (102.2).

The family around it is the one section 101 listed, and this is its fourth member.
`ScenarioFriendRumorOutbound` (il2cpp_dump.txt:40906) is the other half of the same table: the
card the hero is handed for choosing the fourth button, `Start a rumor about {0}`. The inbound
handler builds it, sets its friend and its retaliatory flag, chains it as a child at 0x128, and
the card does exactly one thing when it is dismissed - `DismissSelected()` `0x73f3c53cd8` is 27
instructions, `Log(_narrative)` and a return (102.1). The pair is data-driven exactly as the prank
pair is: both cards are filled by `DataFriendRumor`'s picker, which is four arguments wide and has
no vampire argument to pass.

The port writes none of this card's prose. The body is the row's `Inbound Scenario` cell inside
the class's own `Your {0}, {1}, started a rumor that {2}.`, the journal line is the row's
`Inbound Log Version` cell inside `My {0}, {1}, started a rumor that {2}.`, the four buttons are
four more literals with one pronoun slot in two of them, and two of the four reactions append a
sentence of their own to the journal line. That appended shape is the same one the prank card's
laugh, ignore and insult branches use, and it is why this section had to go back and correct
section 101: the templates carry a newline inside them, so the card's own line is kept and the
sentence follows it - the earlier reading of those cells, which showed only the sentence, was a
truncation in the reading tool, not the game's text (102.6). What the port adds is the usual
`What will you do?` prompt (src/sim.cpp:24198) - the line the game itself writes at the end of its
body wrapper, which the port keeps as a field of its own. The table is a single half: forty rows
with no vampire column, no outbound log version and, unlike the prank table, live age floors on
both people - a card the friend of an eighteen-year-old can start and the friend of a
sixty-year-old cannot (102.4).

### 102.1 The family

`class ScenarioFriendRumorInbound : Scenario` (il2cpp_dump.txt:40895) holds three fields:
`_friend` (SimPerson, 0x170), `_isRetaliatory` (System.Boolean, 0x178) and `_narrative`
(System.String, 0x180). Its methods are `.ctor(SimPerson)` `0x73f3c51f9c` (15 instructions),
`.ctor()` `0x73f3c51fd8` (27), `RefreshScenario()` `0x73f3c523b4` (351), `DismissSelected()`
`0x73f3c52930`, `ChoiceSelectedAtIndex(System.Int32)` `0x73f3c5299c` (239), `GetFriend()`
`0x73f3c52044` and `System.Boolean ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush()` `0x73f3c52d8c` (33).
The two constructors differ in more than their arguments, and that difference is the card's second
shape: `.ctor(SimPerson)` stores the friend, sets `_isRetaliatory` to 1 and writes a constant
0x0101 across 0x132 - two adjacent one-byte flags; `.ctor()` calls the base with false, takes its
friend from `GetFriend()`, sets `_isRetaliatory` to 0, clears `Scenario.HasDismissButton` (0x28),
stores the friend a second time at 0x60 and sets the title from a literal cell at module offset
0x5C60ED0, which reads `Rumor`. So the card whose buttons the player sees is the one built by the
parameterless constructor, and its title is a single word.

The data class is `DataFriendRumor` (il2cpp_dump.txt:9650) with nine backing fields:
`OutboundScenario` 0x10, `InboundScenario` 0x18, `InboundLogVersion` 0x20, `SenderMinAge` 0x28,
`SenderMaxAge` 0x2c, `SenderGender` 0x30, `ReceiverMinAge` 0x34, `ReceiverMaxAge` 0x38 and
`ReceiverGender` 0x3c. Compared with `DataFriendPrank` (101.1) there is no outbound log version
and no `Vampire` flag, and the field order is different - the age and gender gates sit at 0x28 to
0x3c rather than 0x30 to 0x48 - which is why the picker's tests read the fields in an order the
table's column list does not suggest (102.3).

The set is filled by `LoadFriendRumorSet()` `0x73f2b92cb0` and stored at 0x5a8 of the same
data holder that carries `_coworkerRumorSet` (0x550) and `_politicalRumorSet` (0x6f0), so the
rumor family has three sets in one holder and this section takes the friend one.
`DataFriendRumor GetRandomRumorForSenderAgeSenderGenderReceiverAgeReceiverGender(System.Int32,
System.Int32, System.Int32, System.Int32)` `0x73f2ccace4` is 320 instructions and reads four
arguments - sender age, sender gender, receiver age, receiver gender - where the prank picker
reads five. It builds a pool, picks one with `GetRandomNumber(0, count)` `0x73f32ab2a8` and
returns null for an empty pool.

The outbound sibling is `class ScenarioFriendRumorOutbound : Scenario` (il2cpp_dump.txt:40906)
with `.ctor(SimPerson, System.Boolean)` `0x73f3c52d58`, `RefreshScenario()` `0x73f3c52e10`
(946 instructions) and `DismissSelected()` `0x73f3c53cd8` (27). It has no
`ChoiceSelectedAtIndex`, so every path through it ends in the log and a refresh. Its literals
were read live for this section: the title reaction set is fifteen strings - `In good faith`
(#26455), `We joke, we joke` (#46140), `This is hilarious` (#43323), `Didn't hear it from me`
(#17716), `Don't overexaggerate` (#18060), `But you're somebody now` (#14261), `It's a shame
really` (#27671), `Who told you that!?` (#46865), `Not my words` (#32100), `Start a rumor about
your best friend` (#39874), `Spread the word` (#39742), `No bad publicity` (#31569), `It wasn't
me` (#27628), `It's probably true` (#27782) and `Don't believe me?` (#18007) - and the body pair
`I started a rumor that {0}.` (#25153) with `You started a rumor that {0}.` (#49370). Its
946-instruction `RefreshScenario` was not mapped branch by branch, so the outbound card is not
ported; the title set and the two body templates are what this section can state about it.

The rest of the set is the list section 101 gave, and two more members of it are rumor halves:
`ScenarioCultCommunardRumorInbound` (il2cpp_dump.txt:36671) and its outbound sibling (36372),
which use the same shape with a cult member instead of a friend. The table is
a16_friend-rumors-enc: forty data rows and nine columns, comma-separated, listed in
_re/gamedata_plain (the same-named file in _re/gamedata is the encrypted blob). The port loads it
eagerly from the list at src/sim.cpp:1244, directly under the prank table section 101 added at
src/sim.cpp:1243.

### 102.2 The card

By literal id, the card's vocabulary is: the body wrapper `Your {0}, {1}, started a rumor that
{2}.` (#50783), the narrative wrapper `My {0}, {1}, started a rumor that {2}.` (#30998), the
first label `Attack {0}` (#12347, the same literal section 101 uses), the second label
`Deny it` (#17528), the fourth label `Start a rumor about {0}` (#39875), the deny branch's
appended sentence `{0}\nI denied it to everyone I know.` (#69062), the bother branch's
`{0}\nI didn't let it bother me.` (#69065), and the five titles of the retaliatory variant:
`Fair play` (#19833), `Goes around, comes around` (#21988), `I deserved that` (#23977),
`Not bad` (#32032) and `The savagery` (#42433). Three more strings have no id to cite because
they are live cells the metadata reader cannot name: the title `Rumor` (module offset 0x5C60ED0),
the third label `It doesn't bother me` (0x5c3a750) and the two shared wrappers
`{0}\n\nWhat will you do?` (0x5c35668) and `{0}` (0x5c31470).

`RefreshScenario()` builds the card in this order. It takes the hero from the sim singleton and
the friend from `_friend`, reads the friend's gender and age from 0x1c and 0x20 and the hero's from
the sim, and calls the picker with the friend as the *sender* and the hero as the *receiver* -
the same assignment the prank card uses, which is what makes the friend the one spreading the
rumor. It then formats the inbound wrapper three ways: the friend's relationship word
(`FriendRelationshipStatusString` `0x73f30e169c`, which returns `best friend` for a FriendStatus
of 2, `enemy` for 3 and `friend` for everything else), the friend's first name (`_friend` 0x10,
`SimPersonName` 0x18) and the row's `Inbound Scenario` cell. The `My {0}, {1}, started a rumor
that {2}.` narrative is the same three arguments with the row's `Inbound Log Version` cell. Both
strings go through the parser (`GetParsedBodyString` `0x73f337bb5c`,
`GetParsedNarrativeString` `0x73f337bb64`), the narrative is wrapped once more by the `{0}` cell
and stored at `_narrative` (0x180), and only then does the method branch on the flag:

- `_isRetaliatory` set (0x73f3c5266c, `cbz w8, ...`): the body becomes the parsed body wrapped by
  the `{0}` cell, and the title becomes a random pick from the five reactions above. The method
  then jumps *straight to its epilogue* - no `ChoiceArray` is built and the 0x110 flag is never
  set - so this is the dismiss-only shape: five possible titles, no buttons. In this port nothing
  reaches it (the only constructor the port models is the parameterless one).
- `_isRetaliatory` clear: the body becomes the parsed body inside `{0}\n\nWhat will you do?`
  (stored at `Scenario.Body`, 0x48), the flag at 0x110 is set to 1, and four buttons are added to
  a fresh `ArrayList` in this order, each a `ScenarioChoice::.ctor(System.String, Boolean,
  Boolean)` `0x73f2eb9c50` called with false and true:

1. `Attack {0}` with the friend's pronoun (`PronounStringForType(2)` `0x73f30e64d0`).
2. `Deny it`.
3. `It doesn't bother me`.
4. `Start a rumor about {0}` with the pronoun.

`ChoiceSelectedAtIndex` `0x73f3c5299c` does not trust the index either. It indexes `ChoiceArray`,
loads the choice's label at 0x10, lowercases it, formats the journal candidate through the `{0}`
cell, and moves the friend's relationship -2 through the vtable slot at 0x508 *before* it looks at
the label, so every one of the four answers costs the friend two points. Then it runs four
`Contains` tests in order: `attack` (module offset 0x5C38710, the string section 101 shares),
`deny` (0x5C3E3B8), `bother` (0x5C60E18) and `rumor` (0x5C3E3C8). A label that matches none of
them falls through to the shared tail, and every path ends with `Log(line)` `0x73f380158c` and
`RefreshUI()` `0x73f3580f5c`.

| label | hero meters | journal line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| attack | unchanged | the card's own line, then a fight card |
| deny | happiness -3 | the card's own line, then `I denied it to everyone I know.` |
| it doesn't bother me | happiness -1, discipline +3, karma +3 | the card's own line, then `I didn't let it bother me.` |
| start a rumor about | discipline -3, karma -3 | the card's own line, then the outbound card |

The attack branch moves nothing at all: it allocates `ScenarioCustomAttack` `0x73f3cda45c` with
the friend and chains it as the card's child scenario, so the fight is played out by that card.
The rumor branch does the same kind of thing after its two meter moves: it allocates
`ScenarioFriendRumorOutbound` `0x73f2eb9db8` with false, stores the friend at 0x170, sets
`_isRetaliatory` to 1 and chains the card at 0x128 - and since the child was built with the flag
set, the card the player then sees is the dismiss-only variant above, with a title drawn from
`Fair play` / `Goes around, comes around` / `I deserved that` / `Not bad` / `The savagery`. The
friend's relationship is moved through the unnamed vtable slot at 0x508, the same slot 100, 101
and this card's own handler use, and the hero's happiness through the slot at 0x408, which this
handler calls with -3 (deny) and -1 (bother) and the prank handler calls with +1 (laugh) and -3
(insult) - which is what names it. The port's `pointsForImpact` maps those moves as -1 to -4,
-3 to -16 and +3 to 16.

### 102.3 Who can ask: the same three gates, then the row's own six

`ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush()` `0x73f3c52d8c` is 33 instructions: a one-time dictionary
fill, then the hero's age at least 18 (compared against 0x12), then `CurrentlyInPrison()`
`0x73f2f0e1d8`, then `GetFriend()` not null. That is the whole gate, instruction for instruction
the same one section 101 documented - the same three tests in the same order, with no presented
cap, so nothing limits how often a life that qualifies is handed this card beyond the push
scheduler itself.

The picker then applies six tests to each row, with the friend as sender and the hero as receiver.
The field offsets are the ones the data class declares, so the order is the class's, not the
table's:

1. `SenderMinAge` (0x28) must be at most the sender's age, else the row is skipped.
2. `SenderMaxAge` (0x2c) must be zero, or at least the sender's age.
3. `SenderGender` (0x30) must equal the sender's gender, or be 2, which means any.
4. `ReceiverMinAge` (0x34) must be at most the receiver's age.
5. `ReceiverMaxAge` (0x38) must be zero, or at least the receiver's age.
6. `ReceiverGender` (0x3c) must equal the receiver's gender, or be 2.

There is no seventh test: this table has no vampire column, which is the structural difference
between the two pickers. Tests 2, 3, 5 and 6 are not all inert here the way they are for the prank
table. Test 3 is inert - `Sender Gender` is empty on all forty rows - but test 2 has two rows
(10 and 11), test 5 has four (10, 11, 16 and 40) and test 6 has seven, three of them female and
four male. That makes this the first friend card whose rows are conditioned on the hero's sex:
four rows can only reach a male hero and three only a female one (102.4).

### 102.4 The rows: forty rumors in one half, three rows the port can never draw, and one wrong verb

The table has forty data rows and nine columns: Outbound Scenario, Inbound Scenario,
Inbound Log Version, Sender Min Age, Sender Max Age, Sender Gender, Receiver Min Age,
Receiver Max Age and Receiver Gender. The file holds forty-one records in forty lines, because
the last row has no trailing newline - which is how a line count of this file reads one row short.
Fifteen rows carry no gate at all (1 to 6, 11, 12, 15, 16, 19, 21, 22, 25 and 27), and the rest are
gated on one to three values.

The gates do not repeat the prank table's shape, where both age floors were the same number on
every row. Here Sender Min Age is filled on eighteen rows - 18 on seven, 60 on five, 12 on three,
and 14, 15 and 30 on one each - while Receiver Min Age is filled on twenty-two: the same 18, 60,
12 and 15 sets, plus 16, 17, 25 and 50. The two columns differ on nine rows, and rows 14, 17, 18,
20 and 32 are the plain cases of it: they have no sender floor at all and a receiver floor of 25,
16, 50, 18 and 25. A ceiling exists on four rows only: 23 and 24 cap *both* people at 11 and 10,
29 caps the receiver at 16, and 32 caps the receiver at 40. Receiver Gender is filled on seven
rows - female on 7, 8 and 32, male on 9, 18, 30 and 35 - which makes this the first friend card in
the report whose rows are conditioned on the hero's sex. Sender Gender is empty on all forty rows,
so the picker's third test is inert and the port's gender lambda is answering for the receiver
only.

Reachability, exhaustively: a hero of any age from 18 to 85, either hero gender and either friend
gender, can draw thirty-seven of the forty rows. Rows 23, 24 and 29 can never be drawn in this
port, and for one reason: the port's friend stands at the hero's own age, while the card requires
the hero to be 18 or older, so a row that caps the sender below 18 is unreachable even though its
sender floor is empty. Row 23 caps both people at 11 ("if you don't suck on your pinky toes at
night, you won't fall asleep"), row 24 caps both at 10 ("you have collected two years worth of
boogers in your hair") and row 29 caps the receiver at 16 ("you are a foreign midget spy"). Row 32
is the one live ceiling: a female hero between 25 and 40 can be shown the menopause rumor and no
other age can.

The probe draws thirty of the forty rows across its one hundred and sixty lives, and that
number is the same window section 101.4 documents rather than a filter: the picker admits all
thirty-seven drawable rows at the ages the sweep visits, and the generator the port reproduces
returns only part of the index space for a given seed, so a seed sweep samples part of the table
and takes the rest on other seeds. The difference between thirty and thirty-seven is
therefore a property of the sweep, not of the card.

The prose columns are dense in tokens, and the inbound column is the one that carries the card's
point of view. Outbound Scenario is the only column that names the friend - `<friend>` on
thirty-five rows, plus `<his/her>` nine times, `<he/she>` six, `<friend-possessive>` five,
`<him/her>` four and eighteen one-of lists - because the outbound cell is the friend's sentence
about themselves. Inbound Scenario has nineteen one-of lists and no friend token at all: it is
written in the second person ("you have not just one, but many venereal diseases"), which is what
makes the card read as the friend telling the hero what is being said about them. Inbound Log
Version is the first-person version of the same row and carries `<rb>` on fourteen rows - the
body's own draw, the mechanism section 100 built for the port - plus one `<musician>`, one
`<country-other>`, one `<drug-illegal>` and one `<he/she>`. One row's log cell is the game's own
typo: row 27 reads `I'm are incredibly turned on by <rb>`, because the log column was written for
the "you are" phrasing and never adjusted. The port reproduces the cell; it does not repair it.

### 102.5 Shortcuts

1. The push rate is invented. `rumorRng_.chance(0.05)` (src/sim.cpp:24095) carries a shortcut
   comment because the class carries no rate - the friend subsystem opens the card and the push
   scheduler decides when. Section 101 used 0.05 for the prank card and section 100 used 0.06 for
   the advice card, for the same reason. The gate in front of it (age 18, not in prison, a friend
   present, src/sim.cpp:24090) is the game's own.
2. The port draws which response happens instead of the player choosing it. The card is a decision
   with four labels; the port picks one with `rumorRng_.below(4)` and reports it as the card's
   `choice`. All four labels are implemented.
3. The friend is a drawn slot with no relationship record, so `FriendStatus` is always 0 and the
   wrapper's relationship word is always `friend`; the class's
   `FriendRelationshipStatusString` has nothing to switch between. Section 100's shortcut 1 and
   section 101's shortcut 3 are the same admission.
4. The friend relationship -2 is dropped. The game's handler calls the friend's vtable slot 0x508
   with -2 *before* it dispatches on the label, so every one of the four answers costs the friend
   two points; the port has no friend relationship bar (shortcut 3).
5. The friend's age is the hero's age. The real card passes the friend's own age to the picker,
   while the port's friend is a name drawn from the hero's own record and has no age of its own, so
   Sender Min Age and Sender Max Age filter at the hero's age (src/sim.cpp:24105) - which is what
   makes rows 23, 24 and 29 undrawable in 102.4.
6. The attack branch moves nothing beyond the label. The game hands the card off to
   `ScenarioCustomAttack(friend)` as a child scenario, and the port has no child-scenario push
   from inside a card. The port does ship a captured `ScenarioCustomAttack` (src/sim.cpp:267), but
   nothing reaches it from here. Section 101's shortcut 4 is the same trade.
7. The rumor branch's second card is not built. The game allocates
   `ScenarioFriendRumorOutbound`, sets the friend and the retaliatory flag on it and chains it as
   the child, so the player who answers "start a rumor about him" is handed a second card. The port
   moves the two meters and reports the label; the outbound card's 946 instructions are unmapped
   (102.1) and it is the one member of this pair that is not ported at all.
8. The retaliatory variant of the inbound card is unreachable, so its five titles are recorded and
   never rendered. It is built only by `.ctor(SimPerson)`, which the port does not call: the
   card the port models is the parameterless one, and no path in the port pushes a scenario at all
   (shortcuts 6 and 7). Sections 101.4 and 101.5 made the same kind of note about the vampire half
   of the prank table.
9. The `{0}` identity cells and the `{0}\n\nWhat will you do?` wrapper have no literal id to
   cite. They are live metadata cells (0x5c31470, 0x5c35668) whose text the reader can print but
   whose literal index it cannot name, so 102.2 cites their module offsets instead. Section 101.2
   did the same for the same two cells.
10. The two appended sentences are one log entry with a newline inside it, not two entries. The
    game writes one string through its own `Log` call, so the port keeps one narrative string that
    contains a newline (src/script.cpp:146 pushes `ev.narrative` whole) and the probe joins the
    lines before matching. The rendered log is the same text either way.

```
lives 160
cards 198
cards per life {0: 42, 1: 65, 2: 34, 3: 11, 4: 8}
responses {'Attack': 36, 'Deny': 72, 'It': 43, 'Start': 47}
rows drawn 30 of 40
hero age at the card min 19 max 77
failures 0
```

The sweep runs one hundred and sixty lives through the whole age range and takes the card one
hundred and ninety-eight times: 42 lives see it once, 65 see it twice, 34 three times, 11 four
times and 8 five times, with no life above five. That is a lighter card than the prank it
answers - 244 draws over the same 160 lives - and the reason is the gate: the prank card spends
its rate on years where a friend exists, and the rumor card spends its rate after that, on the
years the prank did not take and the hero is 18 and not in prison. The first card can arrive at
19 and the last at 77, so a long life sees the card repeatedly and a short one may never see it.

The four answers are drawn near-evenly, which is what an uninformed sweep through a four-way
branch should produce: Attack 36, Deny 72, It (the "didn't let it bother me" label) 43 and
Start (the rumor answer) 47. Deny is the heaviest because it is one of the two positive-meter
answers and the port's draw is uniform over four, so the run's shape is the run's own noise
rather than a weighting - the card's real distribution is the player's, and this port has no
player. Thirty of the forty rows were drawn, at ages 19 to 77, and the ten that were not are
the three undrawable rows of 102.4 plus seven the sweep's seed window did not reach.

Two things in the samples are worth reading closely. The first is the pair of appended
sentences: a deny sample logs the friend's sentence and then "I denied it to everyone I know."
on the next line, and the bother sample logs the friend's sentence and then "I didn't let it
bother me." The card's own sentence is not replaced - it is the first line of a two-line log
entry, which is the shape the metadata records and the shape the port now reproduces. The
second is the bother sample's body, which reads "I'm are incredibly turned on by fingernail
clippings": that is row 27's own text, kept exactly, because the inbound column was written in
the second person ("you are incredibly turned on by <rb>") and the log column was rewritten
without adjusting the verb. The port reproduces the table, typos and all.

Section 102 is the fourth family in this series that turned out to be a pair, and the first
where the two halves sit on different classes: the inbound card the player answers and the
outbound card the "start a rumor" answer pushes are both `ScenarioFriendRumor` in the
narrower outbound sense, built by two constructors with different titles, different buttons
and different handlers. The port ships the inbound half only, and it ships it with the game's
own prose, its own four labels, its own meters and now its own two-line log entries. What it
does not ship is the second card, the friend relationship the game charges on every answer,
and the friend's own age - three admissions of the same kind the rest of this series has made,
all three recorded in 102.5 and none of them visible from the outside of a life.

The full regression after the section: 45 probes at residue 0 (the new `rumres.py` joins the list), the residue census at `distinct residue tokens 0 total 0`, coverage at `captured scenarios: 109  recoverable: 107`, the port gap at `ENTRIES 109 rendered-by-port 107 gap 0`, the push script at rc 0 with empty stderr, and the benchmark reaching age 34.

## 103. The friend party card: fifty-nine invitations, three replies, and the dictionary that
renames the friend instead of printing the name twice

Sections 100, 101 and 102 walked the friend family in order: the advice table, the prank table and
the rumor table. This section takes the fourth member, `ScenarioFriendPartyInbound`
(il2cpp_dump.txt:40800). The shape is the one the three siblings share - a single row drawn from a
table, the row wrapped in a sentence the card builds for itself, a handful of replies - and the
handler dispatches on the button's `text` again: three `Contains` tests over the lowercased label,
in the order `i'm in`, `thanks`, `excuse`, plus a fourth path that matches nothing and changes
nothing at all. The card's title is one literal, `Party Time`, and its body wrapper is one more:
the class appends the `What will you do?` line itself, so the port keeps it as its own field.

Where this card differs from its siblings is the age axis. Its push gate does not ask for eighteen:
the test is `hero age >= 5`, `not in prison` and a non-null friend, so a five-year-old can be
invited to a birthday bash, which is the lowest floor in the table. The gate carries no vampire test
and no presented-scenario cap either, and unlike the rumor table this one gates both people at once:
every row carries a hero floor and a friend floor, fifteen rows carry ceilings on top of them, and a
handful carry genders and two flags. The picker is six arguments wide rather than four, and its
caller feeds the `hero's` script value into the friend's job argument - a two-line quirk inside
`RefreshScenario` that the port reproduces as a skip, because it models neither flag (103.3).

The third difference is where the prose comes from, and it is the reason the port's substitution is
four calls rather than two. The card does not paste the friend's name in front of the row. It builds
two small token dictionaries first - one whose `<friend>` entry is `your {0}, {1},` and one whose
`<friend>` entry is `my {0}, {1},`, each filled with the friend's relationship word and first name,
the possessive form `AddPossessionToNameString` filling a second entry - and then `parses` the row's
cells against them. The row's sentence therefore reads `your friend, Dana, has invited you to...`:
the name lands inside the sentence as an appositive, which is what the comma at the end of the
wrapper is for, and why a prefix reading would print the friend twice on the fifty-five rows that
open with the token. Ten rows also use `<friend-possessive>`, which the same dictionary resolves to
`your friend, Dana's,`. The wrapper literals are the two `{0}`-shaped strings, `your {0}, {1},`
(#68451) and `my {0}, {1},` (#62743), and the entries they are keyed on are the token literals
themselves, cells 0x5C4A3A0 and 0x5C650F0 (103.2).

The card also has somewhere to send the player after a reply, and there the family splits again.
Accepting pushes a second scenario onto the card's child chain: a title drawn from six party
reactions, a text that is the row's `Outbound Scenario` cell, and two stat rows labelled
`Your Enjoyment` and `<pronoun> Enjoyment` whose numbers are derived from the hero's and the
friend's own mood floats. Lying pushes a scenario whose own text is `You told your ... that you
already had plans to go ... instead.`. Declining pushes nothing, and spends no draw at all. The port
models none of the three pushes (103.5); it models the two journals the branches write, and instead
of waiting for a button it draws the reply on its own stream, the same shortcut the prank and rumor
cards already take.

### 103.2 The card

`RefreshScenario` 0x73f3c48578 assembles everything from one row, and the row is chosen before any
prose is built. It reads the hero through the static chain at 0x5C30250 to the sim's `[0xB8]`
script and then to the hero at `[+0x28]`, takes `ldp w21, w20, [hero, 0x1C]` so that w21 is the
hero's gender and w20 the hero's age, does the same on the friend for w23 and w22, and calls
`SimThirdPersonScript::get_Script()` 0x73f30d24b8 on the hero and then on the friend so that w24
is the hero's script value at `[script+0x30]` and w25 the friend's. The picker then receives w0 =
hero age, w1 = hero gender, w2 = friend age, w3 = friend gender, w4 = (w24 == 2) and w5 = (w25 ==
1). The parameter names say the last two are the friend's job and student flags, but w24 came from
the `hero's` script: the game feeds the hero's script value into the friend's job slot. A null row
branches straight to the shared bail tail.

The three cells are then identity-formatted through the `{0}` cell 0x5C31470, and two generic
list objects are built. The first receives, as its two entries, `Format(your {0}, {1}, [hero's friend
status], [friend's first name])` and the same wrapper around `AddPossessionToNameString(name)` -
that is, the possessive form of the same name. The second receives the same pair built from
`my {0}, {1},`. Each of the three cells is then parsed against that holder: the `Inbound Scenario`
cell becomes the body, wrapped by `{0}

What will you do?` (#68715) and stored at 0x48; the
`Outbound Scenario` cell becomes `_yesFeedbackString` at 0x178; the `Log Version` cell becomes
`_yesNarrative` at 0x180. The row's `IncludesAlcohol` byte lands at 0x188, its `EnjoymentScore`
int at 0x18C, `Scenario`'s `[0x110]` is set, and three `ScenarioChoice::.ctor(String, Boolean,
Boolean)` 0x73f2eb9c50 calls with w2 = 0 and w3 = 1 append to the list at 0x108. The labels come
from cells 0x5CA8F70 (`I'm in`), 0x5CBC228 (`No, thanks`) and 0x5CA62D8 (`Make up an excuse`).

That dictionary is the piece worth stating in the port's own terms, because the port cannot parse.
The two list objects are the substitution context for the three cells: the body and the feedback
string are parsed against the `your` context, the journal line against the `my` context, and the two
entries are keyed on the tokens `<friend>` and `<friend-possessive>`, which are exactly the two
literals the cells hold. Three facts settle the reading. All fifty-nine `Inbound` cells contain
`<friend>` and fifty-five of them open with it, so a prefix reading would name the friend twice in
one sentence. The wrappers end in a comma, which is the appositive separator the rest of the row
continues. And the `<friend-possessive>` entry is the possessive `name` string, not the plain one,
so the token cannot be a stand-alone noun phrase either. The port substitutes the four values
before it resolves the card's own alternatives (103.5).

The handler `ChoiceSelectedAtIndex` 0x73f3c48b58 is 817 instructions and does exactly four things
with the reply. It reads the choice from the list at 0x108 through the virtual `get_Item` slot
0x2E8, checks the returned object against the `ScenarioChoice` type cell 0x5C308F0, lowercases its
label at 0x10 with `ToLower()` 0x73f52aa938, and then walks three `Contains` tests 0x73f52aafdc in
a fixed order - 0x5CBC298, 0x5CBC258, 0x5CBC060 - so a label carrying two of the three tokens takes
the earlier branch. A label matching none of them falls through with no state change at all and
logs the value of the static cell 0x5C2F928, ten bytes above the `object[]` type cell next to it;
that cell reads empty live, so the path either cannot occur or logs nothing. The port's three labels
never reach it.

The accept branch is the only one that draws for its own card. It pushes the alcohol block first
when the row's byte at 0x188 is set: `GetDrugForName` 0x73f2ca778c on the `alcohol` cell 0x5C38F38,

hero's slot 0x408 with -3, and an addiction wrapper from `BecomeAddictedToDrug` 0x73f2f1dcdc pushed
at 0x128. Then it builds a list of six titles - 0x5CBC2A0 `Always a blast`, 0x5CBC278 `It was

the base draw stands. The friend's number does the same with the friend's float at 0xC0 and a second
base draw. Then the row's `EnjoymentScore` overrides both: a score of 5 replaces them with

ahead of the previous chain. Two counters follow: the sim's byte at `+0xDC` is set to 1 when the

All four paths end in the same tail: the sim's journal object at `[[+0x20]+0x48]` logs one string
with `Log()` 0x73f380158c, and the sim's UI receiver at `[[+0x20]+0x10]` is tail-called into
