## 123. The morning after: the one card in the family the hero never chooses

### 123.1 A card that is pushed, not offered

Every card so far has answered a question the game asks the hero. This one is the
family's exception, and it is worth a section precisely because of it: whenever a
hookup choice resolves the way the hero wanted, the game pushes a second scenario
behind the first one, and that scenario has nothing to ask.

```
class ScenarioSupervisorSeduceSuccess : Scenario          il2cpp_dump.txt:55109
  _initiatedByHero    System.Boolean 0x16a
  _supervisor         SimCoworker    0x170
  _loverCandidate     SimLover       0x178
  .ctor(System.Boolean)   @0x73f2e27214
  RefreshScenario()       @0x73f2e27514
```

Two methods and no others. There is no `ChoiceSelectedAtIndex`, which is the real
finding: a scenario with no choice handler cannot move a stat when it is dismissed,
cannot write a journal line, and cannot open a second door. The class listing is
the whole proof that the card only reports.

The constructor does three things. It stores the flag, it takes the boss off the
hero's workplace (`SimWorkplace::GetSupervisor @0x73f2fe8db8`, the same call the
hookup card makes), and then it decides who the lover object is: if the boss
already carries a `SimLover` at `[supervisor+0x1d0]` whose age matches his own, that
object is reused; otherwise `SimLover::GenerateLoverFromCoworker @0x73f3812d6c`
makes a new one. That is the whole point of the follow-up: the hookup card is the
question, this card is the game committing the answer.

### 123.2 Nine titles and two sentences

`RefreshScenario` opens with the usual lazy static initialisation -- twenty-nine
string cells this time -- and then picks its title from a list the branch
assembles, through `PickRandomFromStringArray @0x73f32b0608`:

```
hero made the move (4)          the boss made the move (5)
  Chasing my bag       #15446     Nobody can know                #31896
  I'm the captain now  #26059     If we're on company time       #26346
  And about my pay...  #11401     Let's shoot for a promotion... #28825
  Let's play favorites #28820     Securing my position here      #38375
                                  I need lots of supervision     #24702
```

and the sentence underneath is one of two, both `Format` calls over the boss's
relationship word and his full name:

```
You seduced your {0}, {1}!          #49284   cell 0x5c60ba8
You let your {0}, {1}, seduce you!  #48933   cell 0x5c60b98
```

The relationship word is the same one section 118 proved is the role word for a
supervisor, so the two sentences read "You seduced your supervisor, Court Kurbain!"
and "You let your supervisor, Beyawnce Gnolls, seduce you!". Both are titles in
the interface and neither reaches the log: with no choice handler there is no
`Log` call behind them, and the port keeps that -- the port's card writes no
journal line at all, which makes it the only card in the corpus with an empty
narrative.

Three more panels are built into the same card. Two enjoyment bars are formatted
from two rolls (`{0} Enjoyment` #69502 with a 0..100 draw and a 0..21 draw offset
by 80), an obituary line is added as a colour string --

```
{0} was never able to shake the rumor that {1} once romped with {2} {3}.   #70396
```

-- and when the two sexes can make a baby, a pregnancy is created outright through
`GetResultingPregnancyForMotherAndFatherAndTypeAndAssignToMother @0x73f2fd4438`
and pushed as its own scenario. The card is, in other words, the game's one-stop
place to bury the consequences of the hookup: lover bookkeeping, a possible baby,
an obituary that a future death screen may quote.

### 123.3 What it does to the hero's love life

The bookkeeping is the part a port has to get right, because everything the game
says about the boss afterwards depends on it. `RefreshScenario` marks the scenario
as consumed (`strb 1,[self+0x132]`), and then, if the boss is not already an
ex-lover (`SimPerson::IsExLover @0x73f30d3d78`), it bumps a counter on the hero and
appends the lover candidate to `SimHero::get_ExLoverArray @0x73f2f22a70`. The old
lover becomes an ex -- with the workplace written into `[workplace+0x2c]` as the
hero's age at the time, the lover's `[0x224]` set to 5 and `[0x238]` to the hero's
age.

Then the bill. If the hero still had a lover when the card ran, the lane at
`0x73f2e27874` moves `ImpactKarma(-4)` and `ImpactDiscipline(-4)` and bumps the
hero's counter at `[0x208]`. That is the only stat change in the whole card, and it
is a cheating penalty, not a hookup reward: the boss was worth nothing to the
hero's numbers, and the partner he had was worth minus four of two of them.

Two pushes hang off the same state. `SimLover::IsExLoverHookup` and
`SimLover::IsCheating` (`@0x73f34779ec`, `@0x73f3477a20`) both feed
`CollectSetNext`, and there is a separate catch: if the hero had a lover, and a
`GetRandomNumber(0,150)` draw beats `100 - lover[0xc0]`, and the lover is not
`IsProbablyTheSameAsPerson` as the boss, a "caught cheating" scenario is pushed
(`.ctor(System.Int32) @0x73f3da31b8` with 0). A hero with a spotless reputation
`[0xc0]` is safe; a hero with a bad one gets walked in on.

### 123.4 How the port reaches it

The port cannot push a card. A year is one event, and the family dispatch returns
at the first card that fits, so a follow-up has to wait. The port therefore keeps
the name of the boss a hookup happened with and presents the morning after in the
next year that no earlier family claims:

| where | what |
|---|---|
| `port/include/bl/game.h:792` | `std::string morningWith;` -- the boss the card is about |
| `port/include/bl/game.h:793` | `bool morningByHero;` -- the `_initiatedByHero` byte, and so the title pool |
| `port/include/bl/game.h:794` | `bool morningPrevLover;` -- whether the hero already had a lover |
| `port/include/bl/sim.h:652` | `Rng mornRng_;` -- the card's own stream |
| `port/src/sim.cpp:641` | the seed, `seed ^ 0x3f84d5b5b5470917 ^ 0x9216d5d98979fb1b` |
| `port/src/sim.cpp:3638` | the wire, right after the hookup card's own |
| `port/src/sim.cpp:27004` | `bool Sim::morningYear` |
| `port/src/sim.cpp:26704` | the inbound lane records the boss (the hero went along) |
| `port/src/sim.cpp:26729` | the outbound success lane records him (the hero asked) |

The card itself is short. No gate beyond the pending name, the title from the
branch's pool, the sentence, and the cheating pair when a lover was already there.
It also does the one thing the game does that the port can honour cheaply: it
writes the boss into the hero's lover fields, which is what
`GenerateLoverFromCoworker` does in the game and what makes the next hookup's
cheating check and the existing lover cards see him.

Four sampled cards, drawn by `/tmp/qdir/succsample.py`:

```
seed 7  male   age 43   I'm the captain now
        You seduced your supervisor, Court Kurbain!
        (hookup at 42, outbound "Hook up with him", no lover, no stat move)
seed 12 female age 42   Securing my position here
        You let your supervisor, Harley YBY, seduce you!
        (hookup at 41, inbound "Hit that", no stat move)
seed 11 female age 73   Chasing my bag
        You seduced your supervisor, Ram Smith!
        karma -30, discipline -30   <- she already had a lover
        (hookup at 72, outbound, and the card is the cheating bill)
seed 24 male   age 56   Nobody can know
        You let your supervisor, Selene Gnomez, seduce you!
        (hookup at 51 -- five years earlier, because four years of other cards
         claimed the year first)
```

### 123.5 Shortcuts

* The game shows the card the moment the hookup resolves. The port shows it in the
  next year nothing else takes, which is why the observed delay is one year in
  sixteen of twenty-eight cards and up to seven in the tail. A card that waits is
  still a card; the alternative was a second event per year the loader has no
  shape for.
* `IsExLover`, `CollectSetNext`, the ex-lover array, the enjoyment panels, the
  obituary colour line (#70396), the collectible chain behind
  `IsScavengerHuntAvailable` / `IsDeadlySins2024` / `HasUserFoundCollectible`, and
  the pregnancy push all stay unported: the port carries no ex-lovers, no
  collectibles, no pregnancy and no obituary generator.
* The caught-cheating card (the `0..150` draw against `100 - lover[0xc0]`) is a
  comment. The port has no lover reputation float, and the card it would push is
  another scenario the port does not carry.
* The hero's `[0x70]+0x2c5` byte, set at the end of `RefreshScenario` when the hero
  made the move on a male boss, has no reader in the port.
* The sound at `[self+0x140]` (`csel` between two cells on the hero's gender) is not
  modelled, as in every other card.

### 123.6 Verification

The probe (`/tmp/qdir/succres.py`, eighty lives: seeds 1..40 in both sexes, each
played to eighty) reproduces the card and the hookup that owes it. The check that
matters most is the orphan count -- a morning after with no hookup behind it is the
one way this card can be wrong:

```

who {'boss': 22, 'hero': 6}
titles {'And about my pay...': 4, 'Chasing my bag': 1, 'I need lots of supervision': 2,
        "I'm the captain now": 1, "If we're on company time": 6,

        'Securing my position here': 2}
deltas {'()': 26, "(('discipline', -30), ('karma', -30))": 2}
delay in years (capped at 9) {1: 16, 2: 5, 3: 2, 4: 1, 5: 2, 7: 2}
cards per life {0: 54, 1: 24, 2: 2}

failures 0

RESIDUE 0 {}

Sixty-nine of the eighty lives never see the card, which is what a follow-up should
look like: the hookup card itself was fifty-two cards in the same sweep before this
section added its own draw, and only the hookups that resolved the hero's way owe a

## 124. The job referral: the one card a friend has to hand over

### 124.1 A card for a hero with nothing

The Citizen family so far has been the street's family -- a witness, a bag of
drugs. This one is the family's first career card, and its gate is the shape of
the whole thing:

```
class ScenarioJobReferral : Scenario               il2cpp_dump.txt:42204
  _job          SimJob   0x170
  _narrative    System.String 0x178
  .ctor()                  @0x73f3d12f48   ( 92 B)
  RefreshScenario()        @0x73f3d12fa4   (3120 B)
  ChoiceSelectedAtIndex()  @0x73f3d13fe4   (2356 B)
  GetReferralJob()         @0x73f3d13bd4   (1040 B)
  IsAvailable()            @0x73f3d14918    (556 B)
  EmojiString()            @0x73f3d14b44     (36 B)
```

The availability check @0x73f3d14918 asks for a hero with no work of any kind:
`CurrentlyHasAJob @0x73f2f0e040`, `CurrentlyHasASpecialJob @0x73f2f0b820`,
`CurrentlyInTheMilitary @0x73f2f0e0b4`, `CurrentlyInSchool @0x73f2f0ccf4` and
`CurrentlyInPrison @0x73f2f0e1d8` must all be false, a property at
`[hero+0x140]+0x298` must be false, and `IsARoyal @0x73f2f0e128` must be false
too. Then the age band, in three instructions:

```
ldr w9, [hero+0x20]        ; age
sub w9, w9, #0x42          ; age - 66
cmn w9, #0x2c              ; (age - 66) + 44 == 0  <=>  age == 110
b.lo  -> false             ; so 66 <= age < 110
```

`cmn` is the giveaway: the compiler folded "less than 110" into "not equal to
110" because the value is already known non-negative. What the card is for is
therefore a retired hero -- past sixty-six, out of school, out of the services,
with no job -- and the friend is the only way back in.

Two more tests close the gate. `NetWorth() @0x73f2f08a60` is compared against a
double and the branch that continues is the **negative** one (`fcmp d0,d1; b.mi`),
so the card fires only for a hero whose net worth is *below* the constant; and
`PresentedCountForScenario` must be under three, the same cap sections 121 and 122
carry.

### 124.2 Who is offering, and what is on offer

`RefreshScenario` draws one referrer variant of eight
(`GetRandomNumber(0,7) @0x73f32ab2a8`) and every variant hunts a *living related
person* it can name -- the checks are `LivesInSamePlaceAsHero @0x73f30e6b28`,
`GetTotalHeroRelationshipStrength @0x73f30d284c > 10.0f`, and, per variant, one
field of its own (a sibling comes out of `get_SiblingArray @0x73f3722db0`). The
person is stored at `[self+0x60]`, and two phrases are built from him: the form
of address `your {0}, {1},` (#68451) or `my {0}, {1},` (#62743) over his
relationship word and his name, and his bare name. If no relative matches, the
form of address stays null and the card abandons itself -- there is no referral
without somebody to make it.

The job itself comes from `GetReferralJob @0x73f3d13bd4`, and that is the card's
one structural surprise: it reads no referral table at all. It calls
`RefreshAvailableJobs(true) @0x73f2ec952c` (or
`RefreshAvailableGoldenDiplomaJobs(true) @0x73f2ecb2bc` when
`DoesUserHaveAccessToGoldenResume @0x73f369d580` says the hero has one) on the
hero's `PlaceOfResidence @0x73f30d6494`, shuffles that array with
`RandomizeOrderOfArray @0x73f32a8470`, and hands back the first entry its
predicate accepts. A referral is therefore not a special job: it is whatever the
hero's own town is hiring, delivered by somebody who knows somebody.

```
{0} has a friend who works at {1} and can get you a job there as {2}.   #69985  0x5cc0918
A friend of {0} offered to set me up with a job as {1} for {2}.          #10054  0x5cc0910
```

The first line is the body (`[self+0x48]`, run through
`CapitalizeFirstLetterOfSentenceString @0x73f32afedc`) and takes the phrase, the
employer and the title; the second is `_narrative`, the sentence every journal
line of the card opens with, and it takes the bare name instead. The title slot
`[self+0x38]` is set once, in the constructor, to `'Job Referral'` (#27915,
cell 0x5cc0908) -- the only card in this report whose title is written before any
refresh runs.

An info panel at `[self+0xa0]` carries four rows -- `Title` (#43646),
`Career` (#15198), `Employer` (#18693) and `Salary` (#36642, formatted by
`CurrencyStringForAmount` over `SimJob::Salary @0x73f2fbeaf8`) -- and two
buttons sit at `[self+0xa8]`: `Take the job` (#40908) and
`That's not for me` (#41424).

### 124.3 Two lanes, and what the hero logs

`ChoiceSelectedAtIndex @0x73f3d13fe4` lowercases the label and runs a single
`Contains('take')` test, so the split is a prefix: anything starting with the
word takes the job.

| | take | refuse |
|---|---|---|
| Discipline | +2 | -4 |
| Karma | +2 | -2 |
| Happiness | +4 | -3 |
| job | `StartJob(SimJob) @0x73f2f1c2a4` | -- |
| journal | `<narrative>` | `<narrative> I turned down the opportunity.` (#69634) |

The happiness slot is `[hero+0x408]`, the float sections 116-123 already read as
happiness. The refusal line is a `Format` over the pre-formatted narrative, which
is why the log reads as one sentence with two halves: *A friend of Dana Wilkens
offered to set me up with a job as Cupid for Jacksonville Public Schools. I turned
down the opportunity.*

Accepting pushes a second card behind it: a title from
`PickRandomFromStringArray @0x73f32b0608` over `Welcome aboard` (#46260),
`When can you start?` (#46505), `Bringing home the bacon` (#14039) and
`Perfect fit` (#33566), with the body `Welcome to {0}!` (#46278) over the
employer and its own info panel; `WillOfferNewHouse @0x73f2a12868` may push a
house offer after that. A hero who owns the Hollywood star also gets one appended
line (#13283) about wishing on it before the first day of work -- the same easter
egg section 96 catalogues elsewhere.

### 124.4 The port had to give the hero a retirement

This is the section where the port found a hole in itself. The hero is employed
from the year he turns eighteen, unconditionally: `src/sim.cpp:3485` writes
`h.employed = !student` on every age-up and nothing in the port ever clears it.
The game's own pool is free because a hero *retires*; the port had no retirement,
so a card whose entire gate is "this hero has no job" could never have fired. The
smallest fix that keeps every earlier gate honest is a workforce exit at 66, right
after the job draw:

```cpp
// shortcut: the port has no retirement system and line 3485 leaves every hero
// employed from 18, so the cards that want a hero without work -- the job
// referral (REPORT.en.md 124) is the first of them -- could never fire. The
// hero leaves the workforce at 66; the career track survives, so careerYear's
// promotion lane still reads it and no earlier gate moves before that age.
if (h.age >= 66 && h.employed && !h.military && !h.militaryPending) h.employed = false;
```

`careerYear` gained the matching guard (`h.age < 18 || h.age >= 66` in its
empty-track branch), because otherwise the retired hero would have taken a fresh
career the very next year and the two rules would undo each other annually.

| where | what |
|---|---|
| `port/include/bl/game.h:790` | `int referralPresented;` -- the card's `PresentedCountForScenario` cap of three |
| `port/include/bl/sim.h:505` | `bool jobReferralYear(...)` |
| `port/include/bl/sim.h:656` | `Rng jrRng_;` -- the card's own stream |
| `port/src/sim.cpp:642` | the seed, `seed ^ 0x243f6a8885a308d3 ^ 0xbe5466cf34e90c6c` |
| `port/src/sim.cpp:3513` | the retirement rule in `ageUp` |
| `port/src/sim.cpp:3650` | the wire, after the morning after |
| `port/src/sim.cpp:27078` | `bool Sim::jobReferralYear` |

The port's referrer is the drawn friend slot rather than one of the eight
relationship variants, because the port's relatives carry no relationship
strength to compare against 10; the friend is the one person the card's own
variants always have. The job is drawn from `a16_careers-enc` with the same two
columns `careerYear` reads -- the first step of the Seniority Track, falling back
to the `Career` column when the track has no comma in it, and the employer from
`Company Type` through `companyName`.

`/tmp/qdir/jrres.py`, eighty lives (seeds 1..40, both sexes, played to ninety-five):

lanes {"That's not for me": 7, 'Take the job': 3}
rows drawn 8
ages {67: 2, 68: 2, 70: 1, 73: 1, 76: 1, 81: 1, 86: 1, 90: 1}
cards per life {0: 70, 1: 10}
jobs {'Cupid': 2, 'History Teacher': 2, 'Exotic Dancer': 1, 'Operations Analyst': 1,
      'Line Cook': 1, 'Elf': 1}

```

Ten cards in eighty lives is what the gate asks for: seventy of the lives either

`tools/test_job_referral.py` is the repo's copy: the table and the row, the age

### 124.6 The retirement rule shows up in the workplace counters

The card itself draws on `jrRng_` and perturbs nothing, but the retirement rule
does: a hero of sixty-six and over is no longer employed, so the workplace family
stops offering at that age. That is the correct behaviour -- a retiree has no
supervisor -- and it is the whole of the drift below.

| test | after 123 | after 124 |
|---|---|---|
| hookup cards | 89 | 73 |
| supervisor cards | 101 | 88 |
| after hours cards | 68 | 57 |
| team building cards | 49 | 46 |
| mornings after | 28 | 23 |
| drug cards | 82 | 83 |
| witness cards | 84 | 84 |
| lightning cards | 75 | 75 |
| lightning deaths | 6 | 6 |

A cheap cross-check that the cause is the retirement rule and not the new card's
year consumption: of the supervisor-family cards in the sweep, twenty-two sit
below sixty-six and exactly one above it, with sixty-seven the oldest. Before the
rule the family ran to the end of every life.

### 124.7 Shortcuts


* The net-worth constant is unreadable offline: the `adrp` page is printed
  digit-clipped by the local tooling and the cell it points at holds unrelated
  floats. The port uses $100,000, documented at the branch.
* The eight referrer variants collapse to the drawn friend, because the port has
  no relationship-strength float for a relative.
* `RefreshAvailableJobs` / `RefreshAvailableGoldenDiplomaJobs` and the golden
  resume are not modelled; the port draws a career row instead, with the
  same eligibility blindness `careerYear` already carries.
* The accept's second card (the four follow-up titles and `Welcome to {0}!`), the
  house offer behind `WillOfferNewHouse`, the Hollywood-star wish line, the info
  panels and the salary formatter all stay unported: the port shows one card a
  year and formats no currency in this family.
* The retirement rule is the port's own invention, not the game's: the game's own
  retirement condition was not read. It is deliberately silent -- no event, no
  journal line -- so it changes only which cards the late years can offer.

## 125. The breakup announcement: the first card of the lover family, and the only one that reports instead of asking

The lover family is the largest block the port had not touched: forty-nine
`ScenarioLover*` / `ScenarioExLover*` classes behind the one coarse
`relationshipYear` approximation (src/sim.cpp:27390), which fires the family's
tables on fixed coins instead of reading them. This section starts the block with
its cheapest and most structural card -- the one the game pushes *after* a
relationship has already ended, and the only one in the family with no
`ChoiceSelectedAtIndex` at all.

### 125.1 The card

```
class ScenarioLoverBreakUp : Scenario              il2cpp_dump.txt:43156
  _lover        SimLover      0x170
  _narrative    System.String 0x178
  .ctor(SimLover)          @0x73f3daf62c   ( 44 B)
  RefreshScenario()        @0x73f3daf658   (348 B)
  DismissSelected()        @0x73f3daf7b4   (108 B)
```

No eligibility method, no choice handler, no fields beyond the pair and the
sentence. The constructor is the base call plus one store:

```
73f3daf638  mov w1, wzr            ; base .ctor(false) -- the card takes no forced
73f3daf644  bl  #0x73f2eb9db8      ;   choice and shows no portrait slot
73f3daf648  str x19, [x20, #0x170] ; _lover = the partner passed in
```

### 125.2 RefreshScenario: three formats, two flags, one lowered noun

```
73f3daf6b8  ldr x8, [x19, #0x170]   ; _lover
73f3daf6bc  mov w9, #0x101
73f3daf6c0  strh w9, [x19, #0x132]  ; two adjacent one-byte flags, both 1
73f3daf6c4  cbz x8, throw           ; and a null check on every step below
```

The narrative is built first, out of the partner's full name:

```
73f3daf6d0..6e4   [0x5c46bf0]       ; literal #23656 'I broke up with {0}.'
73f3daf6e4  bl #0x73f2fc62bc       ; SimPersonName.FullName on [_lover+0x10]
73f3daf6f8  bl #0x73f52976b4       ; String.Format(that, FullName)
```

and the title and body follow:

```
73f3daf700  ldr x8, [x21]           ; cell 0x5c3d8f8, literal #38413 'See ya'
73f3daf708  str x8, [x19, #0x38]   ; Scenario.Title
73f3daf714  bl #0x73f30d35a0       ; SimLover.RelationshipStatusString
73f3daf720  bl #0x73f52aa938       ; .ToLower()
73f3daf750  ldr x2, [x8, #0x18]    ; the partner's first name, [_lover+0x10]+0x18
73f3daf75c  bl #0x73f52a71cc       ; String.Format(cell 0x5c46bd8, status, name)
73f3daf764  str x0, [x19, #0x48]   ; Scenario.Body
73f3daf774  bl #0x73f52976b4       ; String.Format(cell 0x5c31470 '{0}', title)
73f3daf77c  str x0, [x19, #0x178]  ; _narrative
```

so the card reads

```
Title      'See ya'                              (#38413, cell 0x5c3d8f8)
Body       'You broke up with your {0}, {1}.'    (#47912, cell 0x5c46bd8)
Narrative  'I broke up with {FullName}.'         (#23656, cell 0x5c31470)
```

The `{0}` is not a literal word: `SimLover.RelationshipStatusString`
@0x73f30d35a0 is a switch on the lover's status at `+0x224` crossed with two
gender bytes, and the cells it can return are the whole noun table the family
uses:

| status `+0x224` | partner male | partner female | other |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (dating) | #13953 `Boyfriend` | #21646 `Girlfriend` | #33399 `Partner` |
| 2 (engaged) | #20033 `Fiancé` | #20034 `Fiancée` | #33399 `Partner` |
| 3 (married) | #23321 `Husband` | #46941 `Wife` | #39735 `Spouse` |
| 4 | #19195 `Ex-Husband` | #19199 `Ex-Wife` | #19196 `Ex-Partner` |
| 5, 6 | #19193 `Ex-Fling` / #19194 `Ex-Girlfriend` | | |

The byte pair `+0x1c` / `+0x44` picks the column: the two are compared, and
equal bytes take the male arm while unequal take the female one. The card then
lowers the word, so the sentence the player reads is
`You broke up with your girlfriend, Alex.`

### 125.3 DismissSelected: one journal line, no state

```
73f3daf800  ldr x0, [x8, #0x48]     ; [[GameReference+0xb8]+0]+0x20 -> the sim
73f3daf808  ldr x1, [x19, #0x178]   ; _narrative
73f3daf818  b #0x73f380158c         ; the sim journal's Log(string)
```

That is the whole method. The card does not remove the partner, reset the score,
or move him into an ex array: by the time it is constructed the relationship is
already over, and the game shows it as a report. The port therefore keeps the
three strings and nothing else.

### 125.4 What the port wires

* `Hero::breakUpPending`, `breakUpWord`, `breakUpName`, `breakUpFull`
  (include/bl/game.h) carry the partner across the year boundary.
* `relationshipYear`'s breakup branch (src/sim.cpp) fills them from the partner
  it is about to clear: the status word from `loverStatus` and `loverFemale`,
  the body's `{1}` from the first token of the name, the narrative's `{0}`
  from the whole stored name.
* `Sim::loverBreakUpYear` (src/sim.cpp) is the card: it rolls nothing, draws on
  no stream, sets `table = "relationship"`, and writes the three strings.
* It is offered at the head of the yearly dispatch, next to the other queued
  report card (`morningYear`), because the game pushes it the moment the breakup
  card resolves and the port shows one card a year.

```
RELATIONSHIP YEAR  breakup row fires  ->  flags set, relation cleared
NEXT AGE-UP        loverBreakUpYear   ->  'See ya'
```

### 125.5 Verification

`tools/test_love_breakup.py` drives 120 lives with `"relationship": true` and
checks every card the port titles `See ya`: the body template against the eight
status words, that no choice and no stat move ever rides along, the
`logLines` entry against the body's own name, and the absence of unresolved
`<brackets>`.

```
breakup cards: 24
status words: {'boyfriend': 15, 'girlfriend': 9}
ok
```

Only the two dating words appear because the port's breakup gate sits at a score
the married branch almost never falls back to; the married and engaged arms stay
in the switch and the test accepts them.

### 125.6 The stale gender the card exposed

The first sweep printed `You broke up with your girlfriend, John.` -- a female
word over a male partner. The pairing behind it is the supervisor hookup
(REPORT.en.md 120), which stores `h.loverName = sup` and never sets
`h.loverFemale`, so every later reader of the partner's gender --
`RelationshipStatusString` here, and the `Straight Only` row gate at
src/sim.cpp:23548 -- saw the previous pairing's value. The hookup now carries the
gender with the name, resolved once from the celebrity name table's `Gender`
column, which is where the first name was drawn from in the first place. The
sweep after the fix prints the male words over male names.

### 125.7 Shortcuts

* The port's partner carries one stored name; the game formats the body's `{1}`
  from the first name and the narrative's `{0}` from `FullName`, so the port
  splits the single string on its first space.
* The ex and neutral-gender arms of the status switch are not reachable in the
  port, because `relationshipYear` only ends dating, engaged and married pairs.
* The game pushes the card immediately; the port shows one card a year, so the
  announcement lands on the following age-up. It consumes no row and draws
  nothing, so no other card's sequence moves.
* `RelationshipStatusString`'s ex sub-flags (`+0x228`, `+0x22c`, `+0x234`,
  `+0x23c`) are recorded above and not modelled: the port has one `exName`
  slot and no ex-lover array yet.

### 125.8 What moved

The card consumes a year and the hookup now writes a gender, so nine of the
sixty-seven probes shift by one or two events. No probe changed its residue
(0 everywhere), none failed, and the bench is byte-identical -- the bench's lives
stop at thirty-four, before any pair forms.

| probe | after 124 | after 125 |
|---|---|---|
| dlres | 731 | 732 |
| fstres | 141 | 139 |
| ftres | 132 | 134 |
| fwres | 86 | 87 |
| ltres | 918 | 916 |
| mafiares | 745 | 743 |
| partres | 279 | 278 |
| polres | 1682 | 1681 |
| prankres | 247 | 248 |

The batch around it stays green: `coverage.py` reports the same two contentless
entries (`ScenarioMiniPaywall` x2), `portgap.py` reports
`ENTRIES 109 rendered-by-port 107 gap 0`, `rescensus.py` reports
`distinct residue tokens 0 total 0`, and all sixty-seven probes exit zero with

## 126. The terminal driver: the engine played instead of scripted

Tier 2 of the plan is not a scenario. It is the driver that turns the same engine
`blsim --script` batches into something a person can sit in front of, and the
whole of its design is one observation about the port's own API:

```
bool Sim::ageUp(Life& life, AgeUp& out, int forcedChoice = -1);
```

The engine already knows how to run the branch the player picked: every card
honours a 0-based `forcedChoice` index. What it cannot do is *show* the card
before that index is known. So the driver asks for the year twice.

### 126.1 Two passes, one of them in a child

```
year N:  fork -> child      sim.ageUp(life, ev, -1)   print the card, discard the state
         parent waits, prints the buttons, reads the answer
         parent             sim.ageUp(life, ev, K)    for real, K = the pressed lane
```

The preview cannot be folded into the commit, because a card bakes its stat move
at build time — `out.karma` *is* the chosen lane's move. And it cannot be a
snapshot either: `Sim` owns sixty-odd `Rng` streams plus twenty-five per-card
caches plus the loaded table cache, so copying it to rewind costs a full table
copy per year, and copying only part of it diverges from a single-pass run the
first time a cache entry is reused. `fork()` sidesteps both: the child inherits
everything copy-on-write, mutates it, prints one line and `_exit`s. The parent's
streams, caches and tables are never touched, so no state is cloned, replayed or
rewound.

Measured: a ninety-one-year life with relationships on, every card answered, runs
in **1.5 s wall** including the six lane probes and the commit for every year.

### 126.2 Finding a card's buttons

The preview returns the lane the port's own draw took, not the menu. The driver
gets the menu by probing the same year in further children, one per index 0..5,
and keeping the probes that land on the same `(table, row)` as the preview:

```
--- age 23 ------------------------------------
  $4210   happiness 71   health 92   smarts 55   looks 64   karma 40   discipline 51

  Job Offer
  A local shop wants you behind the counter.
  [1] Take the job   (the game's own pick)
  [2] Turn it down
  >
```

A card whose `out.choice` is empty has no `ChoiceSelectedAtIndex` at all — the
report cards (`See ya`, the morning after, the witness journal) — and prints
`[enter] continue`.

### 126.3 What the driver reuses

`runScript`'s setup block moved to `bl::setupLife` (src/script.cpp) so a played
life is built by the same `createLife` + country pin + twenty-two `make*`
switches + birth-line draws as a scripted one, in the same order. The stat
clamping in `applyStats` is copied from the same loop for the same reason. Nothing
else moved: `--script` output is byte-identical, which the whole probe battery
depends on.

### 126.4 Verification

`tools/test_play.py` plays a whole life with every card answered by the game's own
lane and asserts the shape (`=== ` banner, ages strictly increasing from 1, a
death or a final age, no unresolved `<token>`), then replays with the first
two-button card answered `2` and asserts the executed narrative is *that* card's
label — the half a scripted run can never check. Finally it replays the identical
answers and asserts the output is byte-identical, which is the claim that the
forked preview leaves nothing behind.

```
played ages: 91 -> 91
lanes answered: 56
ok
```

### 126.5 Shortcuts

* The menu probe caps at index 5. No ported card has more lanes; the cap is the
  shortcut, not a measured maximum of the game's own cards.
* The preview runs the real `ageUp`, so a card that writes to the filesystem or
  a socket would run twice. Nothing in the port does.
* A `--play` session with no `--script` uses `{}`: seed 0, a seed-picked
  country, male. Age cap is `ages` or 120.
* Windows has no `fork`; the driver is POSIX-only and the port's other modes are
  not.

## 127. Tooling: what the game can be asked for, and what it cannot

Three tools, one measurement each. All three exist so that later sections stop
repeating work; none of them changes the port's behaviour.

### 127.1 `tools/literals_dump.py` — the slot table

Every card string is loaded through a slot: the code does `adrp`/`ldr` to a cell
that holds an `Il2CppString*`, filled from the metadata literal table. Reading one
cell needs a Frida attach, so the tool reads the whole slot range at once and keeps
`tools/lit_cells.json`.

Measured, and this is the finding: **the range holds 420 resolved slots at the
menu and 420 after three age-ups.** The slots are not filled at start-up for every
literal the module references; they fill when the code path that loads them first
runs. The consequences are:

* a literal whose card has never fired in the game is not in the cache, so the
  cache cannot replace the per-card read for a card being decoded *first*;
* it is worth keeping anyway, because it is a growing record of every literal the
  game has already handed over — a play session captures the set of cards that
  fired in it, and those rows never need the harness again.

### 127.2 `tools/cards_capture.py` — asking the game for a card

`probeCard` (blh.js) builds a scenario object, runs its own `RefreshScenario` and
reads the `System.String` fields and the `ScenarioChoice` list back. The tool
batches that per class and caches into `tools/cards.json`, so a card captured once
is readable offline forever.

Two hard limits, both measured:

1. `friendCard`/`genPerson` fails with `access violation accessing 0x0` on the
   life loaded *before* its hero chain is captured — `pointers` reports
   `life`/`hero` only after a scenario has fired.
2. A card whose `RefreshScenario` reads state it does not have throws inside the
   call. `LoverPrude` aborted the process; `LoverCounselingPush`,
   `LoverElopePush` and `LoverDemandsBirthControl` threw *after* writing their
   title, which is still a real capture:

```
ScenarioLoverCounselingPush  (RefreshScenario threw)
  Title          'Counseling'
ScenarioLoverElopePush       (RefreshScenario threw)
  Title          'Elope'
ScenarioLoverDemandsBirthControl (RefreshScenario threw)
  Title          'Birth Control'
```

So the tool is a **title oracle with zero setup** and a **full-card oracle only for
cards that need no partner**. Bodies and buttons for state-dependent cards still
come from the binary plus the literal table.

### 127.3 The offline literal table, and where it stops

`tools/metadata_strings.py` already reads the literal table out of
`global-metadata.dat` (71,223 entries; layout documented in
`METADATA_STRINGS.en.md`, which corrected the earlier 8-byte-entry reader). That
half is solved offline: literal index -> text.

The missing half is cell -> literal index. In il2cpp that mapping is the
`metadataUsagePairs` array, and this build's header does not lay it out where the
documented order says. A scan of the whole 18.8 MB file for the two shapes that
array can take —

* 8-byte `(type 1..6, index)` pairs, and
* 8-byte `(start, count)` lists with strictly increasing starts —

finds no region larger than 5,665 entries, and the largest hits are at 17.68 MB
inside a different structure. So the mapping is not reachable offline with what is
on disk today.

**What this means for throughput**, stated plainly: the decode loop keeps reading
cells against a running game, but the two tools above remove the *repeat* half of
that cost — a card captured once is never asked for twice, and every literal the
game has already loaded is cached.

## 128. Tooling: the whole symbol table, and an annotated disassembler that uses it

### 128.1 `tools/symbols_dump.py` — 140,207 methods in four seconds

il2cpp already holds the map. Walking `il2cpp_domain_get_assemblies` ->
`il2cpp_assembly_get_image` -> `il2cpp_image_get_class` ->
`il2cpp_class_get_methods` and taking each `MethodInfo`'s own entry point gives
`addr -> Namespace.Class::Method` for **every** managed method, not just the
scenario classes `il2cpp_dump.txt` lists:

```
methods 140207 in 4.0s -> tools/symbols.json
```

Keys are module-relative (`ptr - module.base`), so the table does not change when
the loader picks a different base; a static address from the .so maps to
`static - 0x73F049A000`.

### 128.2 What it settled on the first lookup

```
0x73f32ab2a8 -> GameReference::GetRandomNumber
0x73f30d35a0 -> SimLover::RelationshipStatusString
0x73f2fc62bc -> SimPersonName::FullName
0x73f52976b4 -> System.String::Format
0x73f30d284c -> SimPerson::GetTotalHeroRelationshipStrength
0x73f2eb9db8 -> Scenario::.ctor
0x73f380158c -> LifeLog::Log
0x73f30c4db0 -> SimChild::IsChildWithLover
0x73f37228d4 -> Life::get_ChildArray
0x73f32a2f10 -> GameManager::get_DevMode
```

Two of those are corrections, not confirmations:

* `0x73f32a2f10` is `GameManager::get_DevMode`, and its body is `mov w0, wzr` --
  a build-time constant, not a stub. The `orr w19, w0, w19` in
  `ScenarioLoverMakeLoveNag`'s eligibility is therefore `devMode || ...`, which
  in a production build is a no-op clause, and the gate is the rest of it.
* `Life::get_ChildArray` + `SimChild::IsChildWithLover` mean the LINQ block in
  that same eligibility is walking **the hero's children**, not a partner list,
  and tracking the youngest. The `minAge > 4` test at the end is a child-age
  test. §125 recorded that block as an unidentified collection walk; it is now
  identified.

### 128.3 `tools/disasm.py` — the decode loop's new front end

```
python3 tools/disasm.py 0x73f3daf658 90            # BreakUp.RefreshScenario
python3 tools/disasm.py 0x73f3daf658 90 --lits     # resolve slots already seen
python3 tools/disasm.py --method ScenarioFriendMeet::RefreshScenario
```

Every `bl` is named exactly, every `adrp`+`ldr` pair is resolved to its slot
offset, and `--lits` prints the literal text for slots `tools/lit_cells.json`
has already seen load. Two deliberate limitations:

* **exact hits only.** The managed table has no entry for the runtime helpers the
  codegen emits (`0x73f26d4860`, the class-init call in every card), and a
  nearest-below guess labelled all of them `Amazon.Util...FillDictionary` before
  the rule was tightened. `--near` opts into a bounded guess and marks it with
  `~`.
* **the immediate is required** on a load: `ldr x8, [x20]` dereferences a pointer
  the code already holds and is not a slot read, which the first cut of the tool
  mislabelled.

Sample, the §125 card re-read through the new tool:

```
73f3daf6e4  bl  #0x73f2fc62bc   ; SimPersonName::FullName
73f3daf6f8  bl  #0x73f52976b4   ; System.String::Format
73f3daf714  bl  #0x73f30d35a0   ; SimLover::RelationshipStatusString
73f3daf720  bl  #0x73f52aa938   ; System.String::ToLower
```

That is the same decode §125 did by hand, in one command, with no attach.

## 129. The split audit: what moves, and what stays

Before cutting `sim.cpp` into per-family translation units, a measurement of what
is actually in it:

```
Sim methods: 225        lines: 28,876
by name bucket: other 44, money 39, infra 36, fame 28, body 24, crime 16,
                work 13, friend 12, school 7, relationship 6
largest methods: load 45,846 B, racingYear 32,264 B, outdoorYear 30,279 B,
                 vampireYear 30,022 B, casinoYear 29,665 B, modelYear 29,123 B,
                 cultYear 28,883 B, tradeYear 28,873 B, sportsSeason 28,450 B,
                 spyYear 27,733 B
```

The name buckets are misleading on their own — the lover family reads as six
methods because it lives inside one `relationshipYear` dispatch rather than one
function per card — but the size list is not: **the mass is a dozen
`*Year`/`*Season` functions, each 27-32 KB, each already self-contained.**

That is the split's boundary, and it is a good one:

* **moves**: `racingYear`, `outdoorYear`, `vampireYear`, `casinoYear`,
  `modelYear`, `cultYear`, `tradeYear`, `sportsSeason`, `spyYear`, and the
  rest of that shape — one file per family, each holding its own `*Year`
  function plus its private helpers and caches.
* **stays** in `sim.cpp`: `load` (45.8 KB, the table/data bootstrap), the shared
  card plumbing every family calls (`renderRow`, `ensureTable`/`tbl`,
  `fire`, `pointsForImpact`, `drawFirstName`, `personName`, `companyName`,
  `resolve`), the RNG streams, and the yearly dispatch that calls the families in
  order.

The dependency test is the practical one: a family function calls only `Sim`
members, so it moves to another .cpp without touching a declaration. What it must
not do is call a `static` file-local helper in `sim.cpp`; each move therefore
needs a compile, and the bench is the regression.

Order of work, cheapest first and one commit each: `racingYear`, `modelYear`,
`tradeYear`, `casinoYear` (small, self-contained), then the rest, with
`bash tools/bench.sh /tmp/trace_c10.json` diffed after every move — the bench has
to stay byte-identical, because a pure split changes no behaviour.

## 130. The first family moves out: racing

`racingYear`, `racingCardRow`, `racingToken`, `racingBuyCar`, `makeRacing`
and their private helpers are now `port/src/fam/racing.cpp`. `sim.cpp` went from
28,876 to 27,874 lines.

### 130.1 What the move needed

The extraction was mechanical — 1,005 contiguous lines, from the family's banner to
the last brace of `racingYear` — but four kinds of symbol had to be dealt with,
and every later family will hit the same four:

1. **helpers in the file-local namespace.** `lower`, `trim`, `splitOn`,
   `weightedPickOf` were defined inside `namespace { }` at the top of
   `sim.cpp`, so they had internal linkage and could not be referenced from
   another translation unit. They moved out of the anonymous namespace, and
   `bl/text.h` now declares them.
2. **`static` free functions.** `toFirstPerson`, `llPossessive`, `llInList`
   were `static`; dropping the keyword gives them external linkage. Their own
   dependencies (`spySwap`, `substAll`) stay internal, which is legal because
   they are used inside the same translation unit.
3. **one function that had to leave the file entirely.** `spyUpperFirst` sat
   inside the anonymous namespace and had no external callers, so the cheapest
   correct home was a new `port/src/text.cpp` holding the body of
   `bl/text.h`'s promises.
4. **the family's private constants** (`kRacStreetTypes`, `kRanks`) came along
   with the block, no changes.

### 130.2 Verification

A pure split changes no behaviour, so both checks are equality checks:

```
bash tools/bench.sh /tmp/trace_c10.json   diff vs §125: 0 lines
python3 /tmp/qdir/racres.py               racing events 180, residue 0, failures 0
```

180 is exactly the count the same probe produced before the move, and the bench is
byte-identical. `blsim --play` still builds and runs (it goes through
`script.cpp`, untouched).

### 130.3 The rule this established

For every later family: move the block, compile, and let the linker name the
symbols that need external linkage. There is no need to guess — `undefined symbol`
lists exactly the helpers to export, and each one is a one-line move. What must not
happen is a second copy of a rule in the new file; that is why `spyUpperFirst`
went to `text.cpp` instead of being duplicated.

## 131. The split becomes a tool: model follows racing

`tools/split_family.py` cuts functions out of `sim.cpp` verbatim (brace-matched),
writes them into `src/fam/<family>.cpp` behind a fixed include block, and reports
what it took:

```
python3 tools/split_family.py model \
  'bool Sim::modelYear(Life& life, AgeUp& out, int forcedChoice) {' \
  'void Sim::makeModel(Life& life) {' \
  'std::string Sim::modelToken(const std::string& token) {' \
  'std::string Sim::modelName(const char* table) {' \
  'int Sim::modelRankIndex() const {' --dry-run

bool Sim::modelYear(...)          564 lines
void Sim::makeModel(Life& life) {  82 lines
std::string Sim::modelToken(...)   36 lines
std::string Sim::modelName(...)    75 lines
int Sim::modelRankIndex() const {   4 lines
```

`--dry-run` first is the habit: it prints the sizes and moves nothing, so a wrong
marker costs nothing.

### 131.1 What model needed that racing did not

One export, found by the compiler in a single pass:

```
model.cpp:189: use of undeclared identifier 'withArticle'
```

`articleFor` and `withArticle` were `static` at file scope in `sim.cpp`.
Both are now declared in `bl/text.h` and their `static` dropped. This is the
pattern the linker enforces: a family that fills an `<article>` token needs the
article rules, and there is exactly one copy of them.

### 131.2 Verification

```
bash tools/bench.sh /tmp/trace_c10.json   diff vs §125: 0 lines
python3 /tmp/qdir/modres.py               model events 123, residue 0, failures 0
```

123 is the pre-move count from the §125 battery, so the family behaves identically.
`sim.cpp` is down to 27,113 lines.

### 131.3 The state of the split

| family | file | lines moved | bench | probe |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| racing | src/fam/racing.cpp | 1,005 | 0 diff | 180 = 180 |
| model | src/fam/model.cpp | 761 | 0 diff | 123 = 123 |

Remaining, in the same order: `tradeYear`, `casinoYear`, `outdoorYear`,
`vampireYear`, `cultYear`, `spyYear`, `sportsSeason`.

### 131.4 trade, and the one thing the tool cannot do

`tools/split_family.py trade` moved 749 lines in five functions. The build then
named seven helpers, and one of them exposed the split's only real trap:

* six were `static` at file scope — `nameTakesSubject`, `heroToFirstPerson`,
  `musicGenreColumn`, `musicGenreFits`, `musicSideFits`, `spySentence`,
  `spyLowerFirst`. Dropping `static` is the whole fix, plus the declaration.
* `spySentence` and `spyLowerFirst` sat **inside** the file-local
  `namespace { }` opened near the top of `sim.cpp`. Dropping `static` there
  changes nothing: an anonymous namespace has internal linkage whatever the
  storage class says. They had to be cut out and re-inserted after the namespace
  closes.

That is the rule worth remembering for the rest of the split: `static` is a
keyword you can delete, an anonymous namespace is a scope you have to leave.

```
bash tools/bench.sh /tmp/trace_c10.json   diff vs §125: 0 lines
python3 /tmp/qdir/traderes.py             music events 1231, residue 0, failures 0
```

1231 is the pre-move count. Split so far: **racing 1,005 + model 761 + trade 749
= 2,515 lines** in three files, `sim.cpp` down to 26,364, bench and probes
unchanged after every move.

## 132. The split finishes: nine families, 6,692 lines out of `sim.cpp`

Five more moves, same tool, same two checks each. `sim.cpp`: 28,876 -> **22,184**
lines.

| family | file | lines | bench vs §125 | probe |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| casino | src/fam/casino.cpp | 653 | 0 diff | 748 = 748 |
| outdoor | src/fam/outdoor.cpp | 695 | 0 diff | 271 = 271 |
| vampire | src/fam/vampire.cpp | 669 | 0 diff | 3288 = 3288 |
| cult | src/fam/cult.cpp | 688 | 0 diff | 212 = 212 |
| spy | src/fam/spy.cpp | 732 | 0 diff | 113 = 113 |
| sports | src/fam/sports.cpp | 678 | 0 diff | 601 = 601 |

### 132.1 Two linkage shapes the tool cannot fix, and both appeared again

* **`spySwap`** (casino) was `static` at file scope: drop the keyword, declare in
  `bl/text.h`, done.
* **`cultGenderFits`** (cult) sat in an *anonymous namespace* together with
  `kCultPhilosophyFlags` / `kCultPhilosophyNames`. Nothing to export — the whole
  block belongs to the family, so the block moved into `cult.cpp`.
* **`ensureCultFields`** was left behind by the first pass because its name does
  not start with `cult`. The build named it, and it moved too. Worth stating
  plainly: **grep by family prefix is not the family** — `makeX`, `ensureXFields`
  and `xToken` are all part of it.

### 132.2 The whole battery, after nine moves

```
python3 /tmp/qdir/allprobes.py   67 probes
```

The battery is the gate that matters here: a family probe catches a count change in
that family, and the bench catches a shared-path change, but only the battery says
the nine moves together left every other family alone. It is green: 67 of 67 exit
zero, zero failures, and every event count equals the §125 baseline.

### 132.3 What the split bought

* **Nine files that can be edited without touching each other** — the throughput
  ceiling the plan identified was "one file, one writer", and that is now nine
  writers.
* **A one-command move** for the rest: `tools/split_family.py <family> '<signature>' ...`,
  with `--dry-run` first.
* **A shared helper surface** in `bl/text.h` that is the single copy of each rule
  (article, first person, sentence hygiene, genre columns, weighted pick). A new
  family that needs one of them gets it by include, not by copy.

`sim.cpp` still holds the bootstrap (`load`, 45.8 KB), the shared card plumbing,
the RNG streams and the yearly dispatch — the part that is genuinely shared.

## 133. Structural 1: a year can owe more than one card

The port's age-up returns exactly one card. The game does not: it can put several
scenarios in front of the player in one year, and the port had been paying for
that by deferring two of them a whole year — the break-up announcement (§125) and
the hookup's morning after (§123).

### 133.1 The change

`Life` gains a queue, and `ageUp` drains it **before** it advances anything:

```cpp
enum PendingCard {
  kPendingBreakUpAnnouncement = 1,  // LoverBreakUp, right after the break-up card
  kPendingMorningAfter = 2,         // SupervisorSeduceSuccess, right after the hookup
};

if (!life.pendingCards.empty()) {
  const int kind = life.pendingCards.front();
  life.pendingCards.erase(life.pendingCards.begin());
  if (kind == kPendingBreakUpAnnouncement) return loverBreakUpYear(life, out, -1);
  if (kind == kPendingMorningAfter) return morningYear(life, out, -1);
  return false;
}
++life.year;
```

Three properties made this the cheap version:

* **the builders already existed.** `loverBreakUpYear` and `morningYear` were
  written to run a year late; draining the queue calls them unchanged, and they
  clear their own flags, so the old path becomes dead code rather than a second
  implementation.
* **draining rolls nothing.** Both builders read state the trigger already fixed
  (`breakUpWord`/`breakUpName`, `morningWith`/`morningByHero`), so no RNG stream
  moves when a card arrives early.
* **the age does not advance while the queue is not empty**, so one year stays one
  year: no second job draw, no second family line, no second dispatch.

The triggers push the kind where they used to only raise a flag: both success
lanes of `seduceYear` and the break-up branch of `relationshipYear`.

### 133.2 Verification

```
same-age delivery   17 of 17 break-up announcements, one per life that has one
                    ages: (1,m) 74, (1,f) 71, (7,f) 64, (12,m) 55 ... all equal
morning after       delay in years: {0: 24}   was {1: 24} before the change
bench               0 lines diff vs §125
```

Both behaviours are now asserted where they belong, not just observed:
`tools/test_love_breakup.py` requires the card to follow the break-up row **at the
same age**, and `tools/test_seduce_after.py` requires `set(delays) == {0}`.

### 133.3 What moved in the counters, and why that is correct

The extra cards are *additional* events in the same year rather than replacements,
so a probe that counts events sees more of them. That is the game's own shape and
the reason the change was made; the bump is the measurement, not a regression.

**39 of 67 probes moved**, all of them exit 0 with zero failures:

```
racing 180 -> 189    lightning 916 -> 926    prism 330 -> 336    zoo 753 -> 747
mafia  743 -> 750    pet      804 -> 814    casino 748 -> 754   cult 212 -> 217
spy    113 -> 120    deal     732 -> 739    fight  208 -> 220   biz 3484 -> 3488
```

Mostly up, because the extra card is a real event that used to be counted a year
later or absorbed into another year's slot. The few that fall (zoo 753 -> 747,
act 143 -> 142, friend-out 85 -> 84) fall for the same reason from the other side:
a card delivered early applies its stat move early, and a later gate in the same
life then reads a different score.

One wrinkle had to be fixed with it: `--script`'s `ages` used to mean "ageUp
calls", and a pending card would have silently eaten one. The loop now counts
**years lived** (`life.hero.age` changed) while `i` stays the card index, so
`choices[]`/`push[]` keep their one-entry-per-card alignment with the bench's
traces. `tools/test_play.py` shows the effect plainly: 94 cards now reach age 92
instead of 91 for the same `ages` budget, because two of those iterations were
extra cards inside a year.

### 133.4 What this unlocks

The queue is now the mechanism for every "this card pushes that card" chain in
the dump — the assault card after the weapon encounter, the follow-up after the
job referral's accept, and the whole `*Push`/`*Complete` family of two-stage
cards. Each is one enum value and one push.

## 134. Structural 2: the ex-lover array

The port kept the most recent ex as two fields, `exName` and `exFemale`, because the
coarse `relationshipYear` pools only ever needed one name to print. The game keeps
an array (`Life.ExLoverArray`) and constructs every `ExLover*` card with one entry
of it, so eighteen classes were unreachable no matter how well they were decoded.

### 134.1 The shape

```cpp
struct ExLover {
  std::string name;
  bool female = false;
  int age = 0;
  std::string status;    // what the pair were when it ended: dating / engaged / married
  int relationship = 0;  // the score at the break-up
  int year = 0;          // the year it ended
};
std::vector<ExLover> exLovers;  // oldest first; the most recent is back()
const ExLover* latestEx() const { return exLovers.empty() ? nullptr : &exLovers.back(); }
```

The five fields are not guesses: the announcements' own nouns come from the status
(§125's `RelationshipStatusString` switch), and the ex pools already asked the
score and the year through their gates.

### 134.2 The eight sites

Only eight places in the port touched the old fields, and every one of them wanted
*the most recent* ex: the token resolver's `<ex>`, the `"Ex Gender"` column check,
the pronoun bracket the ex pools render with, the ex-pool gate, the rekindle lane,
and the two writes at the break-up. They now go through `latestEx()`, so the
array's extra entries cost nothing until a card asks for one.

### 134.3 Verification

Two things had to be true, and only one of them was visible before:

* **nothing changed** -- bench 0 lines, and the card tests (`love_breakup`,
  `job_referral`, `play`, `seduce_after`) all still pass.
* **the array is the record of break-ups** -- `tools/test_ex_lovers.py` drives 120
  lives and requires the entry count to equal the number of `See ya` cards in that
  life, plus `status` in {dating, engaged, married}, `0 <= relationship <= 100`, and
  the entry's year to be one of the ages a `See ya` card appeared.

```
lives with an ex: 23 of 120
ex entries: 25
statuses: {'dating': 24}
ok
```

The one legal exception is asserted rather than tolerated: a run can stop between
the break-up and its announcement (the announcement rides the same year's queue,
§133, and the loop stops at `ages`), so at most **one** trailing entry may lack a
card -- and it must be the final year.

The array is printed in the script JSON (`final.exLovers`) for exactly this reason:
before it, the port had no view of a hero's own relationship history that a test
could read.

Twenty-four of twenty-five entries are `dating` because the port's married branch
almost never falls back to the break-up score; that is the same gap §125 recorded,
now measured.

## 135. Structural 3: a sibling is an actor, not a row

The family list carried a relation, a name, an age, a disease and a job. That is
enough for the "your mother has been promoted" lines and nothing else: every
sibling/child card in the dump needs the relative to *have* state — are they still
at home, who did they marry, when — and the port had no such field.

### 135.1 What the game keeps, read out of its own symbols

`tools/symbols.json` names the whole family surface, which is how the fields were
chosen rather than invented:

```
Life::get_SiblingArray / Life::get_ChildArray         the two arrays
SimSibling::get_MovedOut              +0x1fd  bool
SimSibling::get_Spouse                +0x210  SimPerson
SimSibling::get_AgeAtCurrentSpouseMarriage +0x218 int
SimSibling::ThirdPersonMovesOutAndShouldAnnounce @0x73f30fed68
SimSibling::ThirdPersonMarries                   @0x73f30fed7c
SimSibling::ThirdPersonTriesForBaby              @0x73f30ff0c0
PersonGenerator::GenerateSpouseForThirdPerson    @0x73f3819114
```

And the two lines those flags drive are literals in the metadata:

```
#9396  '<person> married <spouse-description>.'
#9397  '<person> moved out.'
```

`ThirdPersonMovesOutAndShouldAnnounce` is three instructions — `[this+0x1fd] = 1;
return true;` — so the flag is the whole state and the announcement is the caller's
job. `ThirdPersonMarries` generates the spouse, stores it at `+0x210`, and records
the age at `+0x218`.

### 135.2 What the port now has

`Person` gained `movedOut`, `spouse` and `ageAtMarriage`, and `lifecycleLines`
emits both events for siblings (a relation containing "brother"/"sister"), on
their own stream (`Sim::sibRng_`) so every existing family line draws exactly as
before.

### 135.3 A real bug the work exposed

The first version of the test failed for a reason worth keeping: **family lines
were being thrown away on any year a code-built card fired**, because forty-five
card builders start with `out = AgeUp()`, which clears the `extra` vector the
family lines had just been written into.

`ageUp` is now a wrapper around a new `dispatchYear`:

```
ageUp        year/age counters, newborn setup, family lines, pending queue
dispatchYear the card dispatch (the old body, unchanged)
ageUp        family lines go in front of whatever the card wrote
```

That is the order the game logs them in (trace_game9 age 7), and it is now true on
every year rather than only the table-driven ones.

### 135.4 Verification

`tools/test_family.py`, 120 lives:

```
lives: 120
siblings: 120   moved out: 96   married: 87
ok
```

For every sibling it requires the line to be present when the flag is set and
absent when it is not, the marriage line to name the stored spouse, `ageAtMarriage`
to be in `(0, age]`, and a married sibling to have moved out first — the order the
game's own two methods imply.

The script JSON now carries `final.family`, so this is checkable at all.

### 135.5 Drift, and the probes that had to change with it

The bench moved by **4 lines in one record**: at age 24 the port now logs one more
line than the game's trace — a family line that used to be dropped on a
code-built-card year. That is the fix, not a regression.

The battery then caught the other half of the same truth: **eleven probes failed**,
and every one of them had encoded the old behaviour. They asserted
`len(logLines) == 1` and then read `logLines[0]` as the card's own line. Under the
fix a card's log is *the year's family lines, then the card's own line*, so:

* `len(logLines) != 1` became `len(logLines) < 1`;
* `logLines[0]` became `logLines[-1]`;
* `flres.py` matched the joined text with `fullmatch`, so it now tries the tail
  starting at each line until the row's own log version matches.

```
patched probes: fw, fro, fsst, sd, fupr, ai, fst, tb, sup, fuout, ah, unfr, fl
battery after:  probes 68   rc0 67   residue0 65   fails0 68
```

(`rc0 67` of 68 is the MiniPaywall probe that reports its own non-zero status; it
did the same before this round.)

Why this is worth writing down: the probes are the project's independent check, and
a check that encodes yesterday's bug will call today's fix a failure. They were
relaxed in the one dimension the fix changed and in no other — every count, range,
gender and token assertion they make is untouched.

## 136. Structural 4: fame is a float, and the gate is the game's

The port carried `int fame`, written nowhere but the newborn draw, and read by one
cult gate. The Fame family's gates read a **float at `hero+0xb4`**, and the trio
that was blocked on it (`FamePaparazzi`, `FameBook`, `FameCommercial`) could not be
wired to an integer that only ever held 0 or 30.

### 136.1 The arithmetic, read out of `SimPerson::ImpactFame`

`@0x73f30e4d88`, four instructions of arithmetic after one call:

```
s8 = [this+0xb4]
w0 = AttributeAdjustmentPointsForImpactScore(impact)   ; the port's pointsForImpact
s1 = s8 + (float)w0
fcmp s1, #100.0 ; b.ge  -> s1 = 100.0f
fcmp s1, #0.0   ; b.hi  -> s1 = 0.0f
[this+0xb4] = s1
```

Two details worth keeping: the top clamp is **inclusive** (a value landing exactly
on 100 stays 100) and the bottom clamp is **exclusive** (`<= 0` becomes 0), which is
what `b.ge` / `b.hi` mean and what the port now writes.

### 136.2 The gate

`ScenarioFamePaparazzi.ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush` `@0x73f3bd81f8`:

```
73f3bd825c  ldr  s0, [x9, #0xb4]     ; the hero's fame
73f3bd8260  mov  w9, #0x42960000     ; 75.0f
73f3bd8268  fcmp s0, s1
73f3bd826c  b.ge #0x73f3bd82a4       ; famous enough
73f3bd828c  bl   #0x73f32abacc       ; GameReference::DevTestingFame
```

So: `fame >= 75.0f`, or the developer flag. `Sim::isFamous` is exactly that
comparison, and the dev flag is not a thing a shipped build has.

### 136.3 Verification

The port already has the habit of a mode that asserts rather than prints
(`--deckcheck`, `--bagscheck`, `--rngcheck`); `--famecheck` joins them:

```
$ ./build/blsim --famecheck
  famecheck: SimPerson::ImpactFame arithmetic and the Fame gate
    fame 0 impact 0 -> 0
    fame 50 impact -6 -> 0          ; -100 lands exactly on the floor
    fame 50 impact 6 -> 100         ; +100 lands exactly on the ceiling
    fame 90 impact 6 -> 100         ; and holds above it
    fame 99 impact 4 -> 100         ; +30 from 99 clamps
    fame 10 impact -4 -> 0
    fame 50 impact 2 -> 58
    fame 50 impact -2 -> 42
    isFamous 74.9 -> 0   75.0 -> 1
  famecheck failures=0
```

Nine clamp cases and both sides of the gate, exit code 0. `bench` is unchanged and
the card tests are unchanged, which is the point: `fame` moved from `int` to
`float` without a single behavioural draw moving.

### 136.4 What this unlocks

`ScenarioFamePaparazzi`, `ScenarioFameBook` and `ScenarioFameCommercial` can now be
gated with one predicate instead of a guess, and `Sim::impactFame` is the one place
a card has to call to move fame — every later fame card uses it.

## 137. Structural 5: retirement is the country's, not the port's

§124 invented a retirement age because the job-referral card could never fire while
the port kept every hero employed from 18. The invention was `age >= 66`, and the
game has the number in its data:

```
DataCountry::GetRetirementAgeForGender        the accessor
DataCountry::get_RetirementAgeMale            country column
DataCountry::get_RetirementAgeFemale          country column
```

`gamedata_json/a16_countries-enc.json` carries `<RetirementAgeMale>k__BackingField`
and `<RetirementAgeFemale>k__BackingField` for all 102 countries, and they are not
one number:

```
male ages   55, 58, 59, 60, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 67
female ages 50, 55, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64
Afghanistan 60/55   Norway 67/67   Japan 62/62   Brazil 65/60   USA 66/66
```

So the port's 66 was wrong for most of the world, in both directions.

### 137.1 The change

`Country` gained the two columns (parsed by a new `intField`, since these values are
bare numbers rather than strings), `Hero` gained `retirementAge` set at the same
moment the country is pinned, and the two `>= 66` sites now read it.

The second site needed a real fix, not a substitution: the promotion lane reads
`careerTrack`, and the track survives retirement on purpose, so a retired hero was
still being promoted. `careerYear` now returns before both the new-career draw and
the promotion rung once the hero is past his country's age.

### 137.2 Verification

`tools/test_retirement.py` — five country/gender pairs, fifteen lives each:

```
Afghanistan  female retired in 14 lives
Afghanistan  male   retired in 12 lives
Brazil       female retired in 13 lives
Japan        male   retired in 12 lives
Norway       male   retired in  6 lives
ok
```

Per life it asserts three things: `final.retirementAge` equals the country row for
that gender (the data path, end to end), a hero past that age is `employed: false`,
and **no** `I started a new position as …` or `I have been promoted to …` line
appears at or after it. The first version of this test failed at exactly that second
clause — Norway, age 73, `promoted to St. Valentine` — which is how the promotion
bug was found rather than assumed away.

`final` also carries `retirementAge`, `employed`, `job` and `fame` now, so a test can
see the hero's own state without inferring it from cards.

### 137.3 What is still missing

* `Occupation::AgeAtRetirement` and `Occupation::Pension` are not modelled: the
  country decides *when*, and nothing pays anything when it happens. The pension
  needs the occupation's own row, which the port does not keep yet.
* The retirement is still silent — no `JobRetire` card, no pension line. §124's
  note stands: it changes which cards the late years can offer, nothing else.

## 138. The content sprint opens with a token, not a card

The first card of the sprint was going to be `ScenarioFamePaparazzi`, whose gate and
fame move landed in §136. Decoding it stopped on a missing token: its body is
`"<circumstance-public>, a paparazzo calls you <insult> in an attempt to wind you
up."` (`a16_paparazzi-scenarios-enc`), and **`<insult>` had exactly one source in
the port** — `a16_hustler-insults-enc`, reachable only while a *hustler* card was
rendering. The paparazzi, racer and vampire cards all write the same token and got
an empty string.

### 138.1 The general pool

`a16_insults-enc`, 205 rows: `Insult, Plural, Gender, Clean, Vampire`.

* `Gender` is `male` / `female` / `both`. Every card that says `<insult>` is
  addressing the hero, so the pool is filtered on **his** gender.
* `Vampire` marks the 64 rows the vampire family draws for itself; they are
  excluded from the general pool.
* `Clean` marks the safe-for-clean-mode rows. The port has no such setting, so the
  column is recorded and not used — that is a shortcut, written at the code.

`Sim::insultToken()` draws from the filtered pool on a stream of its own
(`insultRng_`), so no existing family's sequence moves.

### 138.2 Order matters, and the first cut got it wrong

The general branch has to sit **after** `hustlerIsToken`, not before: the hustler
family keeps its own pool, and putting the general one first silently replaced it.
`hustres` proves it — 928 events before and after the reorder, i.e. the family's own
cards are untouched.

### 138.3 Verification

`tools/test_insult.py`, 80 lives: no card is allowed to leave `<insult>` verbatim,
at least one table row must actually be read, and the portable pool is checked at
the data level (141 portable rows, 64 vampire-only, no overlap):

```
distinct insults seen: 58
portable rows: 141  vampire-only rows: 64
ok
```

The first version of this test asserted that no *vampire-only wording* appeared in
any card, and failed on `a mosquito`. That assertion was wrong, not the code: the
hustler family's own pool shares wording with this one, so the presence of a word
in a card says nothing about which table produced it. The check moved to where it
can be true — the pools themselves — and the card-level assertion kept to what is
observable: nothing left unresolved.

Bench: 0 lines.

### 138.4 Where the paparazzi stands

Decoded so far, for the next round: gate `fame >= 75.0f` (§136); body and narrative
from a `DataHub::GetRandomPaparazziScenario` row through `BracketParser`; three
buttons built in this order — `Pose for his photo` (#34352), `Pretend he's not
there` (#34511), `Cover my face` (#16565); lane journals `{0} I smiled for his
picture.` (#69613), `{0} I pretended not to notice him.` (#69597), `{0} I covered my
face to make it hard for him to take my picture.` (#69547); and a row containing
`paparazzo` pushes a `ScenarioCustomAttack` with `ImpactDiscipline(3)` +
`ImpactKarma(3)`. Not yet read: which lane owns which impact pair, and the shared
tail's virtual call at `[hero+0x458]`.

## 139. The paparazzi card, and the virtual call that turned out to be fame

§138 stopped on the shared tail's virtual call at `[hero+0x458]`. It is settled, at
runtime rather than by inference: an object of `SimHero` was allocated on the device,
its vtable read, and slot `0x458` resolved to a module-relative `0x2a87f60` —
`SimHero::ImpactFame`, the interface wrapper §136 documented.

```
slot458  0x77aa517f60   - module base  ->  0x2a87f60
static   0x73F049A000 + 0x2a87f60     =   0x73f2f21f60   SimHero::ImpactFame
```

### 139.1 The card

`ScenarioFamePaparazzi` draws one row of `a16_paparazzi-scenarios-enc`
(`Scenario`, `Log Version`), resolves both through the port's bracket parser, and
offers three buttons. `ChoiceSelectedAtIndex @0x73f3bd7e28` dispatches on the
**label text**, not the index:

| lane | gate | journal | impacts |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Pose for his photo` | `Contains(choice,"pose")` | `{0} I smiled for his picture.` #69613 | Discipline 3, Karma 3, **Fame 2** |
| `Pretend he's not there` | fall-through | `{0} I pretended not to notice him.` #69597 | Discipline 2, Karma 2 |
| `Cover my face` | `Contains(choice,"cover")` | `{0} I covered my face…` #69547 | **Fame −1** |

`{0}` is the row's own `Log Version`, resolved. A row whose text contains `attack`
pushes a `ScenarioCustomAttack` with `ImpactFame(4)`; that follow-up card is not
ported, so the port skips it (shortcut at the code).

### 139.2 An arithmetic lesson worth keeping

`ImpactFame` takes an **impact score**, not points: it applies
`pointsForImpact` internally. So `ImpactFame(2)` is **+8 fame**, `ImpactFame(-1)` is
**−4**, and `ImpactFame(4)` is +16. The first version of the test assumed `+2 / -1`
and failed with `final fame 84, want 81` on a life with one pose and one cover —
which is exactly `80 + 8 - 4`. The card was right and the test's model was wrong;
the model was corrected, not the code.

### 139.3 Verification

`tools/test_paparazzi.py`, 40 famous lives:

```
paparazzi cards: 69
lanes: {'Pose for his photo': 31, 'Cover my face': 20, "Pretend he's not there": 18}
lives at fame 75 with a card: 9 of 10
ok
```

Per card: age ≥ 18, the label is one of the three, the journal ends with that lane's
tail, no unresolved `<token>` in body or journal, and the stat deltas equal
`pointsForImpact` of the lane's scores. Per life: `final.fame` equals
`80 + 8·poses − 4·covers`, clamped — the fame wiring checked end to end, not just
the card. Plus the gate: fame 0 and 74 never produce the card, fame 75 does (the
comparison is inclusive, as `b.ge` says).

### 139.4 A spec switch the gate needed

Nothing in the port moves fame except this card, so a famous hero was unreachable in
a scripted life at all. `"fame": 80` is now a spec key, next to `royal`, `vampire`
and the rest: the game earns fame through a career, and the port needs a way to
stand at the gate before the career that feeds it exists.

## 140. A card-shaped view: the decode tool the sprint needed

Two cards in a row ate a whole round each, and neither time was the card the
problem. `ScenarioLoverCounselingPush.ChoiceSelectedAtIndex` is **1,111
instructions**; `ScenarioExLoverPaternityTestCourtOrder`'s pair is 1,500. Almost all
of that is compiler output: `List<T>.Add` closures, LINQ enumerators,
`String::Format` wrappers, il2cpp runtime helpers, vtable stubs. The card itself —
the game methods it calls, the immediate arguments, the fields it writes — is a few
dozen lines buried inside.

`tools/cardview.py` prints those few dozen lines and collapses the rest:

```
python3 tools/cardview.py 0x73f3dee5c4 240
python3 tools/cardview.py --method ScenarioExLoverPaternityTestCourtOrder::ChoiceSelectedAtIndex 200
```

Four rules decide what survives:

* a `bl` to a **managed** method whose name is not framework (`System.`, `<>c`, and
  the SDK namespaces are dropped) — the card's own vocabulary;
* `mov w1, #imm` — the argument the next such call takes, which is how an impact
  value is read;
* `str` into a slot the scenario owns (`0x38` Title, `0x48` Body, `0x108`/`0xb8`
  choice lists, `0x110` and `0x132` flags, `0x170`/`0x178`/`0x180` the class's own
  fields);
* a slot load whose literal is already cached in `tools/lit_cells.json`, printed
  with its text.

Everything else becomes `... N`.

### 140.1 What it turns a card into

`ScenarioExLoverPaternityTestCourtOrder`, both methods, 530 instructions:

```
73f3dee748  mov  w1, #6                ; the argument that follows
73f3dee76c  bl   SimLover::ExRelationshipStatusString
73f3dee7ec  mov  w1, #5
73f3dee7f4  bl   SimPerson::PronounStringForType
73f3dee828  mov  w1, #1
73f3dee834  bl   SimPerson::PronounStringForType
73f3dee8e4  str  x0, [x19, #0x48]     ; Body
73f3deea50  str  x0, [x19, #0x180]    ; _narrative
73f3deea70  bl   ScenarioChoice::.ctor
73f3deeac8  bl   ScenarioChoice::.ctor  ; two buttons
73f3deeb00  str  x21, [x19, #0x108]   ; the choice list
--- handler ---
73f3deec74  mov  w1, #-2
73f3deec7c  bl   SimPerson::ImpactKarma
73f3deec98  mov  w1, #-2
73f3deeca0  bl   SimPerson::ImpactDiscipline
73f3deed20  mov  w1, #0x26            ; crime type 38
73f3deed28  bl   SimHero::GetCrimeScenarioForCrimeType
73f3deed84  bl   Scenario::.ctor       ; the pushed card
73f3deedcc  bl   LifeLog::Log
```

That is the card: two ex-status nouns, two pronouns, a Body and a narrative, two
buttons, one lane that moves karma and discipline by −2 and one that **pushes a
crime scenario for crime type 38** — a court order the ex took out, and breaking it
is a crime the game already models.

### 140.2 Verification

`tools/test_cardview.py` runs the tool on two cards whose calls the report already
knows — `LoverBreakUp` (§125) and the court-order card — and asserts the expected
calls and field writes survive while the kept-line count stays under twenty. A
filter change that hides the logic fails there rather than quietly costing the next
decode an hour.

```
cardview keeps the card and drops the codegen: ok
```

### 140.3 What this changes about the sprint

Every remaining card starts from a 20-40 line view of itself instead of a
1,000-instruction dump. The two cards this round could not finish are now ~20 lines
each, and the third one (`LoverCounselingPush`) shows its skeleton the same way:
`RelationshipStatusString().ToLower()`, two `PronounStringForType`, one Body write,
three `ScenarioChoice` ctors.

## 141. Birth control: the state three lover cards need

The sprint's next three cards are all written around one flag the port does not
have. The game keeps it on the person and stamps two ages on the life:

```
Person::get_OnBirthControl / set_OnBirthControl
Life::get_AgeAtLastWentOnBirthControl / set_AgeAtLastWentOnBirthControl
Life::get_AgeAtLastWentOffBirthControl / set_AgeAtLastWentOffBirthControl
```

`Hero` now carries `onBirthControl` plus the two ages, the script accepts
`"birthControl": true`, and `final` reports it.

### 141.1 What the cards look like, through the §140 view

`ScenarioLoverDemandsBirthControl` (refresh 600 B, handler 1,704 B), decoded far
enough to know its shape:

```
73f3920718  SimLover::RelationshipStatusString        ; {0} of the body
73f392078c  str x0, [x19, #0x48]                      ; Body
73f39207c4  ScenarioChoice::.ctor                     ; buttons 1 and 2
73f3920808  ScenarioChoice::.ctor
73f3920848  mov w1, #2
73f3920854  SimPerson::PronounStringForType           ; {0} of the third label
73f3920890  ScenarioChoice::.ctor                     ; button 3
--- handler ---
73f3920be4  GameReference::GetRandomNumber(0, 100)    ; the argue roll
73f3920c34  ScenarioLoverArgues::.ctor                ; it pushes an argue card
73f3920cb4  SimPerson::ImpactDiscipline(-3)
73f3920d34  DataHub::GetRandomArguerAction
73f3920e48  GameReference::PickRandomFromStringArray
73f3920e74  SimLover::RelationshipStatusString
73f3920f2c  LifeLog::Log
```

and its three literals, read out of the slots:

```
body      'Your {0}, {1}, wants you to go on birth control.\n\nWhat will you do?'
button 1  'Agree to go on birth control'
button 2  'Refuse to go on birth control'
button 3  'Argue with {0}'        ({0} = PronounStringForType(2))
```

`ScenarioLoverStopsBirthControl` is the mirror (2,820 B handler) and
`ScenarioBirthControlHero` is the hero's own.

### 141.2 Why the state landed without a card

All three need the flag to be meaningful, and the flag needs a writer. Porting a
card first would have meant a card whose effect is invisible — accept, and nothing
changes. The order here is deliberate: the state, its spec switch and its JSON view
land first, the card that flips it lands next.

`tools/test_birth_control.py` pins what a state with no card can be pinned on: off
by default in every life, on when the spec says so (both spellings), and a
non-boolean value is a parse error with its own message rather than a silent false.

```
birth control state: ok
```

### 141.3 A parser bug this found

The first cut read `"birthControl": true` as *not a boolean*: `findValue` returns
the position right after the colon, which is a **space** in every JSON this project
writes, and the comparison started there.
## 142. The birth-control demand, and the first lover card of the sprint

`ScenarioLoverDemandsBirthControl` is the first card built on §141's flag. Its three
literals came out of the class's own slots — body `Your {0}, {1}, wants you to go on
birth control.\n\nWhat will you do?`, buttons `Agree to go on birth control` /
`Refuse to go on birth control` / `Argue with {0}`, journals
`I agreed to go on birth control following {0} suggestion.` (#23417) and
`{0} tried to get me to go on birth control but I refused.` (#70365) — and the agree
lane writes the flag on the person (`strb w10, [hero+0x50]`).

The card offers **two** buttons, not three. The third — `Argue with {0}` — opens the
`ScenarioLoverArgues` flow through `DataHub::GetRandomArguerAction` and
`PickRandomFromStringArray`, and that flow is not ported; offering a button whose
consequence the port cannot produce would be worse than not offering it. The
omission is written at the code, next to the lanes that do exist.

```
agree   'I agreed to go on birth control following his/her suggestion.'
        hero.onBirthControl = true, hero.ageWentOnBirthControl = hero.age
refuse  'My girlfriend, Alex, tried to get me on birth control but I refused.'
        no stat move, no state change
```

The card is gated on a partner who exists and is not already satisfied
(`!h.onBirthControl`), which is what the class's own gate reads before it draws.
