## 143. The view's blind spot, and the mirror card's decode

§140's filter drops framework calls, and that included `String::Contains` — which is
how several cards dispatch on the **choice's text**. The paparazzi decode in §139
had to find those comparisons by hand, and the mirror card below is written the same
way, so the rule is fixed before it costs another hour.

`cardview` now keeps `System.String::Contains` / `StartsWith` / `EndsWith` / `Equals`
and marks them:

```
73f3bd7f88  bl  System.String::Contains   <== label dispatch
73f3bd8018  bl  System.String::Contains   <== label dispatch
73f3bd80bc  bl  System.String::Contains   <== label dispatch
73f3bd8140  bl  System.String::Contains   <== label dispatch
```

Four comparisons in the paparazzi handler, which is exactly its dispatch. The test
(`tools/test_cardview_dispatch.py`) requires them to stay visible *and* the card's
own calls (`ImpactDiscipline`, `ScenarioCustomAttack::.ctor`) to stay beside them.

### 143.1 `ScenarioLoverStopsBirthControl`, decoded as far as it goes

The mirror of §142: the partner wants **off** the contraception. Refresh 636 B,
handler 2,820 B. Through the fixed view:

```
RelationshipStatusString          ; the {0} of the body
PronounStringForType(1)           ; the {2} of the body
str x0, [x19, #0x48]              ; Body
ScenarioChoice::.ctor  x3         ; three buttons
--- handler ---
ImpactKarma(-2), ImpactDiscipline(-2)
GetRandomNumber(0, 100)           ; the argue roll
PickRandomFromStringArray
PronounStringForType(4 / 5 / 1)
```

and its literals:

```
body      'Your {0}, {1}, wants to stop taking {2} birth control.'
button    'Yes, stop taking it'          'Disapprove of that idea'
button    'Convincing contraceptive'     'Objection!'   'Why stop?'
journal   "{0} wants to stop taking {1} birth control. I told {2} I don't approve of that."

```

**The lane mapping is not read**, and that is where this round stops. Five buttons'

## 144. The mirror card, and how its mapping actually works

§143 stopped because the lane mapping was unknown. It is known now, and the way it
was found is the lesson: **the handler reads the chosen button's own Title and
dispatches on its text**, exactly like the paparazzi (§139).

```
73f39213e4  ldr  x0, [x19, #0x108]   ; the choice list
73f39213f0  mov  w1, w20             ; the index the game passed in
73f39213fc  blr  [x8, #0x2e8]        ; ArrayList<ScenarioChoice>[index]
73f3921444  bl   System.String::ToLower
73f3921458  ldr  x8, [.., #0x928]    ; slot 0x5ca6b70 = 'disapprove'
73f3921474  bl   System.String::Contains
73f3921478  tbz  w0, #0, #0x73f392193c   ; not "disapprove" -> the other lane
```

So the card is indexed by the engine and then *classified by its own label*. That is
why no `cmp w1, #0/1/2` exists, and why §143 could not find a lane table: there is
none.

### 144.1 The two lanes

| lane | gate | effect | journal |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Yes, stop taking it` (#47510) | not `Contains("disapprove")` | `strb wzr,[hero+0x50]` — birth control **off** | #70379 `{0} wants to stop taking {1} birth control. I agreed that was a good idea.` |
| `Disapprove of that idea` (#17777) | `Contains("disapprove")` | `ImpactKarma(-2)`, `ImpactDiscipline(-2)` | #70380 `{0} wants to stop taking {1} birth control. I told {2} I don't approve of that.` |

Body: `Your {0}, {1}, wants to stop taking {2} birth control.` with `{2}` the
partner's possessive. Ported with two of the game's three buttons — the third opens
the argue flow, which is still unported, and the `GetRandomNumber(0,100)` roll that
follows the disapprove lane is not modelled.

### 144.2 Verification

`tools/test_lover_stops_birth_control.py`, 80 lives that start on birth control:

```
lanes: {'Disapprove of that idea': 15, 'Yes, stop taking it': 15}
lives that stopped: 15
ok
```

Per card: the class's own body sentence, one of the two labels, that lane's journal,
and the deltas — **`karma -8, discipline -8`** for disapprove, nothing for accept,
because the handler passes an impact *score* of −2 (the §139 lesson again). Per life:
whichever birth-control card came **last** decides `final.birthControl`, which is why
the two tests each own their direction: 142 proves the flag gets set, 144 proves it
gets cleared, and neither claims more.

### 144.3 The gate is the mirror

The demand asks only a partner who is **not** on birth control (§142); this card asks
only one who **is**. A hero who starts on birth control is asked to stop; a hero who
is not is never asked. Both directions are asserted.

## 145. What the sprint is actually blocked on, measured

Three cards in a row reached the same wall from different directions, so this round
stops adding cards and records the wall. Every claim below is from the §140 view.

### 145.1 The blockers

| card | needs | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `ScenarioLoverArgues` | a reason switch over ~10 ctors | 10 `.ctor` overloads; Refresh 0x73f3dac5a0 formats `SimDisease`, `SimPet`, `SimJewel`, `SimRichSocialMedia`, `SimMagazineOpportunity`, `SimChild`, `DataCelebrity`, `SimHouse` variants |

Four of the five need **children**. That is the single largest hole left, and it is

### 145.2 Why no card shipped this round

Each of the five can be faked in ten minutes and none can be faked honestly: a
counseling card that never mentions the child it is about, an argue card that picks
a reason the game did not pick, a magazine card with a fabricated opportunity. The
probes would then defend the fabrication — which is exactly the failure mode §135
found in eleven probes that had encoded an older bug.

### 145.4 The order this implies

1. **A child model.** One field set on the live `Life`, born from a partner, aged

## 146. The child model

The game keeps a `SimChild` array on the life. `SimChild` has 86 methods and 30
getters, so the model was scoped to what the blocked cards actually read rather than
to everything the class can do:

```
SimChild.ChildType / RelationshipStatus      who the child is to the hero
SimChild.MovedOut                            has it left home
SimChild.IsChildWithCurrentLover             which partner it belongs to
SimChild.NumTimesHeroAskedToTakePaternityTest the court-order card's own counter
SimChild.Spouse / ExSpouseArray / GrandchildArray      not modelled yet
```

`Life::children` now holds `{name, lastName, female, age, alive, movedOut,
otherParent, withCurrentLover, paternityAsked}`, each child ages with the hero, and
`final.children` prints the array.

### 146.1 What it deliberately does not do

**No birth.** The game gets a child through its baby scenarios; the port has none,
and a lifecycle line invented for it would be text the game does not have — the
exact thing §145 refused. The array is reachable through a script key instead
(`"children": 2`), the same way `fame` (§139) and `birthControl` (§141) were
reachable before the cards that move them existed.

**No name.** The fixture leaves `name` empty rather than drawing one: the cards that
read a child name it from the parent it belongs to, and a name drawn at setup would
not be the one the game would have drawn.

### 146.2 Verification

`tools/test_children.py`:

```
child model: ok
```

No children unless the script asks; the fixture puts them on the life with the right
genders, aging with the hero (`kid.age >= final.age`, since they are born before the
run); `MovedOut` implies an adult; the count is bounded and a bad value is a parse
error with its own message.

Bench: 0 lines. `test_play`, `test_family`, `test_birth_control` unchanged — the
model is additive, and nothing draws from a stream it should not.

### 146.3 What it unblocks

* `ScenarioExLoverPaternityTestCourtOrder` (§143's decode): `_exLover` + `_child`,
  and its `paternityAsked` counter is now a field.
* `ScenarioLoverCounselingPush`: `Life::get_ChildArray` + `IsLivingWithHero` are
  `Life::children` and a per-child flag.
* The whole child family (custody, discipline, paternity results), which the port
  had no state for at all.

### 147.1 The lane rule, proved

The handler classifies the chosen label, as §144 established for this family:

```
73f3deec40  ldr  x8, [.., #0x10]     ; slot 0x5c35010
73f3deec54  bl   System.String::Contains
73f3deec58  tbz  w0, #0, #0x73f3deed40
```

and slot `0x5c35010` holds the literal **`'refuse'`**. So:

* **Refuse to take the test** → `ImpactKarma(-2)`, `ImpactDiscipline(-2)`, then
  `SimHero::GetCrimeScenarioForCrimeType(0x26)` = crime type **38**, a
  `Scenario` is constructed from it and linked at `[self+0x128]`, and the journal is
  logged. Refusing a court order is a crime the game already has a name for.
* **Take the test** → the other branch builds a card, links it the same way at
  `[self+0x128]`, and writes `[new+0x132]` and `[new+0x170]`: it pushes the
  **results** card.

### 147.2 Why the card is not ported yet

Five of the six placeholders are decided: `{0}` the ex's relationship word
(`ExRelationshipStatusString`), `{1}` the ex's name, `{2}` the ex's pronoun
capitalised, and the narrative's `{4}` mirrored. The three that are not are `{3}`
`{4}` `{5}` of the body — the child's relation word, name and age — and the port's
children have **no name** (§146). A card that prints `...the father of your son ,`
with a hole in it is worse than the card not firing.

### 147.3 The next micro-task, stated exactly

Give the child fixture a name and the three body placeholders follow: `{3}` is the
child's relation word, `{4}` its name, `{5}` its age in the family's own phrasing.
The decode above is complete enough that this is now a data question, not a
disassembly question.

## 148. Children are named, and the last placeholder is still open

§147 said the court-order card needed one thing: a named child. That half is done.
`Sim::firstNameFor(bool)` is the public way to the game's own name pool (the one
`drawFirstName` already drew partners and siblings from), and the children fixture
uses it, so `Life::children` now carries real names:

```
[('Kye', False, 6), ('Dula', True, 7)]
```

`tools/test_children.py` requires every child to be named, capitalised and to carry a
first name only. Bench 0 lines.

### 148.1 Where the card still stops

Reading the Refresh's `String::Format` argument array settles four of the five
arguments and not the fifth:

```
73f3dee76c  SimLover::ExRelationshipStatusString(6)   {0} the ex's own word
            [ex+0x10]+0x18                            {1} the ex's name
73f3dee7f4  PronounStringForType(5)                   {2} He / She
73f3dee834  PronounStringForType(1)                   ...
73f3dee860  str  x22, [x21, #0x38]                    the args array, 6 slots
73f3dee8dc  Format(cell 0x5cc5bb0, args)              the body
```

The body reads `...believes you are the father of {3} {4}, {5}.` — `{3}` is a
relation word, `{4}` the child's name and `{5}` still unknown, and the argument array
is built by stores into `[x21, #0x20..0x40]` whose sources are loaded far above the
`Format`. Guessing `{5}` would put a wrong clause in the most legally explicit
sentence in the family.

### 148.2 What that means for the next attempt

Two ways out, in order of cheapness:

1. **Watch it print.** The card only fires for a hero with an ex and a child, which
   the harness can be talked into (`children` fixture + an ex), and one capture of
   the real body answers `{3}`/`{5}` in a single read.
2. **Resolve the argument array backwards** from the six stores to their sources.

Option 1 is one harness session; option 2 is another hour of disassembly for the
same answer. The round records the choice rather than spending it.

## 149. The court-order card, and the six arguments it took

§148 left one placeholder open. Reading the argument array settled all six, and the
body turns out to name the child twice — once by age-and-relation, once by name:

```
args[0] [x21+0x20]  ExRelationshipStatusString(6).ToLower()   'ex-girlfriend'
args[1] [x21+0x28]  [ex+0x10]+0x18                            the ex's first name
args[2] [x21+0x30]  PronounStringForType(5) on the ex          she / he
args[3] [x21+0x38]  PronounStringForType(1) on the ex          her / his
args[4] [x21+0x40]  Format('{0}-year old {1}', age, son/daughter)
args[5] [x21+0x48]  [child+0x10]+0x18                         the child's first name
```

so the card reads *"Your ex-girlfriend, Robin Averill, has obtained a court order
requiring you to take a paternity test. She believes you are the father of her
0-year old son, Kye."* — and the lane rule is `Contains("refuse")`, proved in §147.

### 149.1 Two fixture bugs the card exposed

1. **Children were older than the hero.** The fixture created them at age `1 + c` and
   aged them with him, so a hero of 83 had a "72-year old son". `Child` now carries
   `bornAtHeroAge` (§146's array gained one field) and a child only ages once the
   hero passes it: born at 20, four-year staggered, so a life has children of
   different ages.
2. **A paternity test over a grown man.** Once the ages were right the card still
   fired over a 64-year-old. The game's own gate was not read, so the port now
   refuses to offer it once the child is past infancy — written at the code as a
   shortcut, not disguised as knowledge.

### 149.2 Reaching it on purpose

A court order needs an ex **and** a small child, and a break-up inside two years of
a birth is too rare to test against. The script gained `"ex": true`, which seeds one
named ex-lover and makes the fixture children hers — the same kind of fixture as
`fame`, `birthControl` and `children`.

### 149.3 Verification

`tools/test_paternity_court_order.py`, 30 lives:

```
cards: 2
lanes: {'Take the test': 1, 'Refuse to take the test': 1}
ok
```

The body is matched against the full six-placeholder pattern (ex word, ex name,
pronoun, possessive, child age, son/daughter, child name), the pronoun and possessive
must agree, the journal must open with the ex named the same way, and the lanes move
what the handler moves: **karma −8, discipline −8** on refuse, nothing on take. The
counter `paternityAsked` is what stops the card repeating.

### 149.4 What is still a shortcut

* `Take the test` pushes the results card in the game; the port only moves the
  counter.
* `Refuse to take the test` pushes a crime scenario for crime type **38**; the port
  only moves the stats.
* The card's own gate (`_exLover` + `_child` + not-yet-asked) is inferred from the
  fields; the infancy limit is the port's.

## 150. The result of the test, and a decision the game makes by rolling

`ScenarioExLoverPaternityTestResults` is what the court order's *take* lane pushes,
and it closes the gap §149 left open — a hero who complies now sees an answer.

```
positive  titles  'New responsibilities' / 'Proof is in the pudding' / 'The DNA matches'
          body    'The paternity test for your {0}, {1}, {2} came back positive!'
negative  titles  'One less stress' / 'Positively negative' / 'Get outta here!'
          body    'The paternity test for your {0}, {1}, {2} came back negative!'
          journal both, mirrored in the first person ('for my …')
```

### 150.1 The game rolls; the port stores

The card does not read a fact — it decides one: `GetRandomNumber(0, 1000)` against a
hero field, then a second roll for the branch. Paternity in this game is a coin, not
a record.

The port keeps the answer instead, on the child (`Child::isHeroes`), and says so at
the code. The reason is testability rather than taste: a fixture child that belongs
to the ex must stay hers across runs, or every assertion downstream becomes a coin
flip. It is a **documented divergence**, not a reproduction — the first such one in
this family.

### 150.2 The chain, end to end

```
court order, take lane  ->  life.pendingCards.push_back(kPendingPaternityResults)
same age-up, drained    ->  paternityResultsYear builds the answer
```

That is §133's queue doing the job it was built for, and the first two-card chain in
the port that both cards are real.

### 150.3 Verification

`tools/test_paternity_court_order.py`, extended:

```
cards: 2
lanes: {'Take the test': 1, 'Refuse to take the test': 1}
results: {'positive': 0, 'negative': 1} chained after the court order: 1
ok
```

Per result card: the body is the class's sentence with one of the two endings, a
title is always set, the button is one of the two, the journal is the same sentence
in the first person, and it rides **the same age** as the court order that pushed it.
Bench 0 lines; `test_play` and `test_children` green.

### 150.4 Shortcuts

* the roll is replaced by `Child::isHeroes`, as above;
* the body's three placeholders are filled as *relation-word, child-noun, name* —
  the argument split was not read, and the sentence is correct in English either
  way;
* a positive result does not yet start child support (`SimChild.ChildSupport`), which
  the game's dismiss handler applies.

## 151. A child is born

§146 said the array existed but nothing filled it. It fills itself now.

The game runs birth through `SimPregnancy` and two cards: `ScenarioPregnancy` asks the
hero about the pregnancy and `ScenarioBirth` reports the arrival —
`'{0} just gave birth to a baby {1}{2}!\n\nWhat will you name {3}?'` (#70148).

The port carries the pregnancy as two flags on the hero (`loverPregnant`,
`loverPregnantByHero`) and reports the arrival as a report card:

```
Your wife, Layla, just gave birth to a baby boy!
I named him Minji.
My wife, Layla gave birth to a baby boy named Minji.
```

### 151.1 What the port does differently, on the record

* **the naming question is cut.** There is no text entry in the port, so the body
  stops before `What will you name {3}?` and the child is named from the game's own
  pool instead. The line's two halves are the class's sentence; the question is the
  only part removed.
* **the conception roll is a port coin** (one in twelve per year, partner 18-45).
  The game's own roll lives behind `SimPregnancy` and the hookup cards.
* **`OtherParent` and `isHeroes` are set from the pairing**, so a born child
  belongs to the partner it was born to — which is what the paternity family
  (§149) needed to stop being a fixture.

### 151.2 Verification

`tools/test_birth.py`, 30 lives with partners:

```
births: 6 lives with children: 4
ok
```

Per birth: the body matches the class's sentence (partner word, partner name, boy or
girl), the journal names the child, **that child is on the life** with the partner as
`otherParent`, the right gender, `isHeroes: true`, and an age equal to the hero's age
minus the year of the birth. Per life: no partner, no children.

Bench 0 lines; `test_children`, `test_paternity_court_order` and `test_play` green.

### 151.3 What this unblocks

* `ScenarioLoverCounselingPush` — its handler reads `get_ChildArray` and
  `IsLivingWithHero`, and children now arrive without a fixture.
* The paternity family's `isHeroes` divergence (§150) can finally produce a
  **positive** result, because a born child is the hero's.
* Custody, child discipline, the child's own lifecycle lines: all of it has state to
  stand on now.

## 152. The counseling demand

The card §145 called blocked on children — its handler reads `Life::get_ChildArray`
and `SimChild::IsLivingWithHero` before it formats — is in, and it needed neither:
the child read turns out to be for the *subject* of the session, not a requirement to
hold one.

```
RefreshScenario @0x73f3db367c   Format(cell 0x5cc4418, status lowered, name, pronoun)
  body  'Your {0}, {1}, is demanding that you visit a relationship counselor
         with {2}.\n\nWhat will you do?'
  buttons  'Agree to go' (0x5ca2ae0)   'Refuse to go' (0x5c39c00)
```

### 152.1 The lane rule, and the two extra comparisons

`ChoiceSelectedAtIndex @0x73f3db38c4` compares the label against four literals:

```
0x5c35048  'agree'      -> the session happens
0x5c35010  'refuse'     -> the refusal
0x5c35678  '<disease>'  \  the subject the session is about
0x5c62aa0  '<addiction>' /
```

| lane | effect | journal |
|---|---|---|
| `Agree to go` | `ImpactDiscipline(2)` → +8 | #23416 `I agreed to attend relationship counseling with {0}.` |
| `Refuse to go` | none read | #70366 `{0} tried to make me attend relationship counseling with {1} but I refused.` |

The two `{0}` forms are the partner named twice: capitalised at the start of the
refusal, lower-case mid-sentence in the agreement.

### 152.2 Verification

`tools/test_lover_counseling.py`, 30 lives:

```
lanes: {'Agree to go': 6, 'Refuse to go': 7}
ok
```

Per card: the body matches the class's sentence with the pronoun agreeing with the
partner's own gender, the age is at least 18, the label is one of the two, and the
journal is that lane's sentence — with `discipline +8` on agree and nothing on
refuse. No partner, no card.

Bench 0 lines; `test_birth` and `test_play` green.

### 152.3 Still a shortcut

The `<disease>` and `<addiction>` subjects are not modelled: the port's session is
always about the relationship itself, which is what the body says anyway. The
`GetRandomNumber(0,100)` roll the handler makes after the refusal is not modelled
either.

## 153. The partner argues: one reason out of ten

`ScenarioLoverArgues` is the class both birth-control cards' third button opens, and
§145 listed it as a blocker because it is **one class with ten constructors** and a
Refresh that switches on which object it was built with (pet, jewel, disease,
magazine, gift, child, celebrity, house, string pair, int reason).

The int reason is the one the port can feed, and it is small:

```
73f3dac9ac  ldr  w8, [x19, #0x16c]     ; _reason
73f3dac9b8  cmp  w8, #1
73f3dac9c0  b.eq #0x73f3daca00
73f3dac9e0  slot 0x5cc3fd8             ; '{0} is arguing with you because you cheated on {1}.'
73f3daca28  slot 0x5c42d50             ; '{0} is arguing with you because you gave {1} {2}.'
```

Two flavours: cheating, or a bad gift. The port implements the first.

### 153.1 A report, not a dialogue

The card's buttons are not ported — the handler is as variant-rich as the Refresh —
so it arrives as a **report**, the same shape as the break-up announcement (§125):

```
She is arguing with you because you cheated on your girlfriend, Adele Radkins.
journal: She is arguing with me because I cheated on her.
```

and it rides the same age-up as the hookup that caused it, through §133's queue:
`seduceYear`'s cheating branch pushes `kPendingLoverArgues` where it already applied
the karma and discipline penalty.

### 153.2 Verification

`tools/test_lover_argues.py`, 40 lives:

```
argue reports: 1 same-age as the hookup: 1
ok
NaN

Per report: the subject pronoun opens it, the partner's word is in it, it carries
**no buttons**, and the journal is the first-person form. Per chain: it sits at the
same age as the hookup in the event before it.

Bench 0 lines; `test_play` and `test_lover_counseling` green.

### 153.3 What is left of the class

Nine constructors: pet, jewel, disease, magazine, gift, child, celebrity, house and
the string pair. Each is a branch of the same Refresh and a branch of the same
handler — the shape is now known, so they are content work rather than discovery.
The gift flavour (`reason 0`) is the cheapest of them and needs a gift name the port
already has tables for.

## 154. The gift flavour is not reachable, and that is the finding

§153 called `reason 0` — `'{0} is arguing with you because you gave {1} {2}.'` —
the cheapest of the nine remaining variants, because the port already has the gift
tables. It was wired: the gift card's refusal lane set the gift's own description and
pushed the argue report through the queue.

It never fired. Forty lives, no argue report from a gift — and the reason is one
level down:

```
titles containing 'gift', 40 lives:
  'The worst Christmas gift we ever received'   2   (dumb-scenario pool)
  'Visa gift card'                              1   (dumb-scenario pool)
  'The best gift we ever received'              1   (dumb-scenario pool)
  'Whether or not it is okay to regift a gift'  1   (dumb-scenario pool)
  'A gift refused'                              0   <-- giftYear's own card
```

**`giftYear` (§89) never produces a card in a played life.** Its refusal pool needs a
partner whose pride or craziness is at least 50, and its 30% coin is spent inside
`relationshipYear`, after every earlier pool in that chain has had its own chance to
claim the year. Whatever the exact cause, the effect is measurable: none of the 40
lives spent a year on a gift.

### 154.1 What was done instead of shipping dead code

The flavour was reverted. `loverArguesYear` handles `reason 1` only, and the code says
why: *reason 0 — the refused gift — is not wired: the gift card's refusal pool never
fires in the port.* A branch nobody can reach is not a ported feature; it is a claim
the probes would eventually have to defend.

`test_lover_argues` still passes (the cheating report and its same-age chain), bench
is 0 lines.

### 154.2 The open question this leaves

`giftYear` is a *ported* card (§89) that never appears in play. Either its gate is
wrong, or its place in the chain starves it — both are checkable, and both matter more
than one more argue flavour. That is the next thing worth a round.

## 155. Correction: §154 was wrong about which card never fires

§154 claimed `giftYear` never produces a card. It does. Forty lives, counting events
by the table they came from rather than by their titles:

```
a16_gifts-enc          31 events   ('ShamWow set', 'Nintendo Switch', 'Book', ...)
a16_anniversary-gift-enc  3 events
```

The mistake was in the measurement, not the code: §154 searched **titles** for the
word 'gift', and a gift card's title is the *gift's own name* ('NutriBullet
blender'), not the word 'gift'. Counting `table` instead shows the card firing 34
times across 40 lives.

### 155.1 What is actually unreachable, and why

The refusal lane, and the reason is structural rather than statistical: **the refusal
pools are only consulted for property gifts.**

```cpp
if (!kind.empty() && p.has("Descriptive Name Override")) ...   // the property branch
  std::vector<size_t> refusals;
  for (size_t r = 0; r < pool.size(); ++r) {
    const bool rowPride = pool.flag(r, "Prideful");
    const bool rowCrazy = pool.flag(r, "Crazy");
    if (rowPride == rowCrazy) continue;      // a row names one of the two traits
    ...
  }
```

A shop gift (`a16_gifts-enc`, 31 of the 34 events) has no refusal pool at all: the
hero offers it, the partner takes it, the relationship score moves. A refusal needs a
**house or a vehicle** to be offered — `a16_gift-rejections-house-enc`,
`a16_gift-rejections-vehicle-enc` — which needs the hero to own one and to give it
away.

So `reason 0` of the argue card (`'{0} is arguing with you because you gave {1}
{2}.'`) stays unwired for a precise reason: **the port has no shop-gift refusal**, and
the property-gift refusal it does have is a different sentence. §154's revert was
right; its explanation was not.

### 155.2 The lesson, since two rounds have now paid for it

Counting by **title** is how §154 measured, and titles in this port are content
(gift names, scenario titles), not card names. `table` + `row` is the identity;
`title` is what the player reads. Every future "does card X fire" question should
count `table`.

## 156. A census of the tables a life actually touches

§155 ended with a question: how many other "ported" cards never fire? The check is
mechanical — count the `table` of every event across a batch of lives and diff it
against the `a16_*` names the sources mention.

`tools/tablecensus.py`:

```
python3 tools/tablecensus.py --seeds 20 --ages 70 --only a16_prison \
  --switches '{"prison": true}'

lives: 40
tables referenced in src/: 11
tables a life touched: 8
referenced but never touched: 3
  a16_prison-bully-outbound
  a16_prison-jobs-enc
  a16_prisoner-juvenile-crimes-enc
```

### 156.1 The two numbers that made it honest

The first version diffed the **whole** source against 60 lives and reported **799 of
857** tables untouched — which is true and useless, because the reference set includes
tables named only by a *token* (`resolve()` handles dozens of names it may never see),
and because a single life cannot enable thirty families at once. A whole-source census
measures the batch, not the port.

`--only PREFIX` is the fix: one family at a time, with only that family's switches on.
Then the number means something — 11 referenced, 8 touched, 3 questions.

### 156.2 What the three prison tables are

* `a16_prisoner-juvenile-crimes-enc` — the crime list a juvenile prisoner is drawn
  from; the port's prison cards may never reach a juvenile.
* `a16_prison-jobs-enc` — prison work assignments; if the port has no prison job
  lane, this is a card that was written and never wired.
* `a16_prison-bully-outbound` — the *outbound* half of a bully exchange, which needs
  an inbound bully card to answer.

Each is either an unreachable gate or a two-stage card whose first half never fires —
exactly the shape §154 mis-diagnosed. That is the next question worth a round, and it
now has a tool that asks it per family.

## 157. The census measures the wrong thing three times

§156 shipped `tools/tablecensus.py` with the prison result as its demonstration. Running
it across every family showed the instrument is weaker than that one number suggested,
and the three attempts say something useful about how this port draws its cards.

| reference set | what it counts | silent, all families |
|---|---|---|
| every `a16_*` in the sources | 857 names, including token dictionaries and name pools | **438**, then **799** on a wider batch |
| `fire(` / `pickRow(` / `renderRow(` sites | tables a card or a sentence draws from | **70** |
| `fire("…")` / `renderRow("…")` only | tables presented directly as a card | **0** |

Each number is true and none of them answers the question:

* the first counts tables the port *mentions*, and most mentions are tokens (`<insult>`,
  `<vehicle>`) or name pools that never become an event's `table`;
* the second counts tables a card *reads data from*, and those are never an event's
  `table` either;
* the third counts only the families that name their table at the call site — the
  prison cards do, and cult, hustler, dealer and vampire do not: they fetch a table
  into a variable first and pass it to `renderRow`.

So `silent 0` for cult is not a clean bill of health, it is the tool not seeing the
draw at all. The only family where the instrument is trustworthy is one whose cards
are written as `fire("table", chance)` — the relationship and friend pools, which is
exactly where §155's mis-diagnosis happened.

### 157.1 What the tool is good for, stated narrowly

For a family whose pools are literal `fire("…")` calls, `--only PREFIX` gives a
short, real list of card tables that never fired in a batch: the prison run reported
**11 referenced, 8 touched, 3 silent** under the old reference set and **4 / 7 / 0**
under the draw-site set, which is the difference between "never mentioned in an event"
and "never drawn as a card".

### 157.2 The check this round actually produced

`fire("…")` sites: **16** in `src/sim.cpp` and **0** in every `src/fam/*.cpp`. The
family files ported in §130-132 draw rows through variables, so a future census has to
follow the variable, not the literal — that is a small static analysis, not a grep.

## 158. The engagement, which the port used to skip

`ScenarioLoverCallOffEngagement` is a report card — `RefreshScenario` and
`DismissSelected`, no choices:

```
title      one of 'Let's wait a little longer', 'Just not sure anymore', 'Just kidding'
body       'You called off your engagement with your {0}, {1}.'   #47929
narrative  'I called off my engagement with {0}.'                #23687
extra      '{0} still wants the commitment.'                     #3450
impacts    ImpactKarma(-5) = -50, ImpactDiscipline(-3) = -16
```

Ported as written — and it exposed a hole underneath it.

### 158.1 The status it reads did not exist

The card needs `loverStatus == "engaged"`, and **nothing in the port ever set that
string.** `relationshipYear` jumped straight from `dating` to `married` on the
marriage-nag pool, so every card that reads an engagement — this one, and the wedding
cards after it — was ported against a status the sim never entered.

The nag is now two steps, which is what a proposal is:

```
dating  --fire(marriage-nags, 0.10), relationship >= 55-->  engaged  (relationship 75)
engaged --fire(marriage-nags, 0.14), relationship >= 60-->  married  (relationship 75)
```

and `final.loverStatus` / `final.loverName` / `final.relationship` are in the JSON, so
the status can be observed instead of inferred.

### 158.2 Verification

`tools/test_call_off_engagement.py`:

```
cards: 2
statuses in free play: ['dating', 'engaged', 'married']
ok
```

Per card: the body, the title from the three-item pool, **no buttons**, the journal,
the commitment line, and `karma -50, discipline -16`. Per life: after a call-off the
status is back to `dating` — and in free play all three statuses now occur. The script
also gained `"engaged": true`, the same fixture shape as `ex` (§149), because a
25-year life rarely rolls an engagement on its own.

Bench 0 lines.

## 159. The elopement offer

The wedding chain §145 called blocked on the engagement status has its first card:

```
body     'Your {0}, {1}, has asked you to run off and get eloped.'   #50691
buttons  'Agree to elope' (#11010)   'Plan a wedding instead' (#34055)
handler  Contains('agree') -> pushes ScenarioLoverWeddingPlanning, logs
         Contains('plan')  -> the counter-offer, logs
gate     ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush: not royal, not in prison,
         Life::PresentedCountForScenario, SimLover::WillAgreeToGetEloped
```

### 159.1 Two lanes the port can honour

The planning card is not ported, so the lanes land on the two states the port has:

* **Agree to elope** → `loverStatus = "married"`, relationship 80 — the elopement *is*
  the marriage, which is what eloping means;
* **Plan a wedding instead** → `loverStatus = "engaged"`, relationship 75.

Both journals are the class's own strings, including the second's odd shape
(`'{0} I suggested we plan a normal wedding instead.'` — the partner's name tacked on
with no verb), reproduced as written.

### 159.2 Verification

`tools/test_lover_elope.py`:

```
lanes: {'Plan a wedding instead': 3, 'Agree to elope': 3}
ok
```

Both lanes occur in 20 lives; each one's body, journal ending and age gate are
asserted.

### 159.3 The shortcut, stated

Agreeing marries on the spot instead of pushing `ScenarioLoverWeddingPlanning` →
`ScenarioLoverWedding` (venue, honeymoon, cost) → `ScenarioLoverWeddingAssets`. Those
three cards are the rest of the chain and none is ported.

## 160. The wedding plan, venue half

`ScenarioLoverWedding` is a plan, not a sentence: a venue row from
`a16_wedding-venues-enc` (12 rows, each with a `Cost Score` and a `Lover Happiness
Score`), a honeymoon destination, a total, and three buttons (`do it`, `Edit the
plan`, `Actually, never mind`).

```
73f3dd15c0  DataWeddingVenue::VenueDescription
73f3dd1638  DataVacationDestination::GetDescriptionAndCapitalizeAndUseTrailingCommaIfApplicable
73f3dd1688  DataWeddingVenue::Cost
73f3dd16d8  DataVacationDestination::CostOfVacationForClassAndDaysFromCountry
73f3dd179c  GameReference::CurrencyStringForAmount
```

The port has the venue half:

```
body      'You have chosen to marry {0} at {1}.'          #48760
buttons   'Do it'   'Actually, never mind' (#10716)
called off 'I called off my wedding with {0}.'            #23688
effects   Do it: money -= 1000 * Cost Score, relationship += Lover Happiness Score,
          status married;  Never mind: status dating, relationship 40
```

### 160.1 The shortcut, stated plainly

**The game's wedding cost is a formula** — the venue's `Cost Score`, the destination
and the country's class — and only the venue's own score is read here, priced at 1000
per point. The honeymoon half is not modelled at all: no destination, no vacation
cost, no `Edit the plan`. A player can therefore spend money on a wedding in this port
that the game would have priced differently, and cannot choose where to honeymoon.

### 160.2 Verification

`tools/test_lover_wedding.py`:

```
lanes: {'Actually, never mind': 14, 'Do it': 17}
distinct venues: 12
ok
```

All twelve venues appear across 20 lives, which is the check that the row is really
drawn; every card reports the table it came from, both lanes occur, and the money line
is present on `Do it` while the call-off line is present on the other.

Bench 0 lines; `test_lover_elope` and `test_call_off_engagement` green.

### 160.3 An open question this card exposed

A first attempt asserted `final.loverStatus == "married"` after a `Do it` lane and it
failed on seed 2 with `engaged`. Either a later card re-opens the engagement, or one of
the two new paths that set `married` (§158's nag, §159's elopement) can be overwritten
in the same life. The assertion was removed rather than papered over — but the
inconsistency is real and is the next thing to chase.

## 161. Correction: there was no status overwrite, and the wedding had no money

§160.3 recorded an "open question": a life that chose `Do it` ended `engaged` instead of
`married`, and it was read as one card overwriting another. It was not. The trace:

```
24 | a16_wedding-venues-enc | You have chosen to marry Sam Ellery at the Church.
   | ['The wedding cost $3,000, more than I had.',
      'I could not afford the wedding at the Church.']
```

The card fired, the hero **could not pay**, and it left the engagement exactly where it
was. The behaviour was right; the test's expectation was wrong; and the assertion had
been removed instead of being explained.

### 161.1 Two things that were wrong underneath it

1. **The card offered venues the hero could not afford.** It drew from all twelve rows
   and only discovered the problem after the choice. It now draws only from the rows at
   or below the hero's money, and falls back to the cheapest row when none is — so the
   plan is always the plan the hero could actually make.
2. **There was no way to give a life money.** `"money"` in a spec did nothing (the key
   never existed), so every wedding in every test was unaffordable and the venue table
   looked like it only had one row. The script gained `"cash": N`, the same fixture
   shape as `fame`, `children`, `ex` and `engaged`.

### 161.2 Verification

`tools/test_lover_wedding.py`:

```
lanes: {'Actually, never mind': 8, 'Do it': 8}
distinct venues: 10
ok
```

and the assertion that was removed last round is back, with a paid wedding behind it:
`paid[0]["choice"] == "Do it"` and `final.loverStatus == "married"` on the same seed that
failed before.

`test_call_off_engagement` needed one change of its own: since §159 and §160 landed, an
engagement is usually resolved in the same year, so a life no longer *ends* engaged.
That test now asserts the status is reachable through its fixture instead of waiting for
a random life to end inside one.

Bench 0 lines; `test_lover_elope` and `test_birth` green.

## 162. Auditing the report's own open questions

Two of the last four rounds ended by discovering that a recorded finding was a
measurement error (§154's title count, §160.3's status "overwrite"). That base rate is
high enough to walk the rest, so every note the report carries as *not read* or *open*
was checked against the code.

| note | claim | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| §154.2 | `giftYear` never fires | **wrong**, corrected in §155 — it fires 34 times in 40 lives; only the property-gift refusal pool is unreachable |
| §160.3 | a card overwrites `married` with `engaged` | **wrong**, corrected in §161 — the wedding was unaffordable |
| §147.2 | five of six court-order placeholders known, `{3}`/`{5}` unknown | **resolved** in §149 by reading the argument array |
| §149.4 | the court order's own gate is inferred | **partly resolved** this round, see below |
| §143.1 | the birth-control lane mapping is not readable | **resolved** in §144 (label dispatch) |

### 162.1 The gate that could be read after all

§149 wrote: *the card's own gate is inferred from the fields; the infancy limit is the
port's.* Both halves were placeholders, and the real gate exists — a different class,
which the symbol table had all along:

```
ScenarioExLoverPaternityTest::ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush
  SimHero::CurrentlyInPrison                       -- not while locked up
  ScenarioExLoverPaternityTest::GetEligibleExLover  -- SimPast::ExLoverArray,
      SimPerson::LivesInSamePlaceAsHero @0x73f3ded080, then a child
  ScenarioExLoverPaternityTest::GetEligibleChildFromExLover
      -- also consults SimLover::StepchildArray
  Life::PresentedCountForScenario                  -- the presented cap
```

The infancy limit is gone. The port keeps the one condition it can actually know: a
child whose father is **not** recorded as the hero is the child a test is asked over.
That is a stand-in for `LivesInSamePlaceAsHero`, which the port cannot express — an ex
in this port has a name, a gender and a year, and no place.

### 162.2 Verification

`tools/test_paternity_court_order.py` after the change:

```
cards: 4
lanes: {'Take the test': 1, 'Refuse to take the test': 3}
results: {'positive': 0, 'negative': 1} chained after the court order: 1
ok
```

Twice the cards, because a grown child now qualifies. The remaining notes in the report
(`KeepItClean` at 0x73f32aba1c, the retirement condition) are still genuinely unread and
are recorded as such rather than as facts.

## 163. People get a place

§162 ended with the gap that keeps reappearing: *an ex in this port has a name, a
gender and a year, and no place* — while the game asks
`SimPerson::LivesInSamePlaceAsHero` before several ex and child cards. Three structures
had the same hole, so it was closed once:

```
Hero::ExLover.city   where the ex was living when the pair ended
Child.city           where the child lives
final.city           the hero's own city, now in the JSON
```

Every creation site fills it: the break-up records `h.city` on the ex it pushes, the
birth card records the partner's city on the child, and both fixtures do the same.

### 163.1 The gate it was blocking

`paternityCourtOrderYear` now asks the place question the game asks, instead of only
the stand-in:

```
if (c.isHeroes) continue;                                  // whose child it is
if (!ex->city.empty() && !h.city.empty() && ex->city != h.city) continue;  // nearby
```

An **empty** city means the record predates the field or a fixture did not set it, and
is not evidence of distance — that is deliberate, so old saves and the fixtures behave
as they did.

### 163.2 Verification

`tools/test_places.py`:

```
children and ex-lovers carry a place
ok
```

Every child and every ex-lover in five lives carries a `city`, and each ex's is the
hero's own. Bench 0 lines; `test_birth`, `test_paternity_court_order`,
`test_lover_wedding` and `test_call_off_engagement` all still pass — the change is
additive and nothing reads a place it did not ask for.

### 163.3 What this unblocks

* `SimChild::IsLivingWithHero` — the flag `MovedOut` and `city` now support it.
* Every ex card that only fires when the ex is *nearby*: the stalking, booty-call and
  custody families all ask this question in the game.
* A future move-house card: `city` is the thing it would change.

## 164. The partner ends it, with buttons

`ScenarioLoverLeaves` is the code-built counterpart of the table-driven break-up the
port already had:

         '{0} wants a divorce.'             #70376   (married)
buttons  'Beg {0} to stay' (#13308)   'Wish {0} well' (#47041)
         'Hypnotize {0} to stay' (#23344) -- the vampire lane

Both leaving lanes do what the port's own break-up block does — record the ex, clear
the pairing — and then push `kPendingBreakUpAnnouncement`, so the journal comes from
the announcement card (§125) rather than from a second copy of the text. `Hypnotize`
is offered only when `h.vampire` and keeps the couple together with +20.

`shortcut:` the game's success roll for begging is not read. The port keeps the couple
when `relationship >= 40` and lets them go otherwise.

### 164.2 Verification

`tools/test_lover_leaves.py`:

```
lanes: {'Beg': 5, 'Wish': 3}
ok
```

Both lanes occur; every card's body opens with a capital and ends with one of the two
class sentences; the button always names the partner; a life that wished the partner
well has an ex-lover on record.

### 164.3 The battery, and a reminder about `rc`

Ran mid-round: `probes 68 rc0 66 residue0 63 fails0 68` — two probes reported a

`RESIDUE 0`, `failures 0`). The parallel runner's exit code is not a result;

## 165. The relationship lifecycle, checked across cards

Eleven cards now write `loverName`, `loverStatus`, `relationship`, `exLovers` or
`breakUpPending`. Each has its own test and none of them looks at a whole life, which is
where those writes meet. `tools/test_relationship_lifecycle.py` states the invariants
instead:

```
status is one of dating / engaged / married, or empty
a status implies a name, and a name implies a status
0 <= relationship <= 100, and a married hero has a positive one
every ex-lover has a name, a known status, and a year that is not in the future
```

### 165.1 The trajectory, not just the invariant

Invariants survive a card that never fires, so the test also walks a whole arc:

```
full arcs: 9
```

Nine lives out of 120 ran engagement → wedding → divorce proposal, and each one asserts
the order (`wedding age <= divorce age`) and that the marriage that ended is on record
as a **married** ex-lover, not as a dating one.

### 165.2 A mistake the trajectory caught immediately

The first version counted *every* divorce proposal as an exit and then demanded a
married ex. Seed 2 failed because the hero **begged and stayed** — the proposal is not
the outcome. The trajectory now only counts a proposal whose lane was `Wish … well`,
which is the lane that actually leaves.

### 165.3 Verification

```
lives: 120 weddings: 87 divorce proposals: 22
ok
full arcs: 9
all invariants hold
```

Two fixtures per seed — a plain life and one that starts engaged with cash — so both the
free-running and the scripted routes are covered.

## 166. Card rates, measured for the first time

Nothing in the suite measured *how often* anything fires: the probes check that a card
can fire, the tests check what it does when it does. `tools/cardrate.py` counts cards
per 100 lives, keyed by table plus the first six words of the body so two lanes of one
card are one card:

```
lives: 120 distinct cards: 2831

per 100 lives   count  card
         76.7      92  a16_movies-enc | The movie theater is showing The
         55.0      66  a16_movies-enc | Your mother is taking you to
         51.7      62  a16_street-persons-enc | While on your walk, you witness
         49.2      59  a16_drugs-enc | While on your walk, you come
         36.7      44  - | Even though you have a boyfriend,
         30.8      37  a16_coworker-pranks-enc | You just realized that your coworker,
         27.5      33  relationship | You broke up with your dating,
         24.2      29  celebrity-dating-app | Date the celebrity of your dreams
```

### 166.1 What the numbers say

* **2,831 distinct card faces** fire across 120 lives, which is the real measure of the
  port's content breadth — far more than the ~380 sections suggest.
* **The movie card fires in three of four lives.** That is the port's own yearly coin,
  not the game's schedule; no rate in the port is verified against the game's push
  probabilities, and this one is visibly too high.
* **A break-up in one life in four** (`You broke up with your dating,`), and 0.72
  weddings per life from §165 — the relationship family is the port's most active one.
* A card whose `table` is `-` (`Even though you have a boyfriend,`) is one of the
  code-built cards that reports no table; those are invisible to `tablecensus.py`
  (§157) and are why that tool cannot see the sprint's cards.

### 166.2 The honest state of tuning

This is a **baseline, not a verification**. Every probability in the port was chosen by
reading a pool's shape, not by reading the game's schedule, and the measurement now
exists to show the size of that gap rather than to close it. Closing it needs the
game's own push weights, which the card classes do not carry — they are decided by
whatever constructs them.

## 167. Correction: §166 counted faces, not cards

§166's headline — *"the movie card fires in three of four lives"* — was wrong in the same
way §154 was. A **face** is one title's sentence; a **card** is the pool. The top row,
`a16_movies-enc | The movie theater is showing The` (76.7 per 100 lives), is one film
being drawn often, not the card firing often.

`cardrate.py` now reports both, table first:

```
per 100 lives   count  table (the card)
        742.5     891  a16_dumb-scenarios-universal-enc
        640.8     769  a16_movies-enc
        587.5     705  -                                  (code-built cards)
        445.0     534  a16_pastimes-enc
        438.3     526  a16_dumb-scenarios-political-campaign-enc
        366.7     440  relationship                       (the sprint's cards)
        307.5     369  a16_conversations-enc
```

### 167.1 What the card-level numbers actually say

* `a16_movies-enc` is **6.4 cards per life**, not 77 per 100. Its coin is 0.12 per year
  over ~23 eligible years, so the arithmetic was always consistent — the summary was
  not.
* The busiest card in the port is the universal dumb-scenario pool at **7.4 per life**,
  followed by movies. Both are high-frequency-by-design pools, so neither is the
  anomaly §166 claimed.
* `relationship` — the table every sprint card reports — is **3.7 cards per life**,
  which is the first real measurement of the family this session has been building.

### 167.2 The lesson, third time

§155: count `table`, not `title`. §167: count `table`, not `table | face`. A title is
content, a face is one rendering, and only the pool is the card. The tool now prints
both so the mistake is visible rather than available.

Nothing was tuned on the back of the wrong number — the movies coin was never touched,
which is the one good consequence of §166 having been a summary rather than a fix.

## 168. Where the port actually stands, read off the instruments

Four instruments, each answering a different question, run after eleven sprint cards and
eight structural changes:

```
portgap      ENTRIES 109  rendered-by-port 107  gap 0
rescensus    distinct residue tokens 0  total 0
row_recover  scenarios 5  recovered 4  -> 1 UNRECOVERED
cardrate     2,831 distinct faces across 120 lives; relationship 3.7 cards/life
```

### 168.1 What each number is allowed to mean

* **`gap 0`** — every push the port renders is accounted for: nothing arrives without a
  table/row or a class name. It does **not** say the port renders the game's pushes;
  it says the port's own pushes are explained.
* **`residue 0`** — no `<token>` survived into a rendered line. A token left unsubstituted
  is the most reliable failure this port has, so zero is meaningful.
* **`2,831 faces`** — content breadth, counted by card after §167's correction.
* **`row_recover` 4 of 5** — the one that produced an action.

### 168.2 The one unrecovered row is a card that is not ported

```
age 6  ScenarioOutdoorAgeUpParentsGiveBik  Canyon Neuron 5  UNRECOVERED
```

`ScenarioOutdoorAgeUpParentsGiveBik*` does not exist in `port/src/fam/outdoor.cpp`
(711 lines, no such card), so "unrecovered row" here means *there is no row because
there is no card*. It is a childhood gift push — a parent gives the hero a bicycle —
and it is the kind of card that sits between two families: parents (who give) and
outdoor (which owns the vehicle tables).

Two others in the same run report `row None` rather than `UNRECOVERED`
(`ScenarioSchoolEnroll`, `ScenarioLoverLeaves`) — the class and its text are known, the
*data row* the game drew is not, and the port's version of each builds its body from the
class's own strings rather than from a table row.

### 168.3 The honest summary

Nothing in the four numbers says the port is finished, and two of the four cannot see a
missing card at all: `portgap` only audits pushes the port *already makes*. The real
measure of what is missing is the gap between the game's scenario classes and the
port's — 300-odd classes against ~70 ported families — and no instrument here measures
that. What can be said is narrower and true: everything the port renders is explained,
nothing is left as a token, and the one row that could not be recovered belongs to a
card that has not been written.

## 169. The class census, and why the class count is not the measure

§168 ended by naming the missing instrument: the game's scenario classes against the
port's. It exists now — and it says something other than what was expected.

```
scenario classes in the game:        2719
named somewhere in port/src:           89    (3%)
not named at all:                    2630
```

Read alone, that is damning. It is also the wrong measure, and the second half of the
tool shows why: **the port renders cards from tables, not from classes**. Counting how
many of each family's data tables `port/src` touches:

```
family      tables touched
Zoo           35 /  35
Astronaut     35 /  35
Vampire       44 /  44
Outdoor       42 /  42
Cult          45 /  45
Racing        31 /  31
Fight         38 /  38
Music         58 /  58
Casino        37 /  39
Secret        51 /  60
Dealer        37 /  38
Black         23 /  24
```

### 169.1 What the two numbers actually mean

The game has one **class per card shape** — `ScenarioZooAgeUpAnimalBirth`,
`ScenarioZooAgeUpAnimalBirthFailure`, `ScenarioZooAgeUpAnimalBirthGoldenPacifier` are
three classes for one family's three outcomes. The port has one **table** for that
family and builds each face from a row. So:

* `2,719` is the game's *granularity*, not its content;
* `89` is how much of that granularity the port reproduces as code;
* the table ratios are how much of the **content** the port can render.

Which makes the class count a measure of nothing on its own — the honest statement is
that the port covers its families' data almost completely (Zoo, Vampire, Music, Cult,
Outdoor, Racing, Fight at 100%) and reproduces their *behaviour* case by case.

### 169.2 What is genuinely missing, stated as such

Tables touched is not behaviour implemented. `Secret 51/60`, `Casino 37/39`,
`Dealer 37/38`, `Black 23/24` are real gaps in the data layer; and for every family at
100%, the gap the instruments cannot see is the **gate and the chain** — which cards
follow which, and under what condition they push. That is what §145 listed as blockers
and what §133's queue began to solve.

### 169.3 The instrument's own caveat

"Touched" means the table's name appears in `port/src`; a table can be named and its
rows never drawn. `cardrate.py` (§167) is the instrument that answers *drawn*, and the
two together — named and drawn — are the closest this project can get to a coverage
claim without the game's own push weights.

§170 ended with a warning about its own explanation: *"belongs to an unported card" is
now doing a lot of work.* So each of the twelve was mapped to the class that owns it:

| `secret-agent-hack-mission-*` x2 | no `Scenario*HackMission*` class exists; the strings are consumed by the stealth/briefing chain | not ported |

Both are blocked on something the port does not have, and both are one row deep:

* **`black-market-auction-categories`** is seven categories with a commonness score.
  The port's auction house picks an item type from its own tables; wiring the category
  would need the mapping from category to the item pool, which no table carries.

Neither is a naming exercise, and neither was wired to make a ratio look better.

Ten of twelve are owned by classes the port does not have -- the explanation §170 gave
is now backed by a class name per row rather than asserted. The other two are owned by
cards that exist and are short of *state*, which is a different kind of gap and is
recorded as such.

## 172. Two cards decoded, neither ported, and why

The round went back to cards and came back with two decodes and one refusal.

### 172.1 `ScenarioLoverMakeLoveNag` — already covered, by a table

```
body      'Your {0}, {1}, is nagging you to make love.'   #50731
narrative '{0} nagged me to make love.'                  #70169
buttons   'Make Love' (#29545)   'Hypnotize ' (#23341, vampire)
          '<name> to stop asking' (#3780)
gate      ScenarioIsEligibleForRandomPush: age 18 check, a count == 3, and an fcmp
```

`relationshipYear` already fires `a16_lover-make-love-nags-enc` at 0.07 — the ported
table card for the same beat. Writing the code-built twin beside it would double the
rate, so it was **not** ported. That is a decision, not an omission: the table version
carries the game's own rows and this one carries one sentence.

### 172.2 `ScenarioExLoverInboundSext` — decoded to a hole

```
body      'Your {0}, {1}, just sent you {2}.'            #50742
narrative 'My {0}, {1}, sent me {2}.'                    #30997
buttons   'Send {0} a txxxt back' (#38590)
          'Forward it to my friends' (#20572)
          'Do these save to the cloud?' (#17931)
          'File a restraining order' (#20129)
journal   '{0} I sent {1} back {2}.'  (#69612)
          '{0} I forwarded it to all of my friends.' (#69567)
fields    _exLover, _narrative;  GetTheExLover() picks the ex
```

Everything is known except `{2}` — *what was sent* — and no string table carries it: a
scan of the literal bank for sext/nude/booty content returns the card's own name and a
booty-call line, nothing describing the picture. `{2}` comes from a `DataHub` method, not
from a table, and the port has no such method yet.

### 172.3 Why that stopped the port

A body of `Your ex-girlfriend, Dana, just sent you .` is the failure §147 refused:
the sentence's object is the whole point of the card. Four buttons and two journals are
recorded here so the next attempt starts from them.

### 172.4 What the round produced instead of a card

Nothing shipped, and that is recorded rather than papered over: one card was declined
because it would double a rate, one stopped at a hole. Both decisions are written down
with their evidence so the next round does not spend itself reaching the same two
conclusions.

## 173. The hole was a table the port had never read

§172 stopped the ex-lover sext card at `{2}`. Following the call chain from the
Refresh's body (after its static-init block) found it in two instructions:

```
73f3de551c  bl  DataHub::GetRandomSexyTextItemForGender   ; {2}
73f3de5558  bl  System.String::Replace                     ; '<pronoun>' -> his/her
```

and `GetRandomSexyTextItemForGender` reads **`a16_sexy-text-items-enc`** — 43 rows of
`Item, Gender, Clean`, a table the port had never referenced. The card is ported now:

```
body      'Your {0}, {1}, just sent you {2}.'            #50742
journal   'My {0}, {1} sent me {2}.'                      #30997
buttons   'Send {0} a txxxt back'  'Forward it to my friends'
          'Do these save to the cloud?'  'File a restraining order'
```

* `{2}` is drawn from the pool filtered by the ex's gender, with `<pronoun>` replaced by
  the ex's own possessive — the same substitution the game does, and the reason a
  "wilted celery" row reads "picture of her willy" rather than "picture of <pronoun>
  willy".
* Three of the four buttons are wired; **`File a restraining order`** is not, because it
  opens the court card, which is the one ex-lover chain still unported.

### 173.1 Verification

`tools/test_ex_lover_sext.py`:

```
lanes: {'Forward it to my friends': 2, 'Send Robin Averill': 4, 'Do these save to the cloud?': 6}
distinct items: 10
ok
```

Ten distinct items across 30 lives is the check that the pool is really drawn; no
`<pronoun>` survives into a line; the card reports `a16_sexy-text-items-enc` as its
table. Bench 0 lines.

### 173.2 A filter bug this round produced

The test's first version keyed on the phrase `just sent you` and caught a **prison**
card — *"Hannah dal Vie just sent you a sex video she made with another man while you've
been in prison."* Filtering cards by a phrase in their body is the same class of mistake
as §154's title filter; the filter is now the ex-lover wording itself.

## 174. The ex has married someone else

Second card of the ex-lover family, and the first that needed no new table:

```
body     'Your {0}, {1}, said {2} can't {3} you because {4} is married{5}.'
{3}      'start dating' (#66066)   'get back together with' (#59507)
journal  the same sentence in the first person (#30996)
buttons  'Respect that' (#36054)
         'Ask {0} to come over anyway' (#12217)
         'Convince {0} to divorce {1}' (#16351)
```

### 174.1 The two verbs, and the one placeholder left empty

`{3}` is one of two literals the class carries, and the port picks by what the pair
*were*: a pair who dated can get back together, anything else can only start dating.

`{5}` is left empty on purpose. The sentence ends `... is married` and the game appends
something there; no literal in the bank reads as a completion of it, and a wrong choice
would change the meaning of the sentence rather than its punctuation. That is the same
call as §147's `{3}`/`{5}`, made the same way: an empty tail is visible, a wrong tail is
not.

### 174.2 Lanes

* **Respect that** — nothing but the journal.
* **Ask … to come over anyway** — `karma -8` (impact −2), and the journal says what was
  asked.
* **Convince … to divorce …** — `karma -12` (impact −3); the lane the game opens the
  court chain from, which is still unported (§172), so the port records the attempt and
  stops there.

### 174.3 Verification

`tools/test_ex_lover_married_now.py`:

```
lanes: {'Ask': 4, 'Respect': 5, 'Convince': 2}
ok
```

All three lanes occur in 25 lives; the body carries one of the two verbs and the
journal opens in the first person. Bench 0 lines.

## 175. The wall behind the ex-lover family is a layer, not a card

§174 ported `ExLoverMarriedNow` from literals alone. The next two cards would not go that
way, and the reason is the same for both:

* `ScenarioExLoverSextMisdirect` builds its body from **fragments** — `'your {0}, {1},'`
  (#68451) is one of them, then `String::Format` three times over names it resolves from
  its five person fields;
* `ScenarioExLoverMessage` offers `'Send your {0}, {1}, a text today!'` (#38586) and
  `'Txxxt {0}'` (#44298), and its body comes from a `DataHub` method like the sext's did
  — that one happened to read a table (§173), which is why it was portable at all.

### 175.1 The number

```
DataHub methods in the binary: 2344

DataHub::GetRandomExLoverBootyCallScenarioForHeroGenderAndExGenderAndAge
DataHub::GetRandomExLoverHateScenarioForHeroGenderAndExGender
DataHub::GetCustodyExLoverArgument
DataHub::GetRandomAstronautInboundMessage
DataHub::GetRandomCultRecruitmentMessageSet
DataHub::GetRandomSexyTextItemForGender          <-- the one that was a table
```

`DataHub` is the game's **content layer**: 2,344 methods that pick, template and gender-
and-age-filter strings, and the port has no equivalent. Its cards borrow tables where a
table happens to exist (`a16_sexy-text-items-enc`) and stop where the content is code.

### 175.2 What that means for the remaining 15 ex-lover classes

They are not fifteen decoding jobs; they are **one layer** the port lacks. Writing a
`DataHub`-shaped module — pool selection by gender and age, fragment assembly, and the
`<ex>`, `<ex-possessive>`, `<pronoun>` substitutions the cards expect — would make the
whole family port at once, and would pay again in cult, astronaut and zoo, whose inbound
messages come from the same place.

### 175.3 Recorded rather than started

The round decoded two cards and shipped none. The next step is not another card: it is
whether a `DataHub` layer can be built from what is already extracted — the string bank,
the symbol table and the tables — or whether each method has to be read individually.
**That question is worth a round of its own, and this one ends with it stated.**

## 176. The layer's shape, measured

§175 asked whether a `DataHub` layer can be built from what is already extracted. The
name census answers the shape question before any disassembly:

```
DataHub methods: 2344
  Load*Set  :  928   (build a pool)
  Get*      : 1348   (pick from one)
  other     :   68

  getter unfiltered   731
  getter ...For...     399
  getter ...Gender...  124
  getter ...Age...      94
```

### 176.1 Two halves, and only one of them is work

The layer is **928 loaders and 1,348 pickers**. Three methods sampled from different
families all have the same two-line shape:

```
GetRandomSexyTextItemForGender          -> LoadSexyTextItemSet            -> pick
GetRandomExLoverBootyCallScenario...    -> LoadExLoverBootyCallScenarioSet -> pick
GetRandomAstronautInboundMessage        -> LoadAstronautInboundMessageSet  -> pick
```

* the **picker** is `pick(filtered by gender/age)` — one implementation the port already
  has in `pickRow`/`weightedPick`, and 1,348 methods collapse into it;
* the **loader** is the content: 928 methods that assemble a set from tables, literals or
  both, and those are as varied as their families.

### 176.2 The answer to §175's question

**Partly buildable.** A generic layer covers the picking half entirely — that is where
the 1,348 methods live — and reduces each family to its `Load*Set` counterpart. `§173`
already proved the pattern end to end: `GetRandomSexyTextItemForGender` became one table
read with a gender filter, in ten lines.

What remains per family is the loader, and loaders are the *smaller* half: 928 against
1,348, and most of them name a table the port already opens.

### 176.3 What that changes about "finish tier 3"

The remaining ex-lover, cult, astronaut and zoo cards stop being fifteen-plus decoding
jobs. They become: **find the `Load*Set` the card's getter names, read that set's table,
and let the port's existing pick do the rest** — which is a routine, not a wall.

`tools/datahub_census.py` records the classification so the next round starts from the
numbers rather than from the worry.

## 177. The loaders decrypt, and that is a different job

§176 said the remaining work was "find the `Load*Set` the getter names, read its table".
Testing that on four loaders says otherwise:

```
LoadSexyTextItemSet                       DecodeAndDecryptString
LoadExLoverBootyCallScenarioSet           DecodeAndDecryptString
LoadCultRecruitmentMessageSet             DecodeAndDecryptString
LoadAstronautInboundMessageSet            DecodeAndDecryptString
```

and the routine behind it is a three-stage cipher:

```
73f2802fac  EncryptionManager::DecodeBase64String
73f28030b4  EncryptionManager::ObfuscateString
73f28030c0  EncryptionManager::XORCipherString
73f28030fc  EncryptionManager::EncryptString
```

### 177.1 Why §173 still worked

`a16_sexy-text-items-enc` sits in `gamedata_plain` as plain rows, and the card read them
directly — the game *also* decrypts a handful of strings in that loader, but the item
pool the card formats is the table. So a card ported through the table is right about
its items and silent about whatever the decrypted strings carry.

That distinction is the useful finding: **`gamedata_plain` is not encrypted; the loaders'
extra strings are.** A card whose content lives entirely in tables is portable today; a
card whose content lives in the decrypted strings is not.

### 177.2 What decryption would take, and why it was not started

The chain is Base64 → a fixed obfuscation → an XOR with a key that `XORCipherString`
receives rather than defines, so the key comes from the caller (or a constant beside it).
Reading it is a job of its own: key extraction, a reimplementation in the port, and a
verification path against a string the game renders — three steps, none of them a card.

**Not started.** Recording it is the honest end of this round: the port's remaining
content splits into *table-backed* (portable by the §173 routine) and *cipher-backed*
(blocked on this chain), and only the first kind should be attempted until the second is
decided.

### 177.3 The corrected routine

```
1. read the card's getter name
2. read its Load*Set
3. if the loader reads a table  -> port it (§173)
4. if the loader decrypts       -> stop; it needs the cipher chain (§177)
```

Step 4 is a decision point rather than a dead end, and the numbers for it exist: 928
loaders, of which the sampled four all decrypt.

## 180. The grounded lane, and the risk that a card renders without doing anything

§179 shipped the discipline card with four lanes that differed only in their journal.
That is exactly the risk §179.3 named — faces faster than behaviour — so the handler was
read for the one lane it details:

```
73f3a86710  mov  w1, #0x1e                    ; GetRandomNumber(0, 30)
73f3a86718  bl   GameReference::GetRandomNumber
73f3a86748  bl   System.String::Contains      ; the label dispatch
73f3a8679c  bl   SimPerson::ImpactDiscipline
73f3a867b0  bl   SimPerson::ImpactDiscipline
```

`Contains('ground')` (slot `0x5caeb90`) selects the grounded lane, and that lane has the
class's own sentence:

```
journal   '{0} I grounded {1} for {2} days.'   #69569
button    'You're grounded'                    #49968 (the child's reply)
```

so the port now rolls **1–30 days**, writes the sentence with the number, and moves
`discipline` by `pointsForImpact(+1)` = 4.

### 180.1 What was left alone, and why

Two `ImpactDiscipline` calls sit in the dispatcher and only one lane could be tied to a
literal with confidence; the other assignment is *not* guessed. Yell, Talk and Do-nothing
still carry no stat move, which is recorded rather than filled in.

### 180.2 Verification

`tools/test_child_discipline_lanes.py`:

```

ok
```

The test only asserts on the lane it can: the grounded journal ends `for N days.` with
`1 <= N <= 30`, `discipline` moves by exactly 4, and no other lane's journal claims it
grounded anybody — the negative half is what keeps a lazy `log + sentence` from hiding
a wrong lane. Bench 0 lines.

## 181. A child asks for money, and the row is the card

`a16_child-demands-enc` is a different shape from the last two: the **row contains the
choices**. Age, Amount, and two comma-separated lists — `Boy` and `Girl` — of things the
child might want.

```
4,5,"buy some candy, buy a new app, buy some water balloons, ...","buy a coloring book, ..."
6,10,"buy a toy car, buy an action figure, buy a hamster, ...","buy a figurine, ..."
```

and the class supplies the sentences around it:

```
body     'Your {0}, {1}, is asking you for {2} to {3}.'     #50717
buttons  'Yes, give {0} {1}' (#47505)   'No, {0} has enough' (#31869)
journals 'I gave my {0}, {1}, {2} to {3}.'                  #24224
         'I refused to give my {0}, {1}, {2} to {3}.'       #24941
```

Rendered:

```
Your son, Sugar, is asking you for $5 to get some ice cream.
I refused to give my son, Sugar, $5 to get some ice cream.
```

### 181.1 Two decisions in the port

* the row is the **nearest at or below** the child's age, which is how the table is
  built (4, 5, 6, ...) and what makes a 9-year-old ask a 9-year-old's question;
* the card needs **no partner**, only a child. The first version inherited the
  `relationshipOn` gate from its neighbours and produced one card in 25 lives; a child
  can ask a single parent, so the gate was wrong rather than the rate.

### 181.2 Verification

`tools/test_child_demands.py`:

```

distinct asks: 3
ok
```

The body is matched against a full pattern (relation, name, amount, ask), the ask must
reappear in the journal, and the journal must be **exactly one** of the two — the
`!=` between `gave my` and `refused to give` is what stops a lane from claiming both.
Bench 0 lines.

## 182. The child's arc: an adult leaves home

§181's risk was that the child family had become a set of prompts with no arc: three
cards that all gate on *a child at home*, and nothing that ever ended that state except a
5% coin at 18.

The game's own method for that moment is
`SimChild::ThirdPersonMovesOutAndShouldAnnounce` — it checks `IsLivingWithHero`, calls
`PersonGenerator::GenerateSpouseForThirdPerson`, writes the surname, and (for a royal)
`SimThirdPersonScript::JoinRoyalFamilyWithRankAndSeat`. Its announcement text is in no
table the port has.

### 182.1 What the port does

The **state** change only:

```cpp
if (child.age >= 18 && !child.movedOut) child.movedOut = true;
```

no line, no spouse, no royal seat — because inventing the announcement would be the
failure §147 and §151 both refused. What it buys is real: a child now leaves at 18 in
every life, so `movedOut` is a fact rather than a coin, and the three cards that read it
stop being able to fire on a 40-year-old who still lives at home.

```
seed 3  [(31, True), (27, True), (3, False)]
seed 5  [(9, False), (5, False)]
```

### 182.2 Verification, and a test that had to grow rather than weaken

`test_child_discipline_lanes` failed on this change — `grounded lanes: 1`, because the
eligible years shrank once children leave. The fix was to **widen the sample** (30 → 60
lives), not to lower the bar: `grounded lanes: 5`, `ok`. Every child test passes:

```
test_child_demands: ok   test_child_discipline: ok   test_child_discipline_lanes: ok
test_children: ok        test_places: ok
```

Bench 0 lines.

### 182.3 What is still missing from the arc

An adult child has no marriage, no spouse, no grandchildren, and no announcement. Those
are three more `SimChild` methods whose content is elsewhere — the same shape as §177's
loaders — and they are recorded here rather than approximated.

## 183. The custody family is one card with three stages

The three `a16_custody-*` tables are not three cards. They belong to a single class with
a push chain:

```
class ScenarioChildSupportCustody
    field 0x170 SimLover _exLover
    field 0x178 List<SimChild> _children
    field 0x180 System.String _narrative
    methods  .ctor(SimLover), RefreshScenario, ChoiceSelectedAtIndex,
             PushNextScenario
```

and its three tables are the stages:

```
a16_custody-case-enc            139 rows  Reason, Plural, defendant craziness/money,
                                          unemployed, Case Impact Score, commonness
a16_custody-ex-argument-enc      35 rows  the ex's line, hero/ex gender, ex craziness
a16_custody-child-argument-enc   54 rows  the child's line, gender, age, relationship
```

### 183.1 Why it was not ported this round

`PushNextScenario` is the tell: the card is **interactive over several pushes** — pick
which children are in dispute (`'All of them'` #11108, `'Pick your child'` #33847), then
a case from the 139-row pool, then each side's arguments, then an outcome. That is a
`pendingCards` chain of three or four cards with state held between them, and §133's
queue only carries a kind, not a payload.

Porting it needs one structural step first: **a pending card that carries data** (which
child, which case row) rather than a bare enum. That is a small change to §133's queue
and it is the honest prerequisite, not another card.

### 183.2 The battery, after eleven cards and nine structural changes

```
probes 68   rc0 68   residue0 65   fails0 68
```

Every probe exits zero, no residue, no failures — the child, wedding, paternity,
counseling, argues and sext cards have not disturbed a single one.

### 183.3 The prerequisite, stated as the next step

1. `PendingCard` gains a payload: the kind plus two ints (child index, row index).
2. `ScenarioChildSupportCustody` ports as three pushes that read the payload.
3. The three custody tables become usable at once.

## 184. The queue carries a payload

§183 said the custody card needs a pending card that knows *which child and which row*
it is about. That is now the shape of the queue:

```cpp
struct PendingCard {
  int kind = 0;
  int a = -1;   // child index, or -1
  int b = -1;   // row index, or -1
  PendingCard() = default;
  // Implicit from the kind, so every existing push still reads the same.
  PendingCard(int k, int inA = -1, int inB = -1) : kind(k), a(inA), b(inB) {}
};
std::vector<PendingCard> pendingCards;
```

The implicit constructor is the whole point: **no call site changed**. The seven existing
pushes (`kPendingMorningAfter`, `kPendingLoverArgues`, `kPendingBreakUpAnnouncement`,
`kPendingPaternityResults`) still read `push_back(kPendingX)`, and only the drain reads
`.kind`.

### 184.1 Verification

Bench **0 lines** — the refactor is invisible to the trace, which is the check that the
queue behaves exactly as before. `test_paternity_court_order` (the one card that
already relies on the queue end to end) passes.

### 184.2 A test that was wrong about its own arc

`test_relationship_lifecycle` failed on seed 101 with `{'divorce': 65, 'wedding': 79}`:
a divorce at 65 and a **remarriage** at 79. The test had used `setdefault` to keep the
*first* of each, then asserted `wedding <= divorce` — which is false for a life that
marries twice, and the failure had nothing to do with this round's change.

It now builds both lists and asks the question the arc actually makes: *is there some
wedding at or before some divorce*.

```
full arcs: 9
all invariants hold
```

### 184.3 What the payload unblocks

* `ScenarioChildSupportCustody`: three pushes that read `a` (child) and `b` (case row).
* Any argue chain: the reason index rides in `a`.
* The wedding chain: venue and destination indices ride in `a`/`b`.

## 185. The 103-table worklist is 28 cards and 73 fragments

§179 called the untouched tables a worklist, one card each. Classifying them by their
own headers says otherwise:

```
untouched tables: 101
  card-shaped (Scenario / Log Version / gendered string columns): 28
  everything else:                                                73
```

### 185.1 What the 73 are

```
a16_accessories-headwear-enc    Index, Category, Name
a16_accessories-masks-enc       Index, Name, Commonness Score

```

They are **ingredient tables**: an accessory the hero can own, a part for an aircraft, a
name for a drink, a snippet inside a larger card. None of them is a card, and porting one
alone would produce nothing a player could see — exactly the fake coverage §169.3 warned
about, in the other direction.

### 185.2 What this says about the custody card, and about the plan

The custody tables that started this thread are in the fragment group, and §183's reason
stands: the *card* is `ScenarioChildSupportCustody`, and its body is assembled from
fragments (`'I took '` #25282, `', to court for custody of our children.'` #5910,

```

All of them               #11108
Pick your child           #33847
```

Reproducing that sentence needs the *rendering* the class does, not the fragments in
order — which is the same conclusion §172 and §177 reached from two other directions.

### 185.3 The corrected worklist

**28 card-shaped tables remain**, each with its rows and its own literals, and each a
card the port can render this way. The 73 fragments belong to cards that already exist
in the port or do not exist yet, and they are not work in themselves.

The plan's content sprint is therefore closer to finished than the table count suggested:
28 single-stage cards, not 103 items.
