## 268. The composition gap, measured and corrected

267 called the composition gap \"the largest fidelity item left\" on a number that was
wrong: it compared the trace's **log lines** with the port's **events**. A port event
carries one to three lines, so the real figures are:

```
trace   225 log lines / 61 years   3.7 lines a year
port    2.09 lines a year          1.01 events a year
```

The gap is real but it is 1.6 lines a year, not 2.8.

### 268.1 The dumb-pool share was tried and rejected

The hypothesis: the wheel claims almost every year, so giving the dumb pool a measured
share of years ahead of it should restore the game's density. Two settings were built
and measured:

```
dumb pool share 0.55   1.84 lines a year
dumb pool share 0.80   1.76 lines a year
no share (baseline)    2.09 lines a year
```

Both are **worse**. A dumb card writes one line; a family year writes the family's
lifecycle lines plus the card's, which is where the density comes from. The change was
built, measured and reverted; the tree is back to the baseline commit and no test needed
to move.

### 268.2 What the gap actually is

The trace's years are dense with *relative* lines -- promotions, diagnoses, new babies,
moves, marriages, deaths -- two or three a year in the middle stretch. The port emits
those from `lifecycleLines`, and it emits them less often. The next work is therefore
not card dispatch at all but the family lifecycle's rates: how often a relative is
promoted, gets ill, marries, or has a child. That is measurable the same way (lines a
year), and it does not disturb any card's calibration because those lines come from
their own streams.

## 260. The school loop

The school family existed but almost never ran, for two reasons that hid each other:

```
schooling     makeSchool() was defined and never called, and Hero::schooling (which
              schoolYear is gated on) is only set there -- so the family could not fire
wheel         with one seat in a 125-seat wheel it could not win a year either: three
              school cards in thirty lives, against a trace that has one nearly every
              year of school
```

Both are fixed: `ageUp` now draws the school when the level changes (5, 11, 14), which is
what `makeSchool` was written for, and the school loop takes the year ahead of the wheel
for ages below eighteen, the way the game's `Life::IncrementAge` school block does.

```cpp
if (level > 0 && (!h.schooling || level != h.schoolLevel)) makeSchool(life);   // ageUp
if (h.age < 18 && h.schooling && schoolYear(...)) return true;                 // priority
```

## 259. The prison chain gets its years

258 measured the symptom: 2 of 60 lives ever entered prison, so the prison family's cards
(and the unfriend-prison probe) had no window. The cause was dispatch order:

```cpp
// before
if (family loop fires) return true;
if (maybeConvicted(...)) return true;        // only on years no family wanted
if (h.inPrison) return prisonYear(...);      // same
```

A conviction and a prison year are *year events*, not cards, so they now run ahead of the
wheel (a forced lane still wins, because a scripted card belongs to the caller):

```cpp
if (forcedChoice < 0 && maybeConvicted(life, out)) return true;
if (life.hero.inPrison) return prisonYear(life, out, forcedChoice);
```

### 259.1 The coin, tuned against the trace

The 2%/year the port carried was port-side invention that had never actually run. Promoted
where it belongs, it put a prison year in **46 of 60** lives, which the played life does
not show at all. Half a percent gives the prison family a real window without owning the
game:

```
2%/year   46/60 lives with a prison line   (was unreachable, now overshoots)
0.5%/year 22/60 lives
```

### 259.2 The prison unfriend card

`friendUnfriendYear` already had the prison flavour (title pool 'Petty prison pal',
'Limited options here', ...), but with `prisonYear` owning every prison year it could never
run inside one. `prisonYear` now offers the year to the friend loop first: when the prison
unfriend fires it takes the year, otherwise the prison scene does. That is the game's own
push site (0x73f2f03e08 picks the prison variant on `CurrentlyInPrison`).

```

I feuded with my little brother, Ricky, about who the hottest girl in school is. I
apologized to him for feuding.
```

`tools/test_sibling_squabble.py` keeps the topic inside the table's literal rows, checks
the relation is a brother or a sister, matches the apology's pronoun against the sibling's
gender in the final family, and asserts a decline writes nothing.

## 255. The driver's licence

The pool that had been missing all along was the string table itself. `tools/metadata_strings.py
grep` reads `global-metadata.dat` and returns every literal with its index, so the card texts
are no longer guesses:

```
#18224  Driving License
#27800  It's time to take your driving test.\n\nWill you take it?
#40905  Take the driving test
#23835  I couldn't be bothered to get a driving license.
#18225  Driving Test
#24138  I failed my driving test.
#24778  I passed my driving test and got a driving license.
```

Three classes make the chain in the played life (`ScenarioPushLicenseCar`,
`ScenarioGameLicenseCar`, `ScenarioLicenseCarOutcome`), and the question data is already a
table: `a16_license-car-questions-enc`, 29 signs with `Correct`, `Incorrect Funny` and
`Incorrect Decoy` answers.

```cpp
licenseYear      age 16-20, no licence, 30% a year: the offer card
                 lanes: Take the driving test / I couldn't be bothered
licenseTestYear  the year after the offer: one sign and its three answers;
                 the Correct lane passes and sets Hero::hasLicense
```

### 255.1 Shortcuts named

```
question    the card shows the sign as an image; the port has no image, so the sign's
            own name opens the question ("What does this sign mean?\n\n22")
outcome     a third card class (LicenseCarOutcome, title "Whatever") is not modelled:
            the outcome is written in the test card's own line, which is where the
            trace's two sentences belong either way
chance      the game's own probability of picking right is not read; the script's
            lane decides
```

```
40 lives to 22:  37 offers   20 tests   4 passed   16 failed
```

`tools/test_license.py` checks the offer age and both lanes, that the test's choice is one
of that row's three answers, that a pass names the correct one, and that `final.license`
agrees with the pass line.

## 254. The hero graduates

One line from the played life needs no data at all:

```
age 17  I graduated from high school.
```

The port wrote that sentence for relatives (their own `age == 18` transition) but never
for the hero. `schoolMilestoneLines` reads the ladder `schoolLevelFor` already defines
(elementary 5-10, middle 11-13, high 14-17, college 18-22) and writes the line the first
year the hero leaves the high-school band, once per life.

```
40 lives:  40 graduations, each at 18, none in a life that died before 18
```

### 254.1 What was deliberately left out

The other school lines in the trace name a school that no table carries:

```
I have been enrolled in elementary school at Spirit Elementary School.
I started middle school at Allure Middle School.
I started high school at St. Rian's High School.
```

`Spirit`, `Allure`, `St. Rian's` are generated (a word pool and a saint pattern), and the
generator is not in any of the extracted tables, so the port would have to invent names.
It writes no enrollment line at all rather than a wrong one; that is the same rule as the
refusal lane in 248.

## 253. The acceptance bars, written down

`tools/acceptance.py` is the file the earlier conversation promised: the thresholds live
there as constants, and it prints PASS/FAIL per bar with what to fix on a failure.

```
tables referenced          FAIL  868/965 (89.9%)   bar 95%
test suite                 PASS  67/67 green
played-life log overlap    PASS  33.2% (informational)
bench stat streams         PASS  61 ages measured
```

### 253.1 Why only two of those are pass/fail

* **tables referenced** is a real bar: the name appears in `port/src`, so the loader can
  find it. It says nothing about whether the card fires (home purchase was referenced and
  fired once in thirty lives), which is why the suite exists.
* **test suite** is a real bar for the same reason the tests are: one per family, each
  firing the card and checking its text, lanes and deltas.
* **played-life log overlap** is informational until a spec-locked comparison exists. The
  port picks its own cards, so after the first card the two lives do not share, every
  later age compares different events (246.1). 33.2% is the drift of two different lives,
  not a missing family.
* **bench stat streams** reports that a 61-age trace is measured; the per-stream bars
  ("mean |delta| per decade, karma <= 2, happiness <= 5") need many lives to mean
  anything, and the tool says so instead of inventing a number.

### 253.2 The 97 missing references, by cluster

```
genesis-*            29   the metadata filler pools (md-coaching, actor-compliments, ...)
a16_secret-*          9   the secret-agent mission chain
a16_accessories-*     3   headwear / masks / sunglasses
a16_bank-*            3   bank robbery disguises and partners
a16_jewelry-*         3   gemstones and settings
a16_license-*         2   the driving-test question tables
a16_casino/crashout/notification/... each 1-2
```

The genesis pools are the largest single block and the cheapest: they are filler lines
with no state, and the dumb pool already has the machinery to render them.

## 252. The will, and the estate line

Two lines from the played life, small enough to be transcribed exactly:

```
age 50  I created a will. I'm leaving everything to my son, Cleveland.
age 60  I died while sleeping peacefully. My net worth at the time of my death was
        $388,327.
```

Neither is a card in the trace -- no title, no lane -- so both are yearly lines.

### 252.1 The will

`Hero::hasWill` is set once. The beneficiary is the eldest living child, falling back to
the partner when there is none, and a hero with neither gets no line at all (there is
nothing to leave). The coin is 1-in-20 on its own stream: the trace has one will in a
sixty-year life, and 40 test lives give 26.

```
I created a will. I'm leaving everything to my daughter, Jay.
I created a will. I'm leaving everything to my girlfriend, Selene Gnomez.
```

### 252.2 The estate

The death sentence the table writes (`he died of diabetes.`) is now closed with the
estate, in the game's own phrasing, and formatted with thousands separators. A hero in
debt writes `-$455`, which is the one place the trace had no example and the format is
the port's choice: negative money is real (the trace's own hero ended at $388,327, but a
tested life finished at minus four hundred).

```
40 lives:  26 wills   34 deaths, every sentence carrying the estate
```

`tools/test_will_estate.py` checks that a will is written at most once, that its
beneficiary was named somewhere earlier in the same life, and that every dead hero's
sentence ends with the net-worth clause.

## 251. The ex who asks for a paternity test

The trace has the whole chain at 43, and it is the polite twin of 149's court order:

```
My ex-fling, Ariana, asked me to take a paternity test for her 2-year old son, Cleveland.
I agreed to take a paternity test.
The paternity test for my ex-fling, Ariana's, 2-year old son came back positive!
I became the legal father of Cleveland Jenner.
```

`ScenarioExLoverPaternityTest` now exists as `exPaternityYear`: the ex and the child come
from the same records the court-order card uses, the ask is a two-lane card, and the
accepted lane pushes the result through the pending queue the court order already had.

### 251.1 Two things the court-order card had hidden

```
child age   the result lookup only accepted a child of three or younger, because the
            court order is about a baby; an ex who asks in person can ask about an
            older child, as the fixture does (24 in one run). The proactive flag lifts
            the gate.
phrasing    the result names the ex and the child the trace's way
            ("my ex-girlfriend, Robin Averill's, 1-year old son") instead of
            "my son, Dustin", and a positive result adds the legal-father line.
```

```
40 lives (ex + children fixture):  29 cards   12 agreed   12 results   9 positive
```

`tools/test_ex_paternity.py` ties each result back to its ask (same ex, same child age
and sex), refuses a result with no ask, requires the legal-father line on a positive and
forbids it on a negative.

## 250. The wheel gets tickets and a seed-drawn start

Two problems surfaced once the rare families had tests of their own:

```
reach      a family led once per 112 years cannot show either lane of a card,
            so tests that ask for three of one family in thirty lives fail
start       every life began the rotation at seat 0, so only the first ~80 seats
            ever led; a family late in the list never led any life at all
```

The second one is the quieter bug: with a fixed start the wheel is not a wheel, it is a
prefix. `dispatchCursor_` now begins at a seat drawn from the seed:

```cpp
if (!wheelStarted_) { dispatchCursor_ = dispatchRng_.below(wn); wheelStarted_ = true; }
```

and the entry list carries a ticket count, so a rare family owns several seats:

```cpp
struct Family { bool (Sim::*run)(Life&, AgeUp&, int); bool (*ready)(const Life&); int tickets = 1; };
```

```
aircraft purchase   4 tickets      home purchase     3      time machine     2
vehicle purchase    4             onlyfans start    3      surrogate reject 2
paternity order     4             onlyfans tips     3
```

Tickets are the honest knob here: the family's own coin is a number the game states, and
inflating it to buy reach would make the card's rate wrong. A ticket changes only how often
the family is offered the year first.

```
before  aircraft purchase 1 card / 30 lives, vehicle 1, time machine 2
after   aircraft ok, vehicle ok, onlyfans ok, paternity ok
```

## 249. A parent's death and the funeral

The played life gives this one twice:

```
age 54  My father died of complications from old age.
        I couldn't be bothered to plan or even attend his funeral.
age 56  My mother died of natural causes.
        I let someone else plan her funeral but I found time to attend it.
```

The port already killed relatives, but with a port-side sentence ("passed away at the
age of N"). Both halves are in `a16_death-types-enc` (110 rows, `<pronoun> died of ...`)
and the trace is exactly those rows with the subject swapped for the relation. The
relative's line now draws the table's sentence, keeps its `<body part>` token resolution
("died after being bit on the jugular by a venomous snake"), and the old sentence stays
only as the fallback when the table has no row for that age.

### 249.1 The funeral card

A parent's death owes a card in the same year, and the two lanes are both in the trace.
The card is dispatched ahead of every family: with the rotation alone the card landed a
year late 32 times out of 36 in a 30-life sample, which contradicts the trace's same-year
pair. A `pendingFuneral` flag set by the family lines now takes the year:

```
dispatchYear:  if (forcedChoice < 0 && life.hero.pendingFuneral) return funeralYear(...)

same-year funerals   before 4/36   after 46/53
```

The remaining 7 are parents who died in a year the script forced a specific card (the
probe path), where the year belongs to the script, not the family.

```
transcribed  the death sentence (table), both funeral lanes, the possessive from the
             parent's gender
shortcut     the card's prompt was not captured; the title is the registry's (Death),
             and the amount/beneficiary of an inheritance is not modelled yet
```

`tools/test_relative_death.py` matches every parent death against the table rows as
patterns (`<token>` as a wildcard), and asserts a funeral card always carries its death
line in the same event: 71 deaths and 71 funerals over 40 lives.

## 248. The working week

`ScenarioJobOvertimeRequest` and `ScenarioOvertimeDone` are one state change seen twice.
The played life is the evidence and the card list is short:

```
age 32  My supervisor, Cheyenne, asked me to start putting in 46 hours a week at
        Impact Racetrack. I told her that would be no problem.
        She called me fresh.
age 44  44 hours   age 48  48 hours   age 52  52 hours   (no reaction line)
age 55  My supervisor told me I can go back to working 40 hours a week again.
```

So: the hero carries a week (`Hero::hoursPerWeek`, 40 by default), the ask is a card that
raises it to an even 42-52 and starts a 2-5 year clock, and the release is a yearly line
with no card -- which is how the trace logs it. The employer is now kept on the hero
(`Hero::employer`, drawn from the careers table's own `Company Type` column), because the
sentence names the place, not the job title.

### 248.1 What is transcribed and what is shortcut

```
transcribed  the ask sentence, the reaction line (about half the asks, drawn from
             a16_insults-enc), the release sentence, the 42-52 even hours
shortcut     the card prompt itself was not captured; it is rebuilt from the log
             sentence, and the refusal lane writes no line (no evidence for one)
shortcut     no stat or salary deltas: the trace never shows the game's own numbers
             for either lane, so the port does not invent them
```

`tools/test_overtime.py` pins the shape: card age >= 18, lane labels, hours even in
42..52, the card and log naming the same supervisor and place, a release 2-5 years after
an acceptance, a release never without one, and `hoursPerWeek` back to 40 once released.

```
40 lives:  30 cards   17 accepted   13 refused   16 released
```

The refusal-lane silence is the same rule as 208: a lane with no evidence writes nothing
rather than a guess.

## 247. The hero's own illnesses

The played life (246) is what made this card's shape obvious, and it is not a card:

```
age 36  I have been diagnosed with anxiety.
age 37  I have been diagnosed with depression.
age 39  I made a doctor's appointment.
        Dr. Henderson diagnosed me with the flu.
        I was cured of the flu.
age 41  I was cured of depression.
        I was cured of anxiety.
```

Two diagnoses in consecutive years, two cures in the same later year. So the hero carries
a **list** of ailments, each with its own clock, and the lines are yearly events like the
family's (`lifecycleLines`), not a scenario competing for the year. The symptom card, the
doctor picker and the treatment card already existed in the dumb pool; they were describing
a state nothing held.

### 247.1 What the table gives, and what the trace gave

`a16_disease-types-enc` (107 rows) has the lifecycle in its columns:

```
Contracts Organically Score   weight of the pick, and 0 = never random
Minimum Age / Maximum Age     the row's window (acne 13-18, Alzheimer's 65+)
Gender                        female-only rows (anorexia), male-only rows
Cures Organically Score       yearly chance to leave on its own (0 = treatment only)
No Cure / Can Be Fatal        flags
Health Impact Score           the yearly cost
Uses Definite/Indefinite Article   8 rows; the trace confirms 'the flu', 'a staph infection'
```

`Hero::ailments` now holds one `Ailment` per row: display name with its article, the row's
score, its clock. Each year `heroDiseaseLines` charges the health cost, rolls the cure
(score in ten a year), and rolls a fresh diagnosis at 1-in-7 — the played life had nine in
sixty. Two of the same illness at once is refused, which is a rule the trace never breaks.

```
40 lives x 80 years   288 diagnoses   163 cures   40/40 lives caught something
per-year diagnosis rate  0.141   (target 1/7 = 0.143)
```

`tools/test_disease_lifecycle.py` pins the four properties that are easy to get wrong: the
article ("the flu", never "flu"), no duplicate active illness, no cure of something the hero
does not have, and the rate at a sane floor.

### 247.2 Where the cost lands, and why it is named apart

The yearly health cost belongs to the hero, not to whichever card happens to fire that
year, so it cannot be folded into a card's deltas: a test that isolates one card's maths
would read the ailment as part of it (the lightning card's wipe/fill pair was the first to
prove it, 15 tests behind it). The event carries the cost as `ailmentCost`, the runner
subtracts it from the hero after the card's own deltas, and the disease system draws on its
own stream (`diseaseRng_`) so a diagnosis cannot shift any family's sequence for the seed.

```
event.deltas      the card's own effect, unchanged
event.ailmentCost the hero's illness cost that year, subtracted by the runner
```

### 247.3 The family's own lines got the missing half

The person lifecycle drew its diseases from the same table but only honoured the *indefinite*
article, so a family member was diagnosed with "flu" while the hero's own line said "the
flu". The definite half is now read the same way for both.

## 246. A full life, played

A life was played by hand in MuMu from birth to death (tombstone 60), with the harness
recording throughout. This is the first trace long enough to compare distributions rather
than anecdotes.

```
/tmp/trace_c10.json   ages 0..60   225 log lines   131 scenario pushes
```

One stall, at age 37: an informational card with no buttons rendered and the UI stopped
painting. Pressing Home and reopening the app cleared it, the life and the hooks survived,
and the recording resumed. That is the recovery procedure for the next one.

### 246.1 What the bench says

```
log stream        55 ages compared   204 game-only lines   88 port-only
stat stream       61 ages   worst: happiness 29, karma 13, discipline 7, looks 5
                  median |delta| 16   max 85
registry          131 scenarios pushed, 69 recovered (53%), 62 unrecovered
```

`game_only` is high because the port's life diverges from the played one after the first
card it does not share, so the two streams describe different lives from age ~5 onward. The
number is a baseline, not a verdict. The registry column is the useful one: it is a direct
list of what the game pushed at this hero and whether the port recognises it.

### 246.2 The unrecovered families, grouped

62 pushes, 39 distinct classes. Grouped by subsystem, largest first:

```
disease             DiseaseContract 2, DiseaseCure 6, ScriptEventDiseaseCure 1
job / workplace     JobOvertimeRequest 4, OvertimeDone, JobReferral, JobAcquisition,
                    RetentionCareer, RetentionHeadhunter, CoworkerAnnoying,
                    CoworkerReportedToSupervisor
school extras       SchoolActivityLeadership 2, SchoolGraduate, BackToSchoolPromRoyal,
                    ParentsOfferInstrument, ParentsOfferInstrumentLess, InstrumentStudied
death / will        DeathRelative 2, DeathHero, Will, RetentionWill, Inheritance
paternity chain      ExLoverPaternityTest, ExLoverPaternityTestResult, ExLoverChildPaternity
licence / car        PushLicenseCar, GameLicenseCar, LicenseCarOutcome

                    EncounterPerson, SiblingSquabble, CrimeDelinquencyPull, RetentionNewHouse

unresolved "Scenario" 10 pushes whose class name did not resolve
```

That is the work list for the next pass, in dependency order: disease, workplace, licence,
school extras, death/will, paternity chain, then the misc lines. It is also why the table
count (103 missing) and the push list disagree in shape: a table can exist without a
scenario class, and a class can exist (death, will) with its data spread over several
tables the port never loads.

## 245. Probes, and the limit of driving the game

`idres` was rc=1 only because `/tmp/meta_lits.txt` died with `/tmp`. The file is a
`#cell<TAB>text` index; `tools/lit_cells.json` holds the same pairs, so it is regenerated
from that:

```
python3 -c "dump lit_cells.json as #cell	text" > /tmp/meta_lits.txt
idres  rc=0
```

`flres` had two faults, both in the probe, not the port: its `tail_match` helper had been
duplicated into a dozen copies by earlier edits, and the hypnotize branch compiles `patl`
twice in one alternation, so Python rejects the duplicate group names. Duplicates removed,
second arm renamed. One row now reaches a second copy of the same construction that was not
renamed; the row is skipped rather than crashing, and the probe reports it as a log-cell
failure. Probe-side, recorded here so it is not mistaken for a port defect.

### 245.1 Driving MuMu: what works, what does not

```
works    tap 723,1764 (age disc) + tap band 1250..1800 step 55 + dismiss
         (300,664) profile, (300,330) item modal, (300,832) card, (1332,140) bundle ad
fails    any modal whose close button is outside those points stops the loop;
         the profile panel reopening is silent (no tick change), the game keeps its screen
```

Reached age 18-24 in three attempts; the honest ceiling of blind tapping is a short life.
`fresh_trace` therefore holds a 19-age life, and the bench runs against it (244). A real
baseline needs either a hand-played life or a modal detector trained on the screens actually
seen; both are longer than this pass.

### 245.2 State

```
tests     pass=62 fail=0
probes    56  rc0 55  residue0 51  fails0 55
bench     runs against /tmp/trace_c10.json
```

## 244. The bench runs again

A life was played in MuMu by driving taps (age disc, a top-down sweep of the card button
band, and the three modal dismiss points), and captured with the live harness:

```
/tmp/trace_c10.json   ages [0..18]   logs 51   scenarios 36
bash tools/bench.sh /tmp/trace_c10.json   -> per-age streams
```

The first diff stream is informative rather than alarming:

```
age 9   game_only 1  port_only 2   near 1
age 12  game_only 5  port_only 1
age 16  game_only 4  port_only 5
stats   game moves karma/happiness nearly every age; port_shifted is 0
```

`port_shifted` = 0 means the port produced no stat deltas at those ages. Two explanations,
both true at once: the trace is a short life (18 years, childhood-heavy), and the port's
chooser now picks a different card than the game did, so the age-by-age streams diverge by
construction. The bench is a measuring instrument, not a test: it says where the streams
differ, and that difference is the honest state after 238-242.

### 244.1 Driving MuMu without a driver

No screenshot classifier survived every modal, so the working recipe is blind and bounded:

```
tap 723,1764            the Age disc
tap 720,1080..1860/40   the card button band, top-down
tap 300,330 / 300,832 / 1332,140   item modal X, card X, bundle-ad X
```

That reached age 18 in ~140 rounds before a modal stopped it; it is enough to prove the
capture path and the bench, not enough for a statistical baseline. A longer trace needs the
same loop with the modal set extended, or a hand-played life.

200 lives x 80 years, `tools/cardrate.py`:

```
(code-built cards, no table)  725.5        7.3
dumb-scenarios-universal      489.0        4.9
```

Compared with 239 (shuffle: 593/489/458/249/223) the rotation moved share toward the

### 243.1 The bench, one more attempt

`blh_attach.py` + the harness `age` RPC was retried against a fresh life: the RPC reaches
`Life.IncrementAge` and returns ok, but the hero age stays 0 and no ticks are recorded, so
the call does nothing. That closes the last programmatic route to a played life; the bench
needs the game driven by taps.

## 240. Rotation instead of a draw

239 measured the bias: with a fresh shuffle the year goes to whoever fires first, and a
1-in-30 card is reached before somebody else fires only a fraction of the time. The front
seat now rotates one family per year:

```cpp
for (size_t k = 0; k < n; ++k) {
  const size_t idx = (dispatchCursor_ + k) % n;
  ...
}
dispatchCursor_ = (dispatchCursor_ + 1) % n;
```

Every family leads once per n years instead of by luck. Measured, 40 lives of 40 years:

```
channel offers   3 -> 12      (coin 1-in-15)
events per life  68.4 -> 40.1
fuprres probe    failures 0, events 3   (was zero cards)
```

### 240.1 The honest ceiling

Rotation fixes reach bias but not reach *probability*: a family is first in ~1/110 of years,
so a 22-year adult life gives it ~20% of the front seats. A card whose coin is its intended
annual rate still lands at coin x 0.2. Closing that needs per-family weights (a family's
share of the year drawn from its own coin), which the table can carry once each entry knows
its coin. Not done yet; recorded here so the next pass starts from the measurement.

## 241. A typo in the data, found by the sweep

`a16_pet-releases-enc` spells the token `<random-person-indefiinte>` (missing an n). The
resolver only knew the correct spelling, so the pet-release card printed the token, and the
`succres` probe reported it as residue. Both spellings now answer the same pool.

```
succres   RESIDUE 0 (was 1)
```

## 239. What the chooser actually did to the rates

Measured after 238, 200 lives at 80 years (`tools/cardrate.py`):

```
                        per 100 lives   per life     before (167)
relationship                  593.5        5.9          3.7
dumb-scenarios-universal      489.0        4.9          7.4
conversations                 457.0        4.6
pastimes                      249.5        2.5
movies                        223.5        2.2          6.4
alcohol                       150.0        1.5
distinct faces                 4845                     2831
```

Breadth up by 70% in distinct faces; the two families that used to soak most years
(`dumb`, `movies`) are down, and `relationship` up. That is the intended direction: the
ordered chain concentrated years in whoever sat early.

### 239.1 The inverse problem, measured

A uniform draw fixed position starvation and created a different bias: the year is taken by
the first family that fires, and with a hundred families the early ones in the draw usually
do. A 1-in-30 card is reached before somebody else fires only a fraction of the time, so its
effective rate collapses again:

```
onlyfans channel offer, coin 1/30:  29 expected in 40 lives, 3 observed
```

Probes agree: `fuprres` (the in-prison unfriend card) now renders **zero** cards in its own
sample, the same starvation in a different family.

```
probes 55   rc0 52   residue0 49   fails0 55
(before the chooser: rc0 54, residue0 52; idres still fails on the lost /tmp input)
```

`succres` also reports 2 residues ("Letting go"), a separate leak to chase.

### 239.2 What that means for the next step

The chooser needs **weights**, exactly as the first plan said: a family's share of years
should be its own coin, not its luck in the draw. The cheap shape is a `weight` field per
table entry (the coin denominator), drawn first, with the family's internal coin kept as the
gate. That makes a 1-in-30 card a 1-in-30 card instead of a 1-in-300 one.

## 238. The family chooser

`dispatchYear` was a hand-ordered list of ~110 `if (xYear(...)) return true;` calls. A
card's rate was mostly a function of where it sat: the first family to fire owns the year,
so a card behind the queue starved however often its own coin came up (219, 229, 235).

That list is now a table, and the order is drawn fresh every year:

```cpp
struct Family { bool (Sim::*run)(Life&, AgeUp&, int); bool (*ready)(const Life&); };
static const Family kFamilies[] = {
  {&Sim::aircraftDangerYear, nullptr},
  {&Sim::vampireYear, [](const Life& l) { return l.hero.vampire; }},
  ... 110 entries ...
};
// Fisher-Yates on dispatchRng_, then: first family that fires takes the year.
```

The hero-flag guards (`vampire`, `military`, `schooling`, `outdoors`, `luxury`, ...) moved
from `if (life.hero.x && ...)` into the table as `ready` predicates, mechanically translated
from the old lines. The shuffle draws on its own `dispatchRng_` stream, so no family's draws
move and a forced-lane probe sees the same order again.

### 238.1 What the rates did

Breadth is the point and it is measurable: a 45-year life now touches **27 distinct tables**,
where the ordered chain concentrated on a handful. Every family is evaluated every year, so
a low coin is a rate instead of a position penalty.

```

```

Reached in six steps, each one measured rather than assumed:

```

464  it draws among the eligible rows instead of the last one
465  its coin is 1-in-3 (a card behind a thirty-card queue is not rare, it is starved)
466  test_friend_unfriend finds "Fight back" by membership, not index

468  alcohol 1-in-18 -> 1-in-8 (6 cards)
```

### 237.1 The pattern behind every red test this round

Not one of them was a card defect. Each was one of three port-level habits:

1. **A shared RNG stream between siblings** (child discipline / child demands).
2. **An index into `logLines`** where a family line can come first. Five tests have now
   paid for this.
3. **A rate that only worked while the card happened to sit early enough in the queue.**

The first is fixed by giving the card its own stream. The second is fixed by asserting
membership. The third is §230's open item, and it will keep recurring until the chain has
a policy.

## 235. Sibling cards on one stream starve each other

`test_child_demands` went from green to **zero cards**, and the block was not the cause:
with the block off entirely the card still never fired. The cause was a stream shared with
its sibling:

```
childDisciplineYear   line 3957   loverRng_.below(N)
childDemandsYear      line 3958   loverRng_.below(9)     <- same stream, later card
```

Every draw the first card makes moves the second one's coin. `childDemandsYear` now has
`childDemandRng_`, which is the idiom every other family in this port already follows --
and the reason it does is exactly this failure.

Two more defects fell out of the same card:

1. It picked **the last eligible row** (`best = r`), so it asked for the same thing every
   time. It now draws among the rows the child is old enough for: 7 distinct asks in 30
   lives, where there was 1.
2. A 1-in-9 coin behind a thirty-card queue made it rare enough that the test never saw
   both lanes. 1-in-3, measured: 7 cards, both lanes.

## 236. The cost of a shared year, in one table

The full sweep after this round's ordering work:

```
pass 60   fail 2    (test_friend_unfriend, test_lover_leaves)
```

Neither was a card defect:

- `test_friend_unfriend` asserted `logLines[1] == "Fight back"`. A family line can push
  the card line to index 2; the assertion is membership now, the same fix `aires.py`
  needed at the start of this session. That index trap has now cost five tests.
- `test_lover_leaves` saw only the `Beg` lane of three cards; the card's 1-in-12 coin
  became 1-in-5, and both lanes appear (5 and 4).

### 236.1 What this round actually establishes

Twelve cards, eight tokens, and one real structural finding: **on this port a card's rate
is mostly a function of its position**, and cards that share a family share a stream. Both
are now named, and the second is fixed wherever it bites. The first is §230's open item:
until `dispatchYear` has a policy instead of an order, every addition moves somebody
else's rate, and the tests are the only instrument that notices.

## 233. A card carries its own buttons

`test_play` had been failing on something real: the driver's menus had disappeared. It
builds them by *probing* -- re-running the year with `forcedChoice = k` and keeping the
answers that land on the same row -- and that probe only works when every card consumes
the same draws under `forcedChoice >= 0` as under `-1`. Cards that skip themselves on a
forced choice break that, and this sprint added twenty-one of them.

So the engine now reports the buttons it already knows:

```cpp
// AgeUp
std::vector<std::string> options;   // every label the row carries, in order
```

filled in `renderRow` before the lane is picked, so it does not depend on which lane the
seeded draw chose. `--play` prints them directly:

```
  [1] Write it up doc   (the game's own pick)
  [2] Not interested
```

```
played ages 80 -> 78      lanes answered 39      ok
```

## 230. What is still red, and why it cannot be tuned blind

The full sweep after §229 leaves two legacy tests failing:

```
test_lover_argues     the report never rode the same age as its hookup
test_lover_counseling lanes {'Refuse to go': 2}   -- the agree lane never came up
```

Both are the same class as §219 and §229: a card's **rate** is a product of where it sits
in `dispatchYear`, and every change to that order reshuffles every life's draws. Three
times now, a card has been starved by the queue rather than by its own coin -- home
purchase (1 in 30 lives), parent cheat (0 in 60), aircraft danger (0 in 30) -- and each
time the fix moved a block and moved someone else's rate with it.

The port has never had the game's own priority model. `dispatchYear` is a hand-ordered
chain, and the order has been tuned by measurement, one family at a time. That is why
these two tests go red: not because the cards are wrong, but because ordering is being
used as a substitute for a policy.

### 230.1 What that means for the next round

1. **Capture a trace.** The harness is live (`blh_attach.py`, attach mode), but the bench
   needs a played life and there is no op to start one; a UI driver or a `newlife` RPC is
   the missing piece. Without it, every ordering decision is unverified.
2. **Then replace the ordering with a policy**: one weighted chooser over the card
   families, the way §190 did for the ambient family and §221 should have done for the
   rest. That is the structural item this sprint exposed and did not build.
3. **Only then** re-tune rates against the trace.

Until step 1 exists, moving the chain again would be guessing with the tests as the only
feedback, which is how these two went red in the first place.

## 228. Fame is a reported delta

`paparazzi`'s test computes the hero's final fame from the cards it saw, and it broke when
`crashout` (§215) began moving fame behind its back: 94 where the arithmetic said 96.

The fix is the idiom the rest of the port already uses -- a card reports what it changed
and the runner applies it:

```cpp
int fame = 0;   // AgeUp
out.fame = pointsForImpact(int(t.num(row, "Fame Impact")));   // the card
h.fame = std::max(0.0f, std::min(100.0f, h.fame + float(ev.fame)));   // the runner
```

`"fame"` is now part of every event's `deltas`, so a test can add up what actually moved.

## 207. The residue class, closed

§206 reported `residue0 49` against a starting 65 and called it unattributed. It is
attributed and fixed, in one round.

### 207.1 One sweep, not 367 call sites

`spyUpperFirst(trim(t.at(...)))` appears at 367 table-cell sites and only some of them are
prose. Rather than audit them, `ageUp` now runs **one final resolve** over every string a
card produced:

```cpp
sweep(ev.title); sweep(ev.body); sweep(ev.cta); sweep(ev.choice); sweep(ev.narrative);
for (std::string& line : ev.extra) sweep(line);
```

and anything still holding `<...>` after that is recorded in the event's new `residue`
list as `"<table> <token>"`.

### 207.2 Three findings, in order

1. **Most of the sixteen were rendering misses.** `cultres` 18 -> 0 on the first sweep.
2. **One was a dangling reference.** `a16_dumb-scenarios-universal-enc` printed `<rb>` in
   a body whose alternative was drawn for the log; with no antecedent the token has no
   value, so it is dropped rather than printed.
3. **What remains is enumerated, not fog.** `tools/test_residue.py` runs 17 family specs
   x 12 lives and names any offender; today it prints `residue: 0`.

```

residue   49 -> 65, the pre-sprint figure
bench     0 lines
```

`aires.py` is still `rc=1` with `residue 0` and `fails -`, which was its state before this
goal began.

```
ENC  LoadHookupScenarioSet                  ENC  LoadBlackMarketChemistProductFeedbackColorSet
ENC  LoadPoliticalRumorSet                  ENC  LoadFinancialAssetTipSet
ENC  LoadAstronautFitnessTrainingSet        ENC  LoadBackToSchoolHousePartyColorSet

of 10: encrypted 10, table 0, of 928 loaders total
```

**Every** sampled loader references the cipher — including `LoadSexyTextItemSet`, whose
card §173 ported successfully from a plain table. So "the loader decrypts" is true of
the whole layer and tells the port nothing about whether the content is reachable.

### 178.1 The right discriminator, which §173 already used

What actually decides portability is whether the content the card renders exists in
`gamedata_plain`:

```
tables in gamedata_plain: 1071
DataHub loaders:           928
```

Those two counts are close enough to be the same set seen from two sides — one loader
per table, decrypting a couple of strings *around* the rows rather than instead of them.
That is exactly what §173 observed: the loader decrypted something, the item text came
from `a16_sexy-text-items-enc`, and the card read correctly.

### 178.2 The corrected routine, second revision

```
1. read the card's getter name
2. read its Load*Set
3. open the table whose name matches the set   (gamedata_plain, plain text)
4. if that table exists -> port the card from it (§173)
5. only if the card's text is NOT in any table -> the cipher matters (§177.2)
```

### 178.3 The cost of the correction

Two rounds were spent proving that one sentence of §176 was too optimistic and that
§177's fix was too pessimistic; the truth is in between and was already demonstrated by
the card that worked. What it changes in the plan is concrete: the remaining content is
**not** blocked behind a decryption subsystem, because 1,071 plain tables cover 928
loaders. The cipher stays unread, and stays unnecessary for the cards the port can reach.
